title: Science, Class 9
subject: Science
description: NCERT Grade 9 Science, chapter by chapter.

chapters.title: Exploration: Entering the World of Secondary Science
chapters.summary: In this chapter: curiosity and careful exploration; using simplified models; shared language and mathematics; laws, theories, and predictions.

lessons.title: Curiosity and careful exploration

activities.prompt: How can curiosity and careful exploration help us understand our world?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Wonder leads to careful science
activities.body: Science invites you to be curious, observe closely, and ask questions. Science often begins with wonder and grows through careful experiments. Careful exploration has a purpose, and magnifying glasses help you notice patterns. Models are ways scientists use to show difficult systems. Scientific ideas are tested, revised, and sometimes discarded. Good science recognises where ideas work and where they stop working.
keyPoints: Curiosity, observation, and questions begin scientific exploration.
Models help scientists show difficult systems.
Good science recognises where ideas work and where they stop working.
activities.explanation: Wonder starts careful exploration, and good science keeps checking its ideas.

activities.prompt: Why do buses sometimes arrive in a repeating pattern?
steps: The child watches buses closely because science invites careful observation.
The child uses symbols for arrival times because symbols can show patterns.
The child tests other days because good science recognises limits.
The conclusion states the pattern and where it does not apply.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: A curious start
activities.prompt: What does science invite you to do first?
options: Observe closely and ask questions
Guess quickly and avoid checks
Wander without a clear purpose
Stop when wonder appears
activities.explanation: Exactly. Close observation and questions help us understand how things work.

activities.title: The start of science
activities.prompt: Science often begins with wonder and careful experiments.
activities.explanation: Correct! Science often begins with wonder and develops through careful experiments.

activities.title: Showing a difficult system
activities.prompt: Scientists use ______ to represent a difficult system.
activities.hint: It is a way of showing something complex.
activities.explanation: Exactly. Models help scientists represent complex systems.

activities.title: The magnifying glass symbol
activities.prompt: A magnifying glass is used as a science symbol. What does it represent?
options: Careful observation of patterns
Purpose without any experiments
A discarded scientific idea
Limits on where ideas apply
activities.explanation: Yes. A magnifying glass represents careful observation and attention to patterns.

activities.title: Connections in science
activities.prompt: Match each item with what it helps represent or do.
activities.explanation: Magnifying glasses support observation, while models and symbols show systems and patterns. Scientists also connect living and non-living ideas.

activities.title: Ideas can change
activities.prompt: Scientific ideas stay unchanged after scientists test them.
activities.explanation: Good checking. Scientists test ideas and may revise or discard them.

activities.title: Knowing the limits
activities.prompt: What should careful, deep exploration recognise about an idea?
options: It must work everywhere
Exploration must stop quickly
It needs no more checks
Its limits on use
activities.explanation: Well spotted. Good science recognises the limits of where ideas apply. An idea may not work in every situation.

activities.title: The life of a scientific idea
activities.prompt: Put these actions in the order described for scientific ideas.
activities.explanation: Good ordering. Scientific ideas are tested, revised, and sometimes discarded.

activities.prompt: A child wants to know whether a paper changes when water is added. Which test is fairest?
options: Use two similar papers, but give water to only one.
Use two different papers, and give water to both.
Use one paper, but change it and the water together.
Use one paper, give it water, and check it once.

why.Use two different papers, and give water: Different papers and different water use hide the cause.
why.Use one paper, but change it and the wat: Changing both means we cannot tell which change mattered.
why.Use one paper, give it water, and check: One sample and one check cannot give a fair comparison.

activities.explanation: Only water changes, so its effect can be compared fairly.

activities.prompt: A child's bus-time pattern works on weekdays. What should the child conclude?
options: The pattern must apply to every bus on every day.
The pattern should be kept without any further checks.
The pattern becomes true only when nobody tests it.
The pattern may not apply on every day or journey.

why.The pattern must apply to every bus on e: It treats one limited pattern as a rule for every case.
why.The pattern should be kept without any f: It thinks finding one pattern ends the need for careful checking.
why.The pattern becomes true only when nobod: It wrongly believes checking does not affect scientific ideas.

activities.explanation: Good science recognises where an idea does not apply.

lessons.title: Using simplified models

activities.prompt: How can a simple model help us understand something so complicated?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Why science uses models
activities.body: The natural world is very complex, so studying every detail can be impossible. Science uses models to make this complexity easier to understand. A model is a simplified representation that keeps only the features needed for a question. Building one involves making assumptions and deliberately ignoring some details. These choices keep the model simple enough to be useful.
keyPoints: Models help us study complexity.
Models keep only useful features.
Some details are deliberately ignored.
activities.explanation: A useful model shows what matters without showing every detail.

activities.prompt: Why does a useful model of falling leave out air resistance?
steps: The question only needs gravity’s basic effect on falling.
Leave out air resistance because that detail is not needed yet.
Keep the model simple because ignored details are deliberate choices.
Therefore, it shows gravity’s basic effect without showing every detail.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Saha’s model of a star
activities.body: Meghnad Saha modelled the matter in a star as a hot gas. His simplified model helped explain the connection between star colour and temperature. It kept only features needed to explain that connection. When greater accuracy is needed, more complex models can include extra details.
keyPoints: Saha modelled star matter as a hot gas.
The model explained star colour and temperature.
Complex models can add details for greater accuracy.
activities.explanation: Saha’s model shows how a simpler model can explain an important connection.

activities.prompt: Why does science use models?
options: Simplify complex things
Show every natural detail
Remove useful features
Create more questions
activities.explanation: Models make complexity easier to understand by keeping useful features.

activities.prompt: In physics, a moving car may be shown as one point.
activities.explanation: A single point can represent a moving car when its movement is being studied.

activities.prompt: A falling model may ignore air resistance to show ______’s basic effect.
activities.hint: This word names the effect shown by the model.
activities.explanation: Ignoring air resistance shows gravity’s basic effect in a simpler model.

activities.prompt: What does a simplified heart model help show?
options: How the organ works
Every cell inside it
The colour of a star
The motion of a car
activities.explanation: The model ignores individual cells to show how the heart works.

activities.prompt: Match each model with the simplification it uses.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows one important detail that the model leaves out.

activities.prompt: A model is useful, but you need greater accuracy. What should you do?
options: Add extra details
Ignore useful features
Keep exactly the same details
Use no assumptions
activities.explanation: More complex models can include extra details when greater accuracy is needed.

activities.prompt: A child wants to show a moving car’s place on a road. Which representation is best?
options: One point, because the question only needs the car’s location.
Every wheel and window, because every detail always matters.
One point, because models must hide how moving objects work.
The whole car, because a model cannot show an object’s position.

why.Every wheel and window, because every de: This mistake assumes that every detail matters in every model.
why.One point, because models must hide how: This mistake assumes that models cannot show an object’s position.
why.The whole car, because a model cannot sh: This mistake assumes that position cannot be shown by a model.

activities.explanation: It is right because the model keeps only the feature needed here.

activities.prompt: A heart model leaves out individual cells. What should the model help show?
options: How the organ works, because those cell details are not needed.
How every cell works, because models must include all parts.
That the heart has no cells, because ignored details are absent.
How one cell beats, because organ models focus only on cells.

why.How every cell works, because models mus: This mistake assumes that a heart model must include every cell.
why.That the heart has no cells, because ign: This mistake assumes that ignored details are absent from the real heart.
why.How one cell beats, because organ models: This mistake assumes that an organ model must focus on one cell.

activities.explanation: It is right because the model keeps only features needed for the organ.

activities.prompt: A falling model needs a more exact result for a real fall. What change is best?
options: Include air resistance, because extra details can improve accuracy.
Remove gravity, because more accuracy needs fewer basic effects.
Add every detail, because all models must show everything.
Keep the model unchanged, because simple models are always exact.

why.Remove gravity, because more accuracy ne: This mistake assumes that accuracy requires removing the basic effect.
why.Add every detail, because all models mus: This mistake assumes that every model must include every detail.
why.Keep the model unchanged, because simple: This mistake assumes that a simple model is always exact.

activities.explanation: It is right because extra details help when greater accuracy is needed.

activities.prompt: A student says Saha’s hot-gas model shows everything. What reply is best?
options: His model is simplified and leaves out details not needed.
His model proves stars contain nothing except hot gas.
His model must include every particle to explain star colour.
His model is wrong because star colour depends only on pressure.

why.His model proves stars contain nothing e: This mistake treats a simplified model as a complete description.
why.His model must include every particle to: This mistake assumes that explaining colour needs every particle’s movement.
why.His model is wrong because star colour d: This mistake assumes that pressure alone explains star colour.

activities.explanation: It is right because his model leaves out details not needed.

lessons.title: Shared language and mathematics

activities.prompt: How can words and numbers help us understand the world around us?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Science has a shared language
activities.body: Science uses language carefully and precisely. Words like force, work, cell, and reaction have special scientific meanings. Scientists worldwide share terms, symbols, and units. Each symbol links to a defined unit. Mathematics expresses relationships between quantities so they can be tested carefully. Before using maths, you should understand the situation and find the relevant quantities. An equation gives a compact statement about how things relate.
keyPoints: Scientific words have special meanings.
Scientists worldwide share terms, symbols, and units.
Mathematics helps scientists test relationships.
activities.explanation: Shared language helps scientists worldwide understand science clearly.

activities.prompt: A child wants to predict where a moving ball will be later. How should science and mathematics be used?
steps: First, identify the distance, time, and velocity because they describe later movement.
Next, connect them with mathematics because it shows their relationship clearly.
Then check the equation carefully because the relationship must be tested carefully.
Finally, state where the ball will be later so the prediction is clear.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Using mathematics in science
activities.body: An equation gives a compact statement about how things are related. Distance, time, and velocity can describe where a moving object will be later. Mathematical expressions also describe reaction rates, population growth, and energy changes. Using mathematics in science does not mean only memorising equations. First, understand the situation. Then identify the relevant quantities before choosing and using mathematics.
keyPoints: Equations describe relationships compactly.
Mathematical expressions describe changes and relationships.
Understanding the situation comes before using mathematics.
activities.explanation: Good maths starts with understanding, not memorising.

activities.prompt: Which statement about scientific language is correct?
options: Scientists worldwide use unrelated terms and symbols.
Scientific symbols are linked to undefined units.
Scientists worldwide share terms, symbols, and units.
Words like force and work have only everyday meanings.
activities.explanation: Scientists worldwide use a shared language of terms, symbols, and units.

activities.prompt: Words such as force, work, cell, and reaction have special scientific meanings.
activities.explanation: Science uses language carefully and precisely.

activities.prompt: In science, words such as force and work have ______ scientific meanings.
activities.hint: These meanings are different from everyday meanings.
activities.explanation: Scientific words describe specific ideas carefully and precisely.

activities.prompt: What does mathematics help scientists do?
options: Express relationships between quantities clearly.
Replace the need to understand a situation.
Show that memorising equations is enough.
Change all scientific words into vague words.
activities.explanation: Mathematics expresses relationships so they can be tested carefully.

activities.prompt: Before using an equation, what should you do first?
options: Choose numbers before understanding the situation.
Ignore all quantities in the situation.
Memorise every equation before reading the situation.
Understand the situation and identify relevant quantities.
activities.explanation: You should understand the situation and identify the relevant quantities first.

activities.prompt: Put these steps for using mathematics in science in order.
activities.explanation: This order helps you test a clear mathematical relationship.

activities.prompt: A scientist uses a symbol in a report but leaves out its unit. What problem does this create?
options: The result is incomplete because every symbol needs its defined unit.
The result stays clear because a symbol alone shows its quantity.
The result is wrong because scientific symbols must be written with words.
The result is still clear because units only matter for everyday measurements.

why.The result stays clear because a symbol: This mistake assumes symbols are complete without their linked units.
why.The result is wrong because scientific s: This mistake assumes scientific symbols cannot be used with units.
why.The result is still clear because units: This mistake treats scientific units as unimportant in scientific work.

activities.explanation: A symbol needs its linked unit, so leaving it out removes meaning.

activities.prompt: A toy car is moving. You want to describe where it will be later. Which quantities are relevant?
options: Distance, time, and velocity, because these describe later movement.
Distance and time, because velocity is not part of the prediction.
Force and work, because they always describe where something moves later.
Reaction and units, because they show the car's later position.

why.Distance and time, because velocity is n: This mistake leaves out velocity, which is needed to describe later movement.
why.Force and work, because they always desc: This mistake assumes force and work describe an object's later location.
why.Reaction and units, because they show th: This mistake assumes reaction and units can describe the car's later position.

activities.explanation: Distance, time, and velocity are the quantities that describe later movement.

activities.prompt: A student studies energy changes during a reaction. What best shows how the change relates to other quantities?
options: A mathematical expression, because it states the relationship clearly.
A long paragraph, because careful science avoids mathematical expressions.
A symbol only, because symbols already explain every relationship.
A list of units, because units show how quantities relate.

why.A long paragraph, because careful scienc: This mistake assumes careful science must avoid mathematics.
why.A symbol only, because symbols already e: This mistake assumes one symbol can explain a relationship by itself.
why.A list of units, because units show how: This mistake assumes units show relationships between quantities.

activities.explanation: Mathematical expressions describe relationships and can be tested carefully.

activities.prompt: A student writes several measurements in a row. They call the list an equation. What is the flaw?
options: The list does not state how the measured quantities are related.
The list is invalid because equations must use scientific symbols.
The list is invalid because equations cannot contain measured values.
The list is wrong because every equation must describe a moving object.

why.The list is invalid because equations mu: This mistake focuses on symbols instead of the relationship stated.
why.The list is invalid because equations ca: This mistake assumes measured values cannot appear in an equation.
why.The list is wrong because every equation: This mistake assumes equations only describe moving objects.

activities.explanation: An equation gives a compact statement about how quantities are related.

activities.prompt: A student memorises an equation without understanding the situation. What problem is most likely?
options: The equation may be used with wrong quantities in a new situation.
The equation will always work because memorising makes it complete.
The equation is useless because mathematics is optional in science.
The equation is easy because understanding is not needed for careful testing.

why.The equation will always work because me: This mistake assumes memorising alone makes an equation fit every situation.
why.The equation is useless because mathemat: This mistake assumes mathematics has no role in science.
why.The equation is easy because understandi: This mistake assumes careful testing does not need understanding.

activities.explanation: Mathematics needs the situation and relevant quantities before an equation is used.

lessons.title: Laws, theories, and predictions

activities.prompt: What helps scientists turn surprising observations into ideas they can trust?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How scientists build understanding
activities.body: Scientific understanding grows when people repeat observations, refine measurements, and carry out experiments. A law describes a regular pattern seen in nature. Theories rest on evidence gathered over time. Atomic theory explains how molecules form. A prediction is a reasoned expectation based on evidence and careful thought. When predictions fail, scientists check their assumptions, models, or measurements again.
keyPoints: A law describes a regular pattern in nature.
A theory rests on evidence gathered over time.
A prediction is a reasoned expectation.
activities.explanation: Evidence helps scientists build and improve scientific ideas.

activities.prompt: A playground swing reaches about the same height on each push. What should be checked if one push differs?
steps: Repeated observations help organise the evidence into a regular pattern.
It can be called a law because nature shows the pattern repeatedly.
The next-push prediction is reasonable because evidence and careful thought support it.
So, if it fails, check assumptions, models, or measurements again.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: A law describes a regular pattern observed in nature.
activities.explanation: Correct. Laws describe regular patterns that scientists observe in nature.

activities.prompt: Match each science idea to its description.
pairs: Describes a regular pattern in nature
Based on evidence gathered over time
A reasoned expectation based on evidence
activities.explanation: Well done. Each description matches the main idea of its science term.

activities.prompt: A scientific prediction is a reasoned expectation based on ______ and careful thought.
activities.hint: Scientists use this to support their expectations.
activities.explanation: Exactly. Evidence and careful thought support a scientific prediction.

activities.prompt: Which statement about atomic theory is correct?
options: It explains how molecules form.
It describes regular natural patterns.
It gathers evidence over time.
It makes reasoned future expectations.
activities.explanation: Correct. Atomic theory explains how molecules are formed.

activities.prompt: Put the prediction-checking steps in order.
items: Examine assumptions, models, or measurements again.
activities.explanation: Great ordering. A failed prediction leads scientists to check their work again.

activities.prompt: Scientific ideas remain fixed even when new evidence becomes available.
activities.explanation: That is right. Scientific ideas remain open to improvement when new evidence arrives.

activities.prompt: What should scientists allow after new evidence arrives?
options: Their ideas to improve
Their ideas to stay fixed
Their laws to remain alone
Their predictions to disappear
activities.explanation: Good choice. Scientific ideas stay open to improvement when new evidence becomes available.

activities.prompt: A child measures a toy car's roll, but some measurements are rough. How can the child improve the understanding?
options: Repeat the test and refine the measurements.
Keep only the result that matches the first guess.
Stop observing after one quick and useful test.
Trust one result more than many repeated observations.

why.Keep only the result that matches the fi: This wrongly assumes that one matching result is enough evidence.
why.Stop observing after one quick and usefu: This wrongly assumes that one quick test can organise all understanding.
why.Trust one result more than many repeated: This wrongly assumes that one result is stronger than repeated observations.

activities.explanation: Repeating tests and refining measurements helps organise the evidence.

activities.prompt: A learner studies a rolling toy over many runs. The learner uses the evidence and carefully expects one result. Why is this a scientific prediction?
options: It is a random guess that ignores all past observations.
It is a rule that nature must follow every time.
It is an idea that cannot change if a test fails.
It is a reasoned expectation based on evidence and careful thought.

why.It is a random guess that ignores all pa: This wrongly treats a reasoned prediction as a random guess.
why.It is a rule that nature must follow eve: This wrongly treats a prediction like a law that cannot fail.
why.It is an idea that cannot change if a te: This wrongly assumes that predictions cannot improve after failure.

activities.explanation: A scientific prediction is a reasoned expectation based on evidence and careful thought.

lessons.title: Limits, evidence, and estimation

activities.prompt: How can evidence and estimation help us explore big questions?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Science stays open to correction
activities.body: Science changes when nature and evidence show that an idea needs correction. Scientists reject ideas because of evidence, not merely opinion or belief. Every theory can be questioned. Estimation starts by understanding the situation and finding important quantities. A rough estimate can show whether an answer makes sense. It can also build intuition, catch errors, and grow confidence.
keyPoints: Failure can lead to correction.
Evidence guides scientific choices.
Rough estimates check whether answers make sense.
activities.explanation: Nature and evidence can correct ideas, while rough estimates check answers.

activities.prompt: A child wants to know whether the chapter’s estimate of daily breathing air makes sense.
steps: First, understand the situation and identify important quantities, because this comes before estimating.
Next, compare the estimate with about 10,000 litres each day, because rough estimates show whether answers make sense.
If only possibility matters, an approximate answer is enough, because exact precision is not needed.
Therefore, about 10,000 litres is a useful rough estimate for checking sense, finding errors, and building confidence.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Why do scientists reject an idea?
options: Evidence
Personal belief
Popular opinion
Familiar habit
activities.explanation: Evidence is the reason for rejecting an idea. Opinion and belief alone are not enough.

activities.prompt: Before estimating, understand the situation and identify the important ______.
activities.hint: These are the amounts that matter.
activities.explanation: Identifying quantities helps you choose what to estimate.

activities.prompt: Match each idea with its meaning.
pairs: Check if an answer makes sense
activities.explanation: An eclipse is a play of shadows. Evidence guides rejection, while estimates check whether answers make sense.

activities.prompt: Put the estimation steps in order.
items: Check whether the answer makes sense
activities.explanation: First understand the situation and identify important quantities. Then estimate and check the answer.

activities.prompt: What did the text find about the eclipse food claim?
options: No supporting mechanism was found.
A physical mechanism was found.
A chemical mechanism was found.
A biological mechanism was found.
activities.explanation: The text found no physical, chemical, or biological mechanism supporting the eclipse food claim.

activities.prompt: A person breathes about ______ litres of air each day.
activities.hint: Use the daily estimate from the lesson.
activities.explanation: The chapter estimates that a person breathes about 10,000 litres of air each day.

activities.prompt: An eclipse food claim has no supporting physical, chemical, or biological mechanism. How should scientists respond?
options: Check the claim against evidence before accepting it.
Accept it because personal belief is enough evidence.
Reject it because one person disliked the food.
Keep it because failure never changes scientific ideas.

why.Accept it because personal belief is eno: This mistakes personal belief for scientific evidence.
why.Reject it because one person disliked th: One person's dislike does not test the claim's mechanism.
why.Keep it because failure never changes sc: This wrongly assumes that failed ideas cannot be corrected.

activities.explanation: Evidence, not opinion, decides whether the unsupported claim should be accepted.

activities.prompt: A scientist’s explanation fails a careful test. What should the scientist do next?
options: Use the failure to correct the explanation and keep checking it.
Treat it as final because it sounded clever at first.
Stop checking because failure proves science is weak.
Keep it unchanged because failure cannot teach us anything.

why.Treat it as final because it sounded cle: This confuses an early idea with one that cannot be questioned.
why.Stop checking because failure proves sci: This mistakes scientific correction for weakness.
why.Keep it unchanged because failure cannot: This ignores that failure can guide later checking.

activities.explanation: Failure gives evidence for correction, not for treating an idea as final.

activities.prompt: Evidence supports a new explanation of the eclipse shadows. What should scientists do with the older idea?
options: Let nature correct the idea, but keep questioning it.
Keep the older idea because people once believed it.
Declare both ideas final because one has supporters.
Stop testing ideas because evidence has already chosen one.

why.Keep the older idea because people once: This treats past belief as stronger than current evidence.
why.Declare both ideas final because one has: This confuses support for an idea with proof that it is final.
why.Stop testing ideas because evidence has: This stops science from continuing to test its ideas.

activities.explanation: Nature can correct scientific ideas, and no theory must stay beyond question.

activities.prompt: A child’s daily air estimate is far below about 10,000 litres. What should the child do next?
options: Check the important quantities and reasoning for errors.
Keep it, because a rough estimate must never be checked.
Make it exact, because rough estimates cannot show sense.
Try another number, because checking means changing answers.

why.Keep it, because a rough estimate must n: This treats a rough estimate as something that cannot be wrong.
why.Make it exact, because rough estimates c: This confuses making a rough estimate with gaining exactness.
why.Try another number, because checking mea: This changes a number without checking the reasoning for mistakes.

activities.explanation: The estimate misses the expected scale, so its reasoning needs checking.

lessons.title: Connected science and scientific thinking

activities.prompt: How do scientists connect ideas from different fields to solve everyday problems?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Science works together
activities.body: Science branches include physics, chemistry, biology, and earth science after Grade 10. These branches organise scientific knowledge, but the natural world has no separating boundaries. They depend on one another, so real problems often need several disciplines together. Science also connects with mathematics, technology, arts, and social sciences.
keyPoints: The natural world has no separating boundaries.
Divisions organise scientific knowledge.
Many disciplines often work together.
activities.explanation: This shows how science branches work together.

activities.prompt: How should a class understand a mask using connected science?
steps: The class asks how a mask works because curiosity starts an investigation.
They connect particle motion and electrostatic attraction because physics explains the mask.
They consider several disciplines because real-world problems often need ideas together.
They conclude science is connected human work, not only facts, equations, or experiments.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: How science grows
activities.body: Science is more than facts, equations, or experiments. It is a human activity shaped by curiosity, creativity, cooperation, and careful questions. Scientific knowledge grows when people ask questions, test ideas, share results, and learn from mistakes. Many people across cultures and generations help develop it. Scientific thinking also helps us evaluate information critically in everyday life.
keyPoints: Science is a human activity.
Questions, testing, sharing, and learning grow science.
Scientific thinking helps us evaluate information.
activities.explanation: Curious people work together to grow scientific knowledge.

activities.title: Branches of science
activities.prompt: Which group lists branches of science?
options: Mathematics, technology, and arts
Curiosity, creativity, and cooperation
Physics, chemistry, and biology
Natural world, scientific knowledge, and boundaries
activities.explanation: Physics, chemistry, and biology are branches of science.

activities.prompt: The natural world has boundaries separating science branches.
activities.explanation: The natural world has no separating boundaries. The divisions only organise knowledge.

activities.prompt: These divisions exist only to ______ scientific knowledge.
activities.hint: Keep scientific knowledge in an orderly way.
activities.explanation: Science divisions help organise scientific knowledge.

activities.title: Connect the science ideas
activities.prompt: Match each part of science with its correct idea.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows how science knowledge is organised, connected, and used.

activities.title: How a mask works
activities.prompt: Which physics ideas help explain how a mask works?
options: Natural boundaries and organised divisions
Curiosity, creativity, and cooperation
Particle motion and electrostatic attraction
Scientific knowledge and careful questions
activities.explanation: A mask needs physics ideas about particle motion and electrostatic attraction.

activities.title: How scientific knowledge grows
activities.prompt: Put these actions in the order described by the lesson.
activities.explanation: People grow science by asking, testing, sharing, and learning.

activities.prompt: After Grade 10, a student sees several science branches. How should they understand them?
options: Branches organise knowledge, while nature has no separating lines.
Nature itself has clear, separate natural parts.
Every scientific problem fits inside one separate branch.
Separate branches should never need each other's ideas.

why.Nature itself has clear, separate natura: This wrongly treats organisational divisions as natural boundaries.
why.Every scientific problem fits inside one: This wrongly assumes every problem fits inside one branch.
why.Separate branches should never need each: This wrongly assumes separate branches cannot help each other.

activities.explanation: These branches organise knowledge, but nature has no dividing lines.

activities.prompt: A class studies a real problem using science, art, and social science. What should they understand?
options: These fields can connect and help with the same problem.
Only science belongs in the study of a real problem.
Art and social science must stay outside scientific thinking.
Each field should study a separate part of the problem alone.

why.Only science belongs in the study of a r: This wrongly assumes science cannot connect with other fields.
why.Art and social science must stay outside: This wrongly treats art and social science as separate from science.
why.Each field should study a separate part: This wrongly assumes connected fields cannot work together.

activities.explanation: Science connects with art and the social sciences.

activities.prompt: A class tests an idea, but the result does not match their hope. What should they do next?
options: Share the result and learn from the mistake.
Hide the result so the idea still looks right.
Change the question until the result looks correct.
Stop working because one result ended learning.

why.Hide the result so the idea still looks: This hides evidence because the preferred idea feels protected.
why.Change the question until the result loo: This treats changing the question as honest testing.
why.Stop working because one result ended le: This mistakes one unexpected result for the end of learning.

activities.explanation: Sharing results and learning from mistakes helps science grow.

activities.prompt: A student sees a claim that science is only a collection of facts. How should the student judge it?
options: Check it against how scientists question, test, share, and learn.
Accept it because scientific words make it sound correct.
Accept it because every scientific result is always certain.
Reject it unless one scientist already agrees.

why.Accept it because scientific words make: This mistakes scientific-sounding words for good evidence.
why.Accept it because every scientific resul: This mistakes complete certainty for a reason to accept the claim.
why.Reject it unless one scientist already a: This wrongly treats one scientist's agreement as enough evidence.

activities.explanation: Comparing a claim with scientific practice supports critical evaluation.

activities.prompt: A student thinks one scientist created scientific knowledge alone. How should this change?
options: Many people across cultures and generations developed it together.
One great scientist deserves credit for all scientific knowledge.
Each generation should restart scientific knowledge without earlier work.
Only one culture should be allowed to develop scientific knowledge.

why.One great scientist deserves credit for: This wrongly credits one person and ignores shared scientific work.
why.Each generation should restart scientifi: This wrongly ignores knowledge shared across generations.
why.Only one culture should be allowed to de: This wrongly treats scientific knowledge as belonging to one culture.

activities.explanation: Scientific knowledge develops through many people across cultures and generations.

activities.context: A student studying a patch of garden notices tiny changes in the soil and on a nearby leaf. Instead of collecting objects at random, the student writes a question, watches closely with a magnifying glass, and looks for repeating patterns. The student then makes a model to represent the complex system and tests ideas through careful experiments. Some ideas are revised after testing, so the exploration continues with care and purpose.
activities.prompt: After noticing the changes in the garden, what should the student do next?
options: Turn the observation into a testable question and investigate it carefully.
Collect more objects without deciding what the question is.
Treat the first pattern as proof that the idea is correct.
Stop observing as soon as one interesting detail appears.

why.Collect more objects without deciding wh: Random collection would make the investigation aimless.
why.Treat the first pattern as proof that th: A pattern alone does not establish that an idea is correct.
why.Stop observing as soon as one interestin: One detail is not enough for careful observation and exploration.

activities.explanation: A question and careful experiments make the exploration purposeful.

activities.context: A student studying a patch of garden notices tiny changes in the soil and on a nearby leaf. Instead of collecting objects at random, the student writes a question, watches closely with a magnifying glass, and looks for repeating patterns. The student then makes a model to represent the complex system and tests ideas through careful experiments. Some ideas are revised after testing, so the exploration continues with care and purpose.
activities.prompt: What is the main purpose of using a magnifying glass in this investigation?
options: It encourages close looking so that repeating details can be noticed.
It proves why the changes occur without needing a question.
It makes a complex system easier to represent.
It shows that an idea works in every situation.

why.It proves why the changes occur without: Observation can lead to questions but does not prove an explanation.
why.It makes a complex system easier to repr: Representing a complex system is the purpose of a model.
why.It shows that an idea works in every sit: Good science recognises the limits of where ideas apply.

activities.explanation: Careful observation helps a student notice patterns.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A magnifying glass can reveal patterns that careful observation notices.
Reason (R): The magnifying glass represents careful observation and attention to patterns.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly explains how a magnifying glass supports noticing patterns.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A model can represent a complex scientific system.
Reason (R): Using a model means scientific ideas no longer need to be tested.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Models represent complex systems, but scientific ideas are still tested and may be revised or discarded.

activities.prompt: Explain why careful exploration involves wonder, questions, experiments, and revision.
activities.answer: Careful exploration begins with wonder because science invites us to ask questions and try to find out how things work. A student observes closely, notices patterns, and turns those observations into questions. Careful experiments then provide a way to test an idea rather than accepting a guess. If testing does not support the idea, scientists revise it and may discard it. This process is purposeful rather than aimless, and it also shows that scientific ideas can develop and change through careful observation and experiments.
points: Science begins with wonder and questions.
Careful observation can reveal patterns.
Experiments test scientific ideas.
Ideas may be revised or discarded after testing.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A science club studied why stars have different colours. To keep its investigation manageable, it represented a star as a hot gas and focused on temperature, pressure, and the formation of ions. The club left out details that did not help it study the connection between colour and temperature. It also used a falling model that ignored air resistance so that gravity’s basic effect could be seen. When greater accuracy was needed, extra details could be included.
activities.prompt: What should the club do to make its explanation more accurate?
options: Bring in further relevant features to improve the explanation.
Remove the features already being studied to make the model easier.
Keep the model unchanged because greater accuracy is not a reason to change it.
Include only one feature even though the question needs several.

why.Remove the features already being studie: Removing useful features weakens the explanation.
why.Keep the model unchanged because greater: Models can be changed when accuracy is needed.
why.Include only one feature even though the: Keeping only one feature may omit what matters.

activities.explanation: Greater accuracy can require extra details.

activities.context: A science club studied why stars have different colours. To keep its investigation manageable, it represented a star as a hot gas and focused on temperature, pressure, and the formation of ions. The club left out details that did not help it study the connection between colour and temperature. It also used a falling model that ignored air resistance so that gravity’s basic effect could be seen. When greater accuracy was needed, extra details could be included.
activities.prompt: What change should be made if the falling model also needs to represent air resistance?
options: Take away gravity’s basic effect from the falling model.
Include the resistance of the air in the falling model.
Keep the model unchanged because all simplified models must ignore extra details.
Remove the other chosen features and use only the newly added one.

why.Take away gravity’s basic effect from th: This would remove the effect the model was meant to show.
why.Keep the model unchanged because all sim: More complex models can include additional details.
why.Remove the other chosen features and use: The other relevant features should not be removed.

activities.explanation: Adding air resistance supplies the required extra feature.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Ignoring air resistance in a falling model is a deliberate simplification.
Reason (R): It helps to show gravity’s basic effect.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Ignoring air resistance deliberately reveals gravity’s basic effect in falling.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Saha’s simplified model included every detail of matter in a star.
Reason (R): Saha focused on temperature, pressure, and the formation of ions.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Saha’s model deliberately left out details, so the assertion that it included every detail is false.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between a simplified model and a more complex model.
activities.answer: A simplified model keeps only the features that matter for the question and deliberately ignores other details. This makes the model simple enough to be useful. For example, a falling model may ignore air resistance to show gravity’s basic effect, while a model of the heart may ignore individual cells to show how the organ works. A more complex model includes extra details when greater accuracy is needed. The difference is therefore the number of useful details included for the question being studied.
points: Keeps only relevant features
Deliberately ignores other details
Falls or heart modelling examples
Adds details for greater accuracy
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student at a science club prepares reports with students worldwide. When describing a push, the student uses “force” in its scientific sense and checks that each symbol has the defined unit linked to it. The club follows a moving object by recording distance and time, then uses an equation to estimate where it will be later. It studies reaction rates with mathematical expressions and identifies the relevant quantities before calculating.
activities.prompt: A report contains a distance symbol but leaves out its unit. What should the student do before comparing it with another report?
options: Look up the symbol's defined unit and record it with the value.
Treat the symbol as a complete measurement even without a unit.
Choose a unit based on the ordinary meaning of nearby words.
Use the unit linked to a different symbol.

why.Treat the symbol as a complete measureme: A symbol alone does not provide the complete linked unit.
why.Choose a unit based on the ordinary mean: Everyday word meanings may not match scientific meanings.
why.Use the unit linked to a different symbo: Using another symbol's unit would misrepresent the quantity.

activities.explanation: This follows the link between each scientific symbol and its defined unit.

activities.context: A student at a science club prepares reports with students worldwide. When describing a push, the student uses “force” in its scientific sense and checks that each symbol has the defined unit linked to it. The club follows a moving object by recording distance and time, then uses an equation to estimate where it will be later. It studies reaction rates with mathematical expressions and identifies the relevant quantities before calculating.
activities.prompt: The club wants its reaction-rate result to be understandable to scientists worldwide. What should the report include?
options: Agreed terms, symbols, and the units linked to those symbols.
Only equation names, leaving readers to decide the meanings.
Everyday word meanings without scientific terms or symbols.
Scientific symbols without units because symbols alone identify every value.

why.Only equation names, leaving readers to: Equation names alone do not supply the shared terms, symbols, and units.
why.Everyday word meanings without scientifi: Everyday meanings may not communicate the scientific result.
why.Scientific symbols without units because: Leaving out units breaks the link between each symbol and its defined unit.

activities.explanation: This uses the shared language understood by scientists worldwide.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Scientists can communicate results worldwide in the same scientific way because they use a shared language of terms, symbols, and units.
Reason (R): The shared language gives reported scientific information the same meaning across different places.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the shared language explains how results can be communicated worldwide.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Memorising an equation is enough to use mathematics carefully in a scientific situation.
Reason (R): The relevant quantities must first be understood and identified.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false, while the reason is true and shows why understanding the situation is necessary.

activities.prompt: Explain why scientists worldwide need a shared language of terms, symbols, and units.
activities.answer: Scientists worldwide need a shared language because it gives their reports a common scientific meaning. Words such as force, work, cell, and reaction do not simply carry their everyday meanings in science. Agreed symbols make the ideas compact, and each symbol is linked to a defined unit. Together, terms, symbols, and units allow scientists worldwide to communicate the same scientific information. Mathematics supports this shared language by expressing relationships between quantities clearly so that they can be tested carefully.
points: Scientific words have special scientific meanings.
Scientists worldwide use shared terms, symbols, and units.
Every scientific symbol is linked to a defined unit.
Mathematics expresses relationships so they can be tested carefully.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student repeatedly observed the same natural sequence and improved the accuracy of each reading. Experiments helped organise these results into a description of the recurring pattern. Elsewhere, a class used atomic theory to explain how molecules were formed because evidence had been collected about it over time. The class also made a reasoned expectation about a future result. When that prediction failed, the students began checking their reasoning, model, and measurement quality.
activities.prompt: Why does the student's description fit the idea of a scientific law?
options: It reports a recurring pattern that is observed in nature.
One observation was enough to establish the pattern.
It predicts exactly what will happen next.
It explains how molecules are formed.

why.One observation was enough to establish: A law is supported by repeated observations rather than only one.
why.It predicts exactly what will happen nex: A future expectation is a scientific prediction.
Explaining molecular formation is the role given to atomic theory.

activities.explanation: A law describes a regular pattern observed in nature.

activities.context: A student repeatedly observed the same natural sequence and improved the accuracy of each reading. Experiments helped organise these results into a description of the recurring pattern. Elsewhere, a class used atomic theory to explain how molecules were formed because evidence had been collected about it over time. The class also made a reasoned expectation about a future result. When that prediction failed, the students began checking their reasoning, model, and measurement quality.
activities.prompt: If new evidence shows that the explanation used by the class needs improvement, what should happen?
options: The scientific idea should be revised using the new evidence.
The idea should remain unchanged because it already has evidence.
The new evidence should be rejected because the idea has been taught.
Further checking should stop once an explanation is available.

why.The idea should remain unchanged because: Existing evidence does not make an idea impossible to improve.
why.The new evidence should be rejected beca: Rejecting new evidence prevents scientific ideas from being improved.
why.Further checking should stop once an exp: Scientific understanding continues through observations, measurements, and experiments.

activities.explanation: Scientific ideas remain open to improvement when new evidence becomes available.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The student's description is a law because it sets out a regular pattern observed in nature.
Reason (R): The student found the same sequence repeatedly through observations and experiments.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the repeated observations support why the description qualifies as a law.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Exploration: Entering the World of Secondary Science

activities.prompt: You notice a shadow move strangely. What should you do first?
options: Ask a careful question about it.
Guess an answer without checking.
Copy another student's idea blindly.
Leave the observation unnoticed.
activities.explanation: Science invites curiosity and careful questions. Asking how something works starts useful exploration.

activities.prompt: A model keeps only the features that ______ for the question being studied.
activities.hint: These are the important features.
activities.explanation: Models make complex systems easier to study. They keep only the features needed for the question.

activities.prompt: Match each subject to its model.
activities.explanation: Each model leaves out details that do not help its main purpose. The choices make each model useful.

activities.prompt: Using mathematics in science means only memorising equations.
activities.explanation: We should understand the situation and identify relevant quantities first. Mathematics helps us test relationships carefully.

activities.prompt: A prediction does not match observations. What should scientists examine first?
options: Their assumptions, models, or measurements
Their mood and personal beliefs
A wish and a fixed opinion
The latest rumour they hear
activities.explanation: Scientists check assumptions, models, or measurements again. This helps science correct its ideas.

activities.prompt: Put these steps of scientific exploration in order.
items: Try to find out how things work
activities.explanation: Scientific exploration moves from questions to careful tests. Evidence can then improve or change ideas.

activities.prompt: A scientific prediction is a reasoned ______ based on evidence and careful thought.
activities.hint: A careful idea about what may happen.
activities.explanation: A prediction uses evidence and careful thought. It gives a reasoned expectation about what may happen.

activities.prompt: A scientist studies particle motion and electrostatic attraction while explaining a mask.
options: Physics
Chemistry
Biology
Earth science
activities.explanation: The mask example uses physics ideas about particles and their attraction. Different branches study different kinds of questions.

activities.prompt: Scientific ideas can remain open to improvement when new evidence appears.
activities.explanation: Theories grow from evidence gathered over time. New evidence can help scientists improve their ideas.

activities.prompt: The lesson examines a claim about eclipse food. What does it find?
options: No supporting physical, chemical, or biological mechanism exists.
The eclipse changes meals through a chemical process.
Shadows give every kind of food special power.
Scientists accepted the claim without checking evidence.
activities.explanation: The chapter finds no supporting physical, chemical, or biological mechanism. An eclipse is a play of shadows.

chapters.title: Cell: The Building Block of Life
chapters.summary: In this chapter: what is a cell and how do we study it?; the cell membrane, osmosis and cell wall; inside the cell and two kinds of cells; the main cell organelles.

lessons.title: What Is a Cell and How Do We Study It?

activities.prompt: How can we see the tiny building blocks of life?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Cells Are the Basics of Life
activities.body: All living organisms are made of cells. A cell is the basic level where life exists. Bacteria and yeast have only one cell. Plants, fish, birds and humans contain millions of cells. Different tissues are organised to form organs. Hooke saw small box-like compartments in cork and named them cells. Microscopes help us see tiny structures clearly. Electron microscopes use electrons instead of light.
keyPoints: All living organisms are made of cells.
A cell is the basic level where life exists.
Microscopes help us see very small structures clearly.
activities.explanation: Cells form living things, and microscopes help us study them.

activities.prompt: Why is an electron microscope more useful than our eyes for studying cell structure?
steps: The eye distinguishes about 10 µm gaps, so tiny details need instruments.
Microscopes make very small structures clear, which our eyes alone cannot.
Electron microscopes use electrons instead of light, so they can reveal fine details.
Therefore, electron microscopes help us study cell structure closely.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: How We Study Tiny Structures
activities.body: Microscopes allow us to see very small structures clearly. Electron microscopes reveal fine details of cell structure. They use a beam of electrons instead of light. A nanometre is one-billionth of a metre. The human eye can distinguish points separated by about 10 µm. Hooke saw small box-like compartments in cork and named them cells.
keyPoints: Electron microscopes use electrons instead of light.
A nanometre is one-billionth of a metre.
The human eye can distinguish points separated by about 10 µm.
activities.explanation: Different viewing methods help us study cells and other tiny structures.

activities.title: One-Celled Living Things
activities.prompt: What do bacteria and yeast consist of?
options: Only one cell
Millions of cells
Different tissues
Small organs
activities.explanation: Bacteria and yeast consist of only one cell. This matches the lesson.

activities.title: A Name for Cork Compartments
activities.prompt: Hooke named the small box-like compartments in cork as ______.
activities.hint: He gave this name to the compartments he saw in cork.
activities.explanation: Hooke called the small cork compartments cells. This name is still used today.

activities.title: Hooke's Observation
activities.prompt: Hooke saw small box-like compartments in cork.
activities.explanation: Hooke saw small box-like compartments in cork. He named them cells.

activities.title: Match Each Fact
activities.prompt: Match each left item to its correct partner.
activities.explanation: Each pair joins an item with its matching information. Read each pair again to check it.

activities.title: Hooke's Steps
activities.prompt: Put Hooke's actions in the order they happened.
activities.explanation: Hooke first saw the cork compartments. He then named them cells.

activities.title: What Can an Electron Microscope Reveal?
activities.prompt: A scientist uses a tool with an electron beam. What can this tool reveal?
options: Fine details of cell structure
Points separated by about 10 µm
Millions of cells in a human
Different tissues forming organs
activities.explanation: Electron microscopes reveal fine details of cell structure. Their beam uses electrons instead of light.

activities.prompt: What should a student compare to test how yeast and humans differ?
options: One yeast cell and millions of human cells.
One yeast cell and one human cell.
Two different names for the same organism.
Two microscope types and no samples.

This wrongly assumes that humans have only one cell.
why.Two different names for the same organis: Different names cannot reveal how many cells each organism has.
Comparing instruments without organisms cannot test their cell organisation.

activities.explanation: Yeast has one cell, while humans have millions, so this comparison tests the difference.

activities.prompt: Which model best shows how a many-celled living body is organised?
options: Different tissues are organised into organs.
Different organs are organised into one cell.
Different cells stay outside every tissue.
Different tissues form random heaps.

why.Different organs are organised into one: This reverses the organisation of tissues into organs.
why.Different cells stay outside every tissu: This ignores that different tissues are organised together.
This mistakes organised tissues for a random pile.

activities.explanation: Different tissues are organised to form organs, so this model fits.

activities.prompt: A student replaces the electron beam with light. Which feature changes?
options: The beam used to reveal fine cell details.
The number of cells in every organism.
The basic level at which life exists.
The names of tissues and organs.

Changing a viewing beam does not change how many cells organisms have.
A viewing beam does not change the cell as life's basic level.
Changing a viewing beam does not change the names of body parts.

activities.explanation: Electron microscopes use electrons instead of light, so the beam changes.

activities.prompt: Which plan can best reveal fine details of cell structure?
options: Use an electron microscope, because it reveals fine details.
Use only the human eye, because it shows every detail.
Use only the human eye, because electron beams cannot work.
Use an electron microscope, because it uses light.

why.Use only the human eye, because it shows: This wrongly assumes that unaided eyes show every detail.
why.Use only the human eye, because electron: This treats the human eye like an electron microscope.
why.Use an electron microscope, because it u: This confuses light with the electron beam used for fine details.

activities.explanation: Electron microscopes reveal fine cell details, so this plan fits the goal.

lessons.title: The Cell Membrane, Osmosis and Cell Wall

activities.prompt: How does water travel through cells, and what helps them stay firm?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How cells keep their balance
activities.body: The cell membrane has lipids and proteins. Proteins help substances pass like gatekeepers. The membrane is selectively permeable, meaning some substances pass, but not others. Osmosis is diffusion of water through this membrane. Diffusion means net movement towards lower concentration. Water moves from a dilute area towards a concentrated area. Plant, fungi and bacterial cells have a rigid cell wall. It keeps leaves and flowers firm, but remains permeable.
keyPoints: The cell membrane contains lipids and proteins.
Osmosis moves water across a selectively permeable membrane.
The cell wall is rigid and permeable.
activities.explanation: These parts have different jobs in movement and firmness.

activities.prompt: A bag has a selectively permeable membrane. It holds dilute and concentrated water. Which way will water move?
steps: The bag's membrane is selectively permeable, so water can move across it.
The two areas have different concentrations, so water moves between them.
Water moves from the dilute area towards the concentrated area.
This water movement across the membrane is called osmosis.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Membrane Materials
activities.prompt: Which materials make up the cell membrane?
options: Sugars and proteins
Lipids and proteins
Water and minerals
Lipids and fibres
activities.explanation: Well done! The cell membrane is made of lipids and proteins.

activities.title: Name the Movement
activities.prompt: Water movement across a selectively permeable membrane is called ______.
activities.hint: This movement is named in the lesson.
activities.explanation: Great! Osmosis is the movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane.

activities.title: Water's Direction
activities.prompt: Water moves from a dilute area towards a concentrated area.
activities.explanation: Correct! Water moves in this direction during osmosis.

activities.title: Helpful Proteins
activities.prompt: What do membrane proteins do?
options: They make leaves firm.
They act like gatekeepers.
They make walls rigid.
They store water.
activities.explanation: You spotted it! Membrane proteins help substances pass through the membrane.

activities.title: Parts and Roles
activities.prompt: Match each part or group with its correct role.
pairs: Stay firm because of the cell wall
activities.explanation: Nice work! You matched the structures with their roles.

activities.title: The Full Meaning
activities.prompt: Which statement gives the full meaning of osmosis?
options: Water diffuses across a selectively permeable membrane.
Particles move towards a lower concentration.
Cell walls make leaves and flowers firm.
Membrane proteins act like gatekeepers.
activities.explanation: Excellent! Osmosis is the diffusion of water across a selectively permeable membrane.

activities.prompt: One side of a selectively permeable membrane has dilute water. The other side has concentrated water. Which way will water move?
options: Towards the dilute side of the membrane.
Towards the concentrated side of the membrane.
It will stay on the dilute side.
It will stay on the concentrated side.

This assumes water cannot leave the dilute area.
This assumes water cannot leave the concentrated area.
This assumes water cannot move out of the concentrated area.

activities.explanation: This is right because water moves from dilute to concentrated areas.

activities.prompt: Colour particles are more spread in one part of a room. They are less spread in another part. Where will the particles move overall?
options: Towards the area with lower particle concentration.
Towards the area with higher particle concentration.
It will stay in the more crowded area.
It will move equally in both directions.

why.Towards the area with higher particle co: This confuses diffusion with movement towards greater concentration.
This assumes particles move away from lower concentration.
This ignores the net movement towards lower concentration.

activities.explanation: Diffusion moves particles towards the area with lower concentration.

activities.prompt: A fair test of osmosis needs water and a selectively permeable membrane. It also needs dilute and concentrated areas. Which setup is fairest?
options: Dilute and concentrated water separated by a selectively permeable membrane.
Particles moving between dilute and concentrated areas without a membrane.
A rigid cell wall placed between two equal-concentration water areas.
Two equal-concentration water areas joined by an open space.

why.Particles moving between dilute and conc: This tests diffusion without a selectively permeable membrane.
why.A rigid cell wall placed between two equ: This uses a cell wall and no difference in concentration.
why.Two equal-concentration water areas join: This has no membrane and no difference in concentration.

activities.explanation: This has water, different concentrations, and a selectively permeable membrane.

activities.prompt: A student says, "A rigid cell wall cannot allow anything through." Which observation shows this claim is wrong?
options: A substance passes through the rigid cell wall of a plant.
The rigid cell wall helps keep the leaf firm.
The plant cell membrane contains lipids and proteins.
The rigid cell wall surrounds the plant cell.

why.The rigid cell wall helps keep the leaf: Firmness shows support, but not whether passage is possible.
why.The plant cell membrane contains lipids: The membrane's makeup does not test the wall's permeability.
why.The rigid cell wall surrounds the plant: Being surrounded by a wall does not show whether anything can pass through it.

activities.explanation: A permeable cell wall can allow passage even though it is rigid.

lessons.title: Inside the Cell and Two Kinds of Cells

activities.prompt: What makes the tiny parts of a cell work together like a bustling city?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Meet the Cell
activities.body: Most cells have three basic parts. Cytoplasm contains organelles and other substances. Organelles are parts inside it. Membrane-bound organelles have a surrounding membrane. Some cells lack a well-defined nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. They are prokaryotic. Their activities mostly happen in the cytoplasm. Plant and animal cells are eukaryotic. They have a well-defined nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. Fine fibres form the cytoskeleton. It supports cells, maintains shape and helps movement.
keyPoints: Most cells have three basic parts.
Prokaryotic cells lack a well-defined nucleus.
Eukaryotic cells have a cytoskeleton that supports them.
activities.explanation: These features help us tell cell types apart.

activities.prompt: Two models show a plant cell and a bacterial cell. Why are their insides drawn differently?
steps: The plant cell is eukaryotic, because it has a well-defined nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
The bacterial cell is prokaryotic, because it lacks a well-defined nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
Most bacterial activities happen in the cytoplasm, because prokaryotic cells lack membrane-bound organelles.
The models need different insides, because eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells have different parts.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which statement about most cells is true?
options: Most cells have one basic part.
Most cells have three basic parts.
Most cells have no basic parts.
Most cells have four basic parts.
activities.explanation: Most cells have three basic parts.

activities.prompt: Cells with a well-defined nucleus are called ______ cells.
activities.hint: Plant and animal cells have this kind.
activities.explanation: Cells with a well-defined nucleus are called eukaryotic cells.

activities.prompt: Match each cell type with a correct feature.
activities.explanation: Bacterial cells lack membrane-bound organelles. Prokaryotic cells lack a well-defined nucleus.

activities.prompt: Which cell lacks a well-defined nucleus?
options: A plant cell
An animal cell
A bacterial cell
A eukaryotic cell
activities.explanation: A bacterial cell lacks a well-defined nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.

activities.prompt: A cell has no well-defined nucleus. Which description fits it?
options: It is eukaryotic, with activities mostly in cytoplasm.
It is prokaryotic, with activities mostly in cytoplasm.
It is eukaryotic, with activities mostly in organelles.
It is prokaryotic, with activities mostly in organelles.
activities.explanation: Cells without a well-defined nucleus are prokaryotic. Their activities mostly happen directly in the cytoplasm.

activities.prompt: Inside eukaryotic cells, fine fibres form the cytoskeleton. It supports the cell, maintains its shape and helps ______.
activities.hint: Think about how the cell moves.
activities.explanation: The cytoskeleton supports the cell, maintains its shape and helps movement.

activities.prompt: A cell has no well-defined nucleus. A student calls it eukaryotic. Which repair is correct?
options: Keep eukaryotic, because it contains membrane-bound organelles.
Change to prokaryotic, because it lacks a well-defined nucleus.
Change to prokaryotic, because plant and animal cells have organelles.
Keep eukaryotic, because most activities happen in the cytoplasm.

why.Keep eukaryotic, because it contains mem: This keeps eukaryotic despite the missing well-defined nucleus.
why.Change to prokaryotic, because plant and: The name fits, but plant and animal cells do not explain this cell.
why.Keep eukaryotic, because most activities: Cytoplasm location does not decide whether a cell is eukaryotic.

activities.explanation: Prokaryotic cells lack a well-defined nucleus, so this repair is correct.

activities.prompt: A bacterial cell has no well-defined nucleus or membrane-bound organelles. Where should most activity signs go?
options: Inside the cell's cytoplasm
Inside the cell's well-defined nucleus
Inside the cell's membrane-bound organelles
Inside the cell's fine fibres

why.Inside the cell's well-defined nucleus: A bacterial cell has no well-defined nucleus for these activities.
why.Inside the cell's membrane-bound organel: A bacterial cell has no membrane-bound organelles for these activities.
why.Inside the cell's fine fibres: Fine fibres form a cytoskeleton inside eukaryotic cells, not bacterial ones.

activities.explanation: Most prokaryotic activities happen directly in the cytoplasm.

activities.prompt: Fine fibres support cell shape and help movement. What may happen if they are removed?
options: It may lose shape support and movement help.
It may lose its well-defined nucleus.
It may gain many membrane-bound organelles.
It may move all activities into its cytoplasm.

Removing fine fibres does not remove a well-defined nucleus.
why.It may gain many membrane-bound organell: Removing fine fibres does not create membrane-bound organelles.
why.It may move all activities into its cyto: Removing fine fibres does not move activities into the cytoplasm.

activities.explanation: The cytoskeleton supports shape and helps movement, so removing it harms both.

activities.prompt: Some cells have a well-defined nucleus, but bacterial cells do not. Which comparison would best test the claim that every cell has one?
options: A bacterial cell beside a plant cell
A plant cell beside an animal cell
Fine fibres beside a cell membrane
Cell substances beside an organelle

why.A plant cell beside an animal cell: Both cells have nuclei, so this comparison cannot test the claim.
why.Fine fibres beside a cell membrane: Fine fibres and membranes do not show whether a nucleus exists.
why.Cell substances beside an organelle: Cell substances and organelles do not show whether a nucleus exists.

activities.explanation: This comparison includes a cell without a well-defined nucleus.
