lessons.title: The Main Cell Organelles

activities.prompt: How do the tiny parts inside a cell work together?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Meet the Cell Organelles
activities.body: The nucleus has a double-layered nuclear membrane. Chromosomes carry inherited information, and the nucleolus makes ribosomal subunits. Ribosomes make proteins. The endoplasmic reticulum transports proteins, fats and some hormones. The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts and packages proteins and lipids. Lysosomes break down unwanted materials. Mitochondria are cell powerhouses, while ATP stores energy released by respiration. Leucoplasts are colourless plastids. The vacuole stores water, minerals, sugars and waste.
keyPoints: nuclear membrane: double-layered covering
ribosomes: sites of protein synthesis
lysosomes: break down unwanted materials
activities.explanation: These organelles have different jobs inside a cell.

activities.prompt: How does a cell make a protein and prepare it for use?
steps: Ribosomes make the protein because they are the sites of protein synthesis.
The endoplasmic reticulum helps synthesise and transport proteins, fats and some hormones.
The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts and packages proteins and lipids.
Conclusion: Making and handling proteins involve several organelles.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which part covers the nucleus with two layers?
options: nuclear membrane
nucleolus
vacuole
leucoplast
activities.explanation: The nuclear membrane is the double-layered covering around the nucleus.

activities.prompt: Ribosomes are the sites of protein ______.
activities.hint: This word means making proteins.
activities.explanation: Ribosomes are the sites of protein synthesis.

activities.prompt: Match each organelle with its work.
pairs: stores water, minerals, sugars and waste material
activities.explanation: Lysosomes break down unwanted materials. The vacuole stores water, minerals, sugars and waste material.

activities.prompt: Which organelle helps synthesise and transport proteins, fats and some hormones?
options: endoplasmic reticulum
Golgi apparatus
lysosomes
mitochondria
activities.explanation: The endoplasmic reticulum helps synthesise and transport proteins, fats and some hormones.

activities.prompt: Match each cell part with its described role.
pairs: helps synthesise and transport proteins, fats and some hormones
called the powerhouses of the cell
activities.explanation: The endoplasmic reticulum helps transport proteins, fats and some hormones. Mitochondria are called the powerhouses of the cell.

activities.prompt: Put these Golgi apparatus actions in working order.
activities.explanation: The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts and packages proteins and lipids.

activities.prompt: A cell's ribosomes make fewer proteins. What will most likely happen?
options: Less protein will be produced in the cell.
More protein will be produced in the cell.
More lipids will be produced in the cell.
More water will be stored in the cell.

why.More protein will be produced in the cel: This reverses the effect of having fewer working ribosomes.
why.More lipids will be produced in the cell: This confuses ribosomes with the endoplasmic reticulum's fat-making job.
This confuses protein production with the vacuole's storage job.

activities.explanation: This is right because ribosomes are the sites of protein synthesis.

activities.prompt: A cell is handling a protein. Which sequence best fits the organelle jobs?
options: Ribosomes make it; endoplasmic reticulum transports it; Golgi packages it.
Endoplasmic reticulum helps make it; Golgi packages it; ribosomes transport it.
Golgi makes it; endoplasmic reticulum helps transport it; ribosomes sort it.
Lysosomes make it; vacuole transports it; Golgi sorts it.

why.Endoplasmic reticulum helps make it; Gol: This mixes up making, packaging, and transport.
why.Golgi makes it; endoplasmic reticulum he: This gives ribosomes a sorting job instead of protein synthesis.
why.Lysosomes make it; vacuole transports it: This mixes up lysosomes, the vacuole, and the Golgi apparatus.

activities.explanation: This is right because each organelle does the matching job.

activities.prompt: A learner wants evidence that Golgi modifies proteins. Which comparison is best?
options: Compare proteins before and after they pass through the Golgi.
Compare different proteins only before they pass through the Golgi.
Compare proteins before and after they pass through lysosomes.
Compare proteins before and after they pass through the vacuole.

why.Compare different proteins only before t: This changes the proteins and does not show what Golgi does.
why.Compare proteins before and after they p: This confuses Golgi modification with lysosome breakdown.
This confuses Golgi modification with vacuole storage.

activities.explanation: This is right because it compares proteins before and after the Golgi.

activities.prompt: A cell contains many mitochondria. Which cellular activity do they best support?
options: Storing energy released during respiration in ATP.
Making ribosomal subunits inside the nucleolus.
Breaking down unwanted materials inside lysosomes.
Storing water, minerals, sugars, and waste.

why.Making ribosomal subunits inside the nuc: This confuses energy support with the nucleolus making subunits.
why.Breaking down unwanted materials inside: This confuses energy support with lysosome breakdown.
why.Storing water, minerals, sugars, and was: This confuses energy support with vacuole storage.

activities.explanation: This is right because mitochondria are powerhouses and ATP stores released energy.

activities.prompt: A child claims ATP carries inherited information. Why is this claim flawed?
options: ATP stores released energy; chromosomes carry inherited information.
ATP makes ribosomes; chromosomes store water and minerals.
ATP stores water; chromosomes make ribosomal subunits.
ATP packages proteins; chromosomes break down unwanted materials.

why.ATP makes ribosomes; chromosomes store w: This swaps ATP's energy role with the nucleolus and misplaces storage.
why.ATP stores water; chromosomes make ribos: This confuses ATP with vacuole storage and chromosomes with the nucleolus.
why.ATP packages proteins; chromosomes break: This confuses ATP with Golgi packaging and chromosomes with lysosomes.

activities.explanation: This is right because ATP stores energy while chromosomes carry inherited information.

lessons.title: Cell Growth, Mitosis and Meiosis

activities.prompt: How do our cells grow, repair themselves, and help make babies?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Cells Grow and Divide
activities.body: Body cells can grow and divide. This replaces old, dead or damaged cells and helps your body grow and repair tissues. Cell division makes new cells from cells that already exist. Mitosis makes two daughter cells, meaning two new cells with the same DNA. Meiosis divides one parent cell twice. It makes four daughter cells, creates variation and halves chromosomes. It also produces gametes, cells used for sexual reproduction.
keyPoints: Body cells divide to support growth and repair.
Mitosis makes two daughter cells with the same DNA.
Meiosis makes four daughter cells with half the chromosomes.
activities.explanation: These are the main ideas you will practise in this lesson.

activities.prompt: A child has a cut on the skin. What should happen so the damaged cells can be replaced?
steps: The cut damages body cells, so repair is needed.
Body cells divide because new cells can replace damaged ones.
The new cells come from pre-existing cells, so they are not made from nothing.
Therefore, cell division helps the body repair the cut.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: How does body growth happen?
options: Cells store more food for later.
Cells divide and form new cells.
Cells shrink and leave the body.
Cells stop making new cells.
activities.explanation: Body growth happens because cells divide and form new cells.

activities.prompt: Mitosis produces ______ genetically identical daughter cells.
activities.hint: Count the daughter cells made by mitosis.
activities.explanation: Mitosis produces two genetically identical daughter cells.

activities.prompt: Match each part of cell division to its description.
activities.explanation: Mitosis makes two identical cells. Meiosis makes four cells and produces gametes.

activities.prompt: Put the meiosis events in order.
items: Each daughter cell has half the chromosomes
activities.explanation: The parent cell divides twice. This forms four daughter cells with half the chromosomes.

activities.prompt: What does a daughter cell receive from mitosis?
options: The same chromosome number as its parent
Twice the chromosome number of its parent
No chromosomes at all
Half the chromosome number of its parent
activities.explanation: A mitosis daughter cell receives the same DNA and chromosome number as its parent.

activities.prompt: What does fertilisation do after meiosis?
options: It makes four gametes.
It restores the original chromosome number.
It makes two identical daughter cells.
It replaces damaged body cells.
activities.explanation: Meiosis reduces the chromosome number. Fertilisation restores the original number.

activities.prompt: A child cuts a finger while playing. Which change would best help repair the cut?
options: Body cells divide and replace the damaged cells.
Body cells grow but never make new cells.
Gametes join and repair the damaged body cells.
Body cells divide twice and make four daughter cells.

why.Body cells grow but never make new cells: This mistakes cell growth for the division that makes replacements.
why.Gametes join and repair the damaged body: This wrongly uses sexual reproduction to explain tissue repair.
why.Body cells divide twice and make four da: This mistakes meiosis's two divisions for ordinary body-cell division.

activities.explanation: This uses body-cell division to replace the damaged cells.

activities.prompt: A child is growing taller. What must be happening in the child's body?
options: Body cells are dividing and forming new cells.
Body cells are dying without making new cells.
Gametes are joining to make the child's body grow.
One body cell is dividing twice and making four cells.

why.Body cells are dying without making new: This mistakes loss of cells for the division needed for growth.
why.Gametes are joining to make the child's: This wrongly links gamete joining to ordinary body growth.
why.One body cell is dividing twice and maki: This applies meiosis's two divisions to growth in the body.

activities.explanation: Body growth happens because dividing cells form new cells.

activities.prompt: A student wants to test if mitosis makes identical daughter cells. Which comparison is fairest?
options: Compare each daughter's DNA and chromosomes with its parent.
Compare one mitosis daughter with one meiosis daughter.
Compare daughter cells from two different parent cells.
Compare the parent cell with a gamete from meiosis.

why.Compare one mitosis daughter with one me: This mixes mitosis with meiosis, which make different daughter cells.
why.Compare daughter cells from two differen: Changing the parent does not fairly test one parent's daughters.
why.Compare the parent cell with a gamete fr: This compares mitosis with meiosis instead of checking mitosis daughters.

activities.explanation: This checks each daughter against the same parent's DNA and chromosomes.

activities.prompt: One gamete made by meiosis joins another gamete. What should happen to the chromosome number?
options: It should return to the original number.
It should be reduced to half again.
It should stay at the reduced number.
It should be restored before the gametes join.

This wrongly treats fertilisation as another reduction instead of restoration.
This wrongly assumes the reduced chromosome number stays reduced.
why.It should be restored before the gametes: This puts restoration before gametes join, when fertilisation happens.

activities.explanation: Fertilisation restores the original chromosome number after meiosis halves it.

activities.prompt: Every cell division gives four daughter cells with half the chromosomes. Which observation shows this claim is wrong?
options: Mitosis gives two daughter cells with the parent's chromosomes.
Meiosis gives two daughter cells with the parent's chromosomes.
Mitosis gives four daughter cells with half the chromosomes.
Meiosis gives four daughter cells with the parent's chromosomes.

why.Meiosis gives two daughter cells with th: This wrongly gives mitosis the result of meiosis.
why.Mitosis gives four daughter cells with h: This wrongly gives mitosis the result of meiosis.
why.Meiosis gives four daughter cells with t: This mixes meiosis's cell count with mitosis's chromosome number.

activities.explanation: Mitosis gives two identical daughters with the parent's chromosome number.

lessons.title: Cell Theory and Cell Life

activities.prompt: What helps a tiny cell know when to grow, divide, or rest?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Cells Live and Divide
activities.body: All living organisms have one or more cells. Cells grow and divide in a controlled way. Every cell has a definite life span. New cells replace dead cells and perform the same function. Animal cells usually stop dividing when they touch neighbours, a process called contact inhibition. Cancer cells keep dividing without control. Plant cells do not show contact inhibition. Programmed Cell Death means cell death controlled by genes.
keyPoints: Living organisms contain cells.
Cells grow, divide, and have a definite life span.
New cells replace dead cells and perform the same function.
activities.explanation: This card shows the main rules of cell growth, division, and replacement.

activities.prompt: A scrape removes some skin cells. Why can the skin still work afterward?
steps: Cells have a definite life span, so some skin cells eventually die.
A scrape can kill cells, so the injured area loses its cells.
New cells replace the dead cells and perform the same function.
Therefore, the repaired skin can continue doing its normal work.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What is true of every living organism?
options: Every living organism contains cells.
Every living organism has only one cell.
Only some living organisms contain cells.
Some living organisms contain no cells.
activities.explanation: The lesson says that every living organism has one or more cells.

activities.prompt: All cells arise from cells that already exist.
activities.explanation: A pre-existing cell is a cell that already existed. All new cells come from such cells.

activities.prompt: Cells grow and divide in a ______ way.
activities.hint: This helps keep cell growth and division under control.
activities.explanation: The lesson says cells grow and divide in a controlled way.

activities.prompt: Match each cell type with the correct statement.
activities.explanation: These pairs show what happens to cells during division or cell formation.

activities.prompt: What usually happens when two animal cells touch?
options: They usually stop dividing.
They divide much faster.
They lose their life span.
They become plant cells.
activities.explanation: Touching neighbouring cells usually stops animal cell division. This process is called contact inhibition.

activities.prompt: Put these events in the order they happen.
items: Every cell reaches the end of its life span.
New cells replace the dead cell.
The new cells perform the same function.
activities.explanation: Every cell has a definite life span, and replacement cells perform the same function.

activities.prompt: Which statement about Programmed Cell Death is correct?
options: It is genetically regulated and organised.
It is random and unplanned.
It happens only in cancer cells.
It stops every kind of division.
activities.explanation: Programmed Cell Death is genetically regulated and organised.

activities.prompt: What can a mature plant cell do?
options: Form different types of cells.
Show contact inhibition.
Keep dividing without control.
Arise from no pre-existing cell.
activities.explanation: A mature plant cell can form different types of cells. Plant cells also do not show contact inhibition.

activities.prompt: Animal cells grow until they touch nearby cells. What happens next?
options: Their division stops because touching causes contact inhibition.
Their division speeds up because they touch nearby cells.
Their division stops because all nearby cells have died.
Their division continues without limit because the cells touch.

why.Their division speeds up because they to: This mistake thinks touching cells make division speed up.
why.Their division stops because all nearby: This mistake thinks touching nearby cells means they died.
why.Their division continues without limit b: This mistake ignores the stopping effect of contact inhibition.

activities.explanation: This is right because contact inhibition stops animal cell division.

activities.prompt: Plant cells grow beside each other. How will contact affect their division?
options: It will not stop their division because plants lack contact inhibition.
It will stop their division as soon as the cells touch.
It will stop their division because every plant cell dies.
It will speed up their division because the cells touch.

why.It will stop their division as soon as t: This mistake applies the animal cell rule to plant cells.
why.It will stop their division because ever: This mistake thinks touching cells means neighbouring cells have died.
why.It will speed up their division because: This mistake thinks contact always makes cell division faster.

activities.explanation: This is right because plant cells do not show contact inhibition.

lessons.sceneAlt: Onion skin cells are seen under a microscope.
lessons.sceneCaption: Onion skin cells under a microscope.

activities.context: Riya’s class is preparing a cell display about cork. Hooke saw small box-like compartments there and named them cells. Their teacher says an electron microscope uses a beam of electrons instead of light and reveals fine details of cell structure. Riya wants to compare bacteria and yeast with plants, fish, birds and humans. She is checking whether printed points are about 10 µm apart for the human eye. She will explain how tissues are organised to form organs.
activities.prompt: The display needs to show fine details of cell structure. What should the group change next?
options: Switch from a light microscope to an electron microscope.
Keep using light and rely on the larger printed points.
Examine the cork with the unaided eye instead.
Replace the cell image with the tissue-and-organ diagram.

why.Keep using light and rely on the larger: A light microscope does not use the electron beam described in the case.
why.Examine the cork with the unaided eye in: The unaided eye has a limit of about 10 µm for distinguishing points.
why.Replace the cell image with the tissue-a: A tissue-and-organ diagram would not reveal the cell structure directly.

activities.explanation: An electron microscope uses electrons and reveals fine structural details.

activities.context: Riya’s class is preparing a cell display about cork. Hooke saw small box-like compartments there and named them cells. Their teacher says an electron microscope uses a beam of electrons instead of light and reveals fine details of cell structure. Riya wants to compare bacteria and yeast with plants, fish, birds and humans. She is checking whether printed points are about 10 µm apart for the human eye. She will explain how tissues are organised to form organs.
activities.prompt: Which information corrects a display note that says every organism contains only one cell?
options: Bacteria and yeast have one cell, while plants, fish, birds and humans have millions.
Every organism has one cell because the cell is the basic level of life.
Plants, fish, birds and humans have one cell each, but cork has millions.
Hooke’s cork compartments prove that all living things contain one cell.

why.Every organism has one cell because the: The basic level of life does not mean that every organism has only one cell.
why.Plants, fish, birds and humans have one: The statement gives the wrong cell numbers for both groups.
why.Hooke’s cork compartments prove that all: Hooke’s observation of cork compartments does not prove this for every organism.

activities.explanation: This correctly separates the one-celled organisms from the many-celled organisms.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Using a beam of electrons instead of light enables an electron microscope to reveal fine details of cell structure.
Reason (R): An electron microscope uses a beam of electrons instead of light.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly explains why the electron microscope reveals fine structural details.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Yeast consists of only one cell.
Reason (R): Humans contain millions of cells.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but the number of cells in humans does not explain why yeast has only one cell.

activities.prompt: How does an electron microscope help us study cells, and how is its method of viewing different from a microscope that uses light?
activities.answer: Electron microscopes help us study cells by revealing fine details of cell structure. They do this by using a beam of electrons instead of light. A microscope that uses light also allows us to see very small structures clearly, but the electron microscope is the instrument described here for revealing fine details. For the display, the group can link Hooke’s cork observation with the viewing method. Hooke saw small box-like compartments in cork and named them cells, while the electron microscope can reveal fine structural details in the sample.
points: Electron microscopes reveal fine cell details.
They use electrons rather than light.
Ordinary microscopes make very small structures visible.
The display can connect Hooke’s cork observation with microscopy.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A plant leaf is placed in concentrated liquid, while the water inside its cells is dilute. The membrane around each cell is selectively permeable and is made of lipids and proteins. The leaf also has a rigid but permeable cell wall. Water moves out of the cells, and the leaf remains firm. A student must explain the water movement, the work of membrane proteins, and the cell wall's role.
activities.prompt: Why does water leave the leaf cells in this case?
options: The dilute water inside moves towards the concentrated liquid by osmosis.
Water moves from the concentrated liquid towards the dilute water inside the cells.
Diffusion of particles towards a lower concentration pushes water out of the cells.
The permeable cell wall draws water out of the cells.

why.Water moves from the concentrated liquid: This reverses the stated direction of water movement.
why.Diffusion of particles towards a lower c: The lower-concentration region is inside the cells, so this movement would be inwards.
why.The permeable cell wall draws water out: Permeability allows passage but does not cause water to leave.

activities.explanation: Water crosses a selectively permeable membrane towards a more concentrated area.

activities.context: A plant leaf is placed in concentrated liquid, while the water inside its cells is dilute. The membrane around each cell is selectively permeable and is made of lipids and proteins. The leaf also has a rigid but permeable cell wall. Water moves out of the cells, and the leaf remains firm. A student must explain the water movement, the work of membrane proteins, and the cell wall's role.
activities.prompt: Why can the leaf remain firm even though water is leaving its cells?
options: The rigid cell wall helps leaves and flowers remain firm.
The lipids in the cell membrane make the leaf firm because they can move and rotate.
The membrane proteins make the leaf firm by helping substances pass through.
Osmosis makes the leaf firm by moving water into its cells.

why.The lipids in the cell membrane make the: Moving and rotating membrane molecules does not explain the leaf's firmness.
why.The membrane proteins make the leaf firm: The proteins' stated role is to help substances pass through.
why.Osmosis makes the leaf firm by moving wa: Osmosis explains water movement, while the cell wall explains firmness.

activities.explanation: The wall is rigid and helps leaves remain firm.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Water moved from the dilute interior of a leaf cell towards the concentrated liquid outside.
Reason (R): This movement was osmosis because it was diffusion of water across a selectively permeable membrane.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the reason correctly explains the movement of water.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The rigid cell wall prevents all substances from passing through it.
Reason (R): Although the cell wall is rigid, it is permeable.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false because the cell wall is permeable, while the reason is true.

activities.prompt: Explain how osmosis and diffusion are related.
activities.answer: Osmosis is a special case of diffusion. Diffusion is the net movement of particles towards lower concentration. In osmosis, the particle moving is water, and it moves across a selectively permeable membrane from a dilute area towards a concentrated area. Thus, osmosis can be described as the diffusion of water across a selectively permeable membrane. The two ideas are connected because both describe net movement caused by concentration differences, but osmosis has the extra conditions of water and a selectively permeable membrane.
points: Defines diffusion as net movement towards lower concentration.
Identifies water as the substance moving in osmosis.
Includes the selectively permeable membrane condition.
Explains that osmosis is a type of diffusion.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student studying a bacterial cell notices that it has no well-defined nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles. The student learns that most activities in this cell happen directly in the cytoplasm. When checking plant and animal cells, the student finds a well-defined nucleus, membrane-bound organelles, and fine fibres forming a cytoskeleton. The student is asked how these differences affect the cells’ organization and support.
activities.prompt: Based on the bacterial cell described, how should the student classify it?
options: A prokaryotic cell
A eukaryotic cell
A plant cell
An animal cell

why.A eukaryotic cell: Cells without a well-defined nucleus are prokaryotic.
why.A plant cell: It does not have the features of plant or animal cells.
why.An animal cell: A eukaryotic cell has a well-defined nucleus.

activities.explanation: It lacks a well-defined nucleus.

activities.context: A student studying a bacterial cell notices that it has no well-defined nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles. The student learns that most activities in this cell happen directly in the cytoplasm. When checking plant and animal cells, the student finds a well-defined nucleus, membrane-bound organelles, and fine fibres forming a cytoskeleton. The student is asked how these differences affect the cells’ organization and support.
activities.prompt: Which part of the plant and animal cells should the student identify as helping to maintain cell shape and movement?
options: The cytoskeleton
The cytoplasm
The well-defined nucleus
The membrane-bound organelles

why.The membrane-bound organelles: The other listed parts are not identified as helping movement.

activities.explanation: Fine fibres form the cytoskeleton.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The bacterial cell in the case is a prokaryotic cell because it lacks a well-defined nucleus.
Reason (R): Cells without a well-defined nucleus are called prokaryotic cells.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly explains why the bacterial cell is called prokaryotic.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Most activities in a plant cell take place directly in the cytoplasm.
Reason (R): Most activities in prokaryotic cells take place directly in the cytoplasm.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The statement about a plant cell is false, while the reason about prokaryotic cells is true.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.
activities.answer: Prokaryotic cells, such as the bacterial cell in the case, lack a well-defined nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. Most activities in prokaryotic cells take place directly in the cytoplasm. Eukaryotic cells include plant and animal cells. They have a well-defined nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. Fine fibres form a cytoskeleton inside eukaryotic cells. This cytoskeleton supports the cell, maintains its shape, and helps movement. Therefore, the main difference used here is whether the cell has a well-defined nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
points: Prokaryotic cells lack a well-defined nucleus.
Prokaryotic cells lack membrane-bound organelles.
Eukaryotic cells have a well-defined nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
The cytoskeleton supports eukaryotic cells.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student studying a plant cell observed that the vacuole contained water, minerals, sugars and waste material. The cell also had colourless plastids, which the student recognized as leucoplasts. Lysosomes, enzyme-filled sacs, were present to break down unwanted materials. When the cell needed proteins, ribosomes made them. The proteins were then handled by the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus before being used by the cell. The student also saw mitochondria and learned that respiration released energy stored in ATP.
activities.prompt: If unwanted materials began to build up in the cell, which response is most appropriate?
options: The sacs containing enzymes would act on the unwanted materials.
The vacuole would use enzymes to break down the unwanted materials.
The Golgi apparatus would sort the unwanted materials into lipid packages.
The mitochondria would use ATP to destroy the unwanted materials.

why.The vacuole would use enzymes to break d: The vacuole stores materials; it does not make enzymes for this purpose.
why.The Golgi apparatus would sort the unwan: The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts and packages proteins and lipids.
why.The mitochondria would use ATP to destro: Mitochondria release energy during respiration; they do not destroy unwanted materials.

activities.explanation: Lysosomes are enzyme-filled sacs that break down unwanted materials.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The endoplasmic reticulum helps transport proteins made by ribosomes.
Reason (R): Ribosomes are the sites of protein synthesis, and the endoplasmic reticulum helps synthesise and transport proteins, fats and some hormones.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Reason explains the connection between ribosome-made proteins and their transport by the endoplasmic reticulum.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Cell: The Building Block of Life

activities.title: The basics of life
activities.prompt: Which statement about cells is correct?
options: All living organisms contain cells.
Only animals consist of cells.
Cells are the basic level of life.
Large plants contain no cells.
activities.explanation: All living organisms are made of cells. The cell is the basic level where life exists.

activities.prompt: Diffusion moves particles towards a higher concentration.
activities.explanation: Diffusion is the net movement of particles towards lower concentration.

activities.title: Movement of water
activities.prompt: Water moves from a dilute area towards a ______ area.
activities.hint: This area has more dissolved substances.
activities.explanation: This movement across a selectively permeable membrane is called osmosis.

activities.title: Match organelles to their jobs
activities.prompt: Match each organelle with its correct job.
pairs: Modify, sort and package proteins and lipids
activities.explanation: Each organelle has the listed role inside the cell.

activities.title: Replace old cells
activities.prompt: Put these steps for replacing body cells in order.
activities.explanation: Growing and dividing body cells form replacements for old, dead or damaged cells.

activities.title: Inside a bacterial cell
activities.prompt: Which pair correctly describes a bacterial cell?
options: A defined nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
No defined nucleus or membrane-bound organelles.
A defined nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles.
No defined nucleus and some membrane-bound organelles.
activities.explanation: Bacterial cells lack a well-defined nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.

activities.prompt: Fine fibres support eukaryotic cells and help them move.
activities.explanation: The cytoskeleton supports the cell, maintains its shape and helps movement.

activities.title: Microscopes and tiny measurements
activities.prompt: Match each discovery or tool with its correct detail.
pairs: Reveal fine details of cell structure
Use a beam of electrons instead of light
Distinguishes points separated by about 10 µm
activities.explanation: These pairs link early cell study with the instruments and units used.

activities.title: The cell membrane
activities.prompt: The cell membrane is made of lipids and ______.
activities.hint: These parts help substances pass through the membrane.
activities.explanation: Membrane proteins help substances pass through like gatekeepers.

activities.title: Meiosis and fertilisation
activities.prompt: Put the events in order during sexual reproduction.
activities.explanation: Meiosis produces gametes for sexual reproduction. Fertilisation restores the original chromosome number.

chapters.title: Tissues in Action
chapters.summary: In this chapter: cells, tissues and division of labour; meristematic tissues and plant growth; protective and supporting plant tissues; conducting tissues and tissue systems.

lessons.title: Cells, Tissues and Division of Labour

activities.prompt: What makes cells team up and help your body work?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Cells Build a Working Body
activities.body: A single cell can divide repeatedly and produce many cells. These cells can form skin, muscles, bones, nerves and organs. Cells with similar structures and functions group together to form a tissue. A tissue is a group of similar cells that works together. Division of labour means different groups of cells have different functions. It increases the body's efficiency.
keyPoints: One cell can divide repeatedly.
Similar cells work together as a tissue.
Division of labour increases the body's efficiency.
activities.explanation: Different cells work together, helping the body work more efficiently.

activities.prompt: An animal has many cell types. How is its work shared?
steps: Many cells divide, allowing skin, muscles, bones, nerves and organs to form.
Similar cells group into tissues, so each group can work together.
Different organs form organ systems, so jobs are shared at another level.
This division of labour increases the body's efficiency.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Different Levels of Organisation
activities.body: An organism may have several organ systems. Different organs form organ systems, and organ systems form an organism. Cells with similar structures and functions make a tissue. Division of labour increases the body's efficiency. A unicellular organism has just one cell. This one cell carries out all the functions of life.
keyPoints: Organ systems form organisms.
Division of labour increases the body's efficiency.
One cell handles all life functions in a unicellular organism.
activities.explanation: Different levels of organisation help the body work efficiently.

activities.title: Cells That Belong Together
activities.prompt: Cells with different structures and functions group together to form a tissue.
activities.explanation: A tissue contains similar cells with similar structures and functions.

activities.title: A Strong Plant Cell
activities.prompt: A plant cell wall provides ______ and strength.
activities.hint: This helps the cell keep its shape.
activities.explanation: A plant cell wall provides rigidity and strength.

activities.title: Plant and Animal Features
activities.prompt: Match each cell or tissue with its correct feature.
pairs: Use solar energy to make food components
activities.explanation: Plant cell walls provide rigidity and strength. Animal cells can change shape because they lack rigid walls.

activities.title: From Small to Large
activities.prompt: Put these body levels in order, from smallest to largest.
activities.explanation: Similar cells form a tissue. Organs form organ systems, and organ systems form an organism.

activities.title: The Helpful Division of Labour
activities.prompt: What does division of labour increase in the body?
options: It makes the body efficient
It makes the body weaker
It makes each organ equal
It stops body functions
activities.explanation: Division of labour increases the efficiency of the body.

activities.title: Working Towards an Organism
activities.prompt: Different organs form organ systems, and organ systems form an organism.
activities.explanation: Organs work together in organ systems. These systems together form an organism.

activities.prompt: A plant loses its cell walls. What is most likely to happen?
options: The plant loses support and may fall over.
The plant gains support and grows taller.
The plant makes food faster than before.
The plant changes shape more easily than before.

why.The plant gains support and grows taller: This reverses the effect of losing the cell wall.
Making food faster is not the support effect described.
why.The plant changes shape more easily than: This confuses plant cells with animal cells, which lack a rigid wall.

activities.explanation: The cell wall normally gives the plant rigidity and strength.

activities.prompt: One cell is called more efficient. Why is this claim weak?
options: Many cell groups can divide the work between them.
One cell must do every function of life.
Several organs can each handle one kind of job.
One cell needs no similar cells around it.

This confuses doing every job with doing them efficiently.
why.Several organs can each handle one kind: This describes many organs, but does not compare the two body plans.
why.One cell needs no similar cells around i: This mistakes being alone for being more efficient.

activities.explanation: Division of labour lets many cells increase the body's efficiency.

activities.prompt: Several organs belong to organ systems. What must also be true?
options: The organ systems together form the organism.
Each organ will divide into one cell.
The organ systems will form separate tissues.
Each cell will perform every body function.

Division makes more cells, not one cell from an organ.
why.The organ systems will form separate tis: Tissues come from similar cells, not from organ systems.
why.Each cell will perform every body functi: This confuses an organism's parts with a one-cell organism.

activities.explanation: Different organ systems form the whole organism.

activities.prompt: A teacher shows one cell and a skin tissue. Which sample shows division of labour?
options: The skin tissue, because similar cells work together.
The single cell, because it performs every life function.
The skin tissue, because one cell does every job.
The single cell, because it contains organ systems.

why.The single cell, because it performs eve: This confuses a separate cell with a whole one-cell organism.
why.The skin tissue, because one cell does e: This mixes the right sample with the wrong reason.
why.The single cell, because it contains org: This confuses organ systems with a single cell.

activities.explanation: The skin tissue has similar cells sharing work, which shows division of labour.

lessons.title: Meristematic Tissues and Plant Growth

activities.prompt: What do tiny plant cells do to help a plant grow?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Plants Grow
activities.body: Meristematic tissue is made from actively dividing cells. Roots grow from their tips, where cells divide continuously. Plants also have growth zones at shoot tips. The apical meristem is growth tissue for length. Actively dividing cells in a ring increase a stem's thickness. This growth tissue is called the lateral meristem. The intercalary meristem lies at the lower end of an internode. Differentiation changes meristematic tissue into specialised permanent tissue.
keyPoints: Actively dividing cells form meristematic tissue.
Root tips and shoot tips have growth zones.
Differentiation produces specialised permanent tissue.
activities.explanation: These tissues help plants grow in length and thickness.

activities.prompt: A gardener sees a root getting longer and a stem getting thicker. Why did both changes happen?
steps: Actively dividing root-tip cells form meristematic tissue and make roots longer.
The apical meristem supports length growth because its cells keep dividing.
A dividing ring is lateral meristem, and it increases stem girth.
Thus, different meristematic tissues explain both length growth and girth growth.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What is meristematic tissue?
options: Actively dividing cells
Stopped dividing cells
Specialised permanent tissue
Non-dividing stem cells
activities.explanation: Meristematic tissue forms from actively dividing cells. These cells help a plant grow.

activities.prompt: Roots grow only from their tips.
activities.explanation: Root-tip cells divide continuously, helping roots grow.

activities.prompt: Where is the intercalary meristem located?
options: At an internode's base
At a root tip
In a stem ring
At a shoot tip
activities.explanation: The intercalary meristem is located at the base of an internode.

activities.prompt: Actively dividing cells arranged in a ______ increase a stem's girth.
activities.hint: Think of the shape formed by these cells.
activities.explanation: A ring of actively dividing cells increases a stem's girth.

activities.prompt: Match each growth tissue with its place or role.
activities.explanation: Each tissue has a special place or role in plant growth.

activities.prompt: What happens to meristematic tissue during differentiation?
options: Becomes specialised permanent tissue
Forms a ring around a stem
Grows at a shoot tip
Turns into root-tip cells
activities.explanation: Differentiation turns meristematic tissue into specialised permanent tissue.

activities.prompt: The lateral meristem is located at the tip of each root.
activities.explanation: Root-tip cells divide continuously. The lateral meristem increases a stem's girth.

activities.prompt: Put this growth change in order.
activities.explanation: Differentiation turns meristematic tissue into specialised permanent tissue.

activities.prompt: Roots grow only from their tips. A gardener sees one getting longer. What cell activity causes this?
options: Cells divide continuously there
Stem cells divide in a ring
Tip cells change into permanent tissue
Root-tip cells remain still

why.Stem cells divide in a ring: This confuses root growth with the ring that increases stem girth.
why.Tip cells change into permanent tissue: This confuses cell division with differentiation into permanent tissue.
why.Root-tip cells remain still: This confuses active cell division with cells that do not divide.

activities.explanation: Root-tip cells divide continuously, so they make the root longer.

lessons.sceneCaption: A stained onion root tip squash showing all stages of mitosis: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, and telophase.

lessons.title: Protective and Supporting Plant Tissues

activities.prompt: What hidden helpers protect, support, and feed plants as they grow?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Inside Plant Tissues
activities.body: A complex permanent tissue contains more than one type of cell. The epidermis forms the outermost layer of the plant body. Stomata are pores in the epidermis of leaves. Root hairs increase the surface area for absorbing water and minerals. Parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma support plants. Parenchyma stores food. Collenchyma has living cells with unevenly thickened corners. Sclerenchyma has thick walls because lignin is deposited in them.
keyPoints: Epidermis forms the outermost layer.
Stomata are pores in leaf epidermis.
Parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma support plants.
activities.explanation: Epidermis forms the outside layer. Supporting tissues differ in their cell-wall features.

activities.prompt: An aquatic plant contains thin-walled parenchyma and air spaces. What helps it float?
steps: Parenchyma contains living cells with thin walls.
Specialised parenchyma forms air spaces inside aquatic plants.
The air spaces help the plant float, so they explain its floating.
Therefore, specialised parenchyma helps this aquatic plant float.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Outside Layer
activities.prompt: Which tissue forms the outermost layer of the plant body?
options: Epidermis
Parenchyma
Collenchyma
Sclerenchyma
activities.explanation: The epidermis forms the outermost layer of the plant body.

activities.title: Root Hair Job
activities.prompt: Root hairs increase the surface area for absorbing water and ______.
activities.hint: Plants need this from soil, just as they need water.
activities.explanation: Root hairs increase the surface area for absorbing water and minerals.

activities.title: Tissue Features
activities.prompt: Match each supporting tissue to its cell-wall feature.
pairs: Living cells with unevenly thickened corners
activities.explanation: Parenchyma has thin walls. Collenchyma has unevenly thickened corners. Sclerenchyma has lignin deposits in thick walls.

activities.title: Food Storage
activities.prompt: What does parenchyma do?
options: Absorbs water
Forms pores
Stores food
Deposits lignin
activities.explanation: Parenchyma contains living cells with thin walls. It stores food.

activities.title: Floating Help
activities.prompt: What helps aquatic plants float?
options: Air spaces
Uneven corners
Thin cell walls
Lignin deposits
activities.explanation: Specialised parenchyma forms air spaces that help aquatic plants float.

activities.title: Check the Features
activities.prompt: Which statement about supporting tissues is correct?
options: Collenchyma has thin walls, and parenchyma has uneven corners.
Parenchyma has lignin walls, and collenchyma has thin walls.
Sclerenchyma has thin walls, and collenchyma has uneven corners.
Parenchyma has thin walls, and collenchyma has uneven corners.
activities.explanation: Parenchyma has living cells with thin walls. Collenchyma has living cells with unevenly thickened corners.

activities.prompt: After a plant is moved, some tiny root hairs break off. What will likely happen next?
options: The plant will have less area for absorbing water and minerals.
The plant will have more area for absorbing water and minerals.
The plant will float better because of new specialised air spaces.
Broken root hairs will gain thicker walls because of lignin.

why.The plant will have more area for absorb: More root hairs would increase, not decrease, the absorbing area.
why.The plant will float better because of n: This mistake confuses floating air spaces with root-hair absorption.
why.Broken root hairs will gain thicker wall: This mistake confuses lignin deposition in sclerenchyma with root-hair repair.

activities.explanation: Fewer root hairs mean less surface area for absorbing water and minerals.

activities.prompt: A cut plant part shows several kinds of cells together. What can the student conclude?
options: The student has found a permanent tissue with one cell type.
The student has found only the plant's outer epidermis.
The student has found a complex permanent tissue.
The student has found only thin-walled living cells.

why.The student has found a permanent tissue: This mistake ignores the several kinds of cells observed in the cut.
why.The student has found only the plant's o: This mistake confuses a tissue's position with its cell types.
why.The student has found only thin-walled l: Thin walls describe parenchyma, but other cell types may also be present.

activities.explanation: More than one cell type means the tissue is complex permanent tissue.

activities.prompt: A leaf's outermost layer has tiny pores in it. What does this observation show?
options: These tiny pores are root hairs in the epidermis.
These tiny pores are stomata in the epidermis.
These tiny pores are air spaces in parenchyma.
These tiny pores are lignin deposits in sclerenchyma.

why.These tiny pores are root hairs in the e: Root hairs increase absorption, and they are not leaf pores.
why.These tiny pores are air spaces in paren: Air spaces occur inside specialised parenchyma, not in the leaf surface.
why.These tiny pores are lignin deposits in: Lignin thickens sclerenchyma walls, but it does not form pores.

activities.explanation: Stomata are pores in the leaf epidermis, which is its outermost layer.

activities.prompt: A plant section shows living cells with unevenly thickened corners. Another section shows thick lignin walls. What can we say?
options: These are parenchyma and epidermis, both supporting tissues.
These are collenchyma and parenchyma, both supporting tissues.
These are epidermis and sclerenchyma, both supporting tissues.
These are collenchyma and sclerenchyma, both supporting tissues.

why.These are parenchyma and epidermis, both: Parenchyma has thin walls, while the epidermis forms the outermost layer.
why.These are collenchyma and parenchyma, bo: Both are supporting tissues, but lignin-thick walls rule out parenchyma.
why.These are epidermis and sclerenchyma, bo: This mistake treats the epidermis as supporting and misses uneven corners.

activities.explanation: Uneven corners show collenchyma; lignin-thick walls show sclerenchyma, both supporting tissues.

activities.prompt: A student compares green and pale parts of a plant. Both contain parenchyma. Where can photosynthesis happen?
options: In the pale part, because its parenchyma can photosynthesise.
In the green part, because its parenchyma can photosynthesise.
In both parts, because every parenchyma cell can photosynthesise.
In neither part, because parenchyma only stores food.

why.In the pale part, because its parenchyma: The pale part is not green, so photosynthesis is not supported there.
why.In both parts, because every parenchyma: This mistake ignores that photosynthesis is allowed in green plant parts.
why.In neither part, because parenchyma only: This mistake ignores that green parenchyma can also photosynthesise.

activities.explanation: Parenchyma can photosynthesise in green plant parts, such as the green part.

lessons.title: Conducting Tissues and Tissue Systems

activities.prompt: How do plants move water, food, and nutrients around their bodies?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Plant tissues at work
activities.body: Xylem and phloem are specialised conducting tissues. Together, they form complex permanent tissues. Xylem also provides strength to the plant. Phloem is mostly made of living cells. Its sieve tubes carry food from leaves to other plant parts. Companion cells monitor sugar loading and unloading in sieve tubes. Plant tissues are organised into three tissue systems. These include dermal, ground, and vascular tissue systems.
keyPoints: Xylem and phloem conduct materials in plants.
Xylem provides strength, while phloem contains mostly living cells.
Dermal, ground, and vascular systems organise plant tissues.
activities.explanation: These tissues help plants transport materials and grow strongly.

activities.prompt: How does a plant carry food, gain strength, and stay covered?
steps: Xylem and phloem are specialised conducting tissues, so they help conduct materials.
Xylem also gives strength, so it helps support the plant.
Sieve tubes carry food from leaves to other parts, while companion cells monitor sugars.
The dermal system covers the outside, while ground tissue forms the main body.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which pair are specialised conducting tissues?
options: Xylem and phloem
Ground and dermal
Vascular and dermal
Dermal and ground
activities.explanation: Xylem and phloem are the specialised conducting tissues.

activities.prompt: Xylem and ______ together form complex permanent tissues.
activities.hint: This tissue is mostly made up of living cells.
activities.explanation: Xylem and phloem together form complex permanent tissues.

activities.prompt: Which tissue system forms the main body of a plant?
options: Ground tissue system
Dermal tissue system
Vascular tissue system
Complex permanent tissues
activities.explanation: The ground tissue system forms the main body of a plant.

activities.prompt: Match each tissue system with its role or contents.
activities.explanation: Each tissue system has a clear role in the plant.

activities.prompt: What do companion cells monitor?
options: Loading and unloading sugars
Transporting food between leaves
Providing strength to plants
Forming the outer covering
activities.explanation: Companion cells monitor sugar loading and unloading in sieve tubes.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in order for food movement through sieve tubes.
items: Sugars are loaded in sieve tubes
Sieve tubes transport food from leaves
Sugars are unloaded in sieve tubes
activities.explanation: Food moves through sieve tubes, while companion cells monitor sugar loading and unloading.

activities.prompt: Sieve tubes in a leaf are blocked. What is most likely to happen?
options: Less food reaches other parts of the plant.
More food reaches other parts of the plant.
Sieve tubes carry food in the opposite direction.
Companion cells become the plant's outer covering.

why.More food reaches other parts of the pla: Blocking them should reduce, not increase, food transport.
why.Sieve tubes carry food in the opposite d: Blocking a tube does not reverse its food-carrying direction.
why.Companion cells become the plant's outer: This mistake confuses sugar monitoring with forming an outer covering.

activities.explanation: Sieve tubes normally carry food from leaves to other plant parts.

activities.prompt: Which comparison best tests whether xylem gives strength to plants?
options: Compare two plants differing only in having xylem.
Compare two plants differing only in having phloem.
Compare xylem parenchyma cells with sieve tube cells.
Compare xylem cells with ground tissue cells.

why.Compare two plants differing only in hav: This tests phloem, but the strength belongs to xylem.
why.Compare xylem parenchyma cells with siev: This compares cell parts instead of plants with and without xylem.
why.Compare xylem cells with ground tissue c: This compares two tissues instead of testing the presence of xylem.

activities.explanation: This changes xylem while keeping other plant features the same.

activities.prompt: Sugars are not loaded or unloaded properly. Which cells are directly involved?
options: Companion cells
Xylem parenchyma cells
Sieve tube cells
Ground tissue cells

why.Xylem parenchyma cells: This mistake confuses a living xylem part with sugar monitoring.
why.Sieve tube cells: Sieve tubes carry food, while companion cells monitor sugar loading.
why.Ground tissue cells: This mistake confuses main-body tissue with sugar monitoring.

activities.explanation: Companion cells monitor sugar loading and unloading in sieve tubes.

lessons.title: Animal Tissues and Their Functions

activities.prompt: What helps protect your body and keep its organs working smoothly?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Different tissues have different jobs
activities.body: Epithelial tissue covers the body and lines organs such as the mouth and lungs. Its cells are closely packed. Blood and bone are connective tissues, but blood has a soft watery matrix and bone has a hard rigid one. Skeletal muscles make voluntary movements. Smooth muscles support slow, continuous movements like digestion. Cardiac muscles occur only in the heart. Nervous tissue forms the body's control and coordination network.
keyPoints: Epithelial tissue covers the body and lines internal organs.
Blood and bone are connective tissues with different matrices.
Different muscles make different kinds of movements.
activities.explanation: Learning these roles helps you identify each tissue.

activities.prompt: A child compares the body's outer covering with the lining inside the mouth. Why can both be made of closely packed epithelial cells?
steps: Both the outer covering and the mouth lining use epithelial tissue.
This fits because epithelial tissue covers the outside and lines organs.
Epithelial cells are closely packed, so very little space appears between them.
Therefore, both places have continuous layers with almost no space between cells.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The body's outer covering
activities.prompt: Which tissue forms the body's outer covering?
options: Connective tissue
Nervous tissue
Muscle tissue
Epithelial tissue
activities.explanation: Epithelial tissue forms the outer covering of the body.

activities.title: An organ lined by epithelial tissue
activities.prompt: Which of these is an internal organ lined by epithelial tissue?
options: Mouth
Blood
Bone
Haemoglobin
activities.explanation: Epithelial tissue lines internal organs such as the mouth and lungs.

activities.title: Two connective tissues
activities.prompt: Blood and ______ are connective tissues.
activities.hint: This tissue has a hard, rigid matrix.
activities.explanation: Both blood and bone are connective tissues.

activities.title: Match each tissue to its role
activities.prompt: Match each tissue or muscle to its correct feature.
activities.explanation: Each tissue and muscle has the feature shown beside it.

activities.title: Blood's red colour
activities.prompt: What gives blood its red colour?
options: Bone matrix
Cardiac muscle
Haemoglobin
Nervous tissue
activities.explanation: Haemoglobin is an iron-rich protein that gives blood its red colour.

activities.title: A muscle found in one place
activities.prompt: Which muscle type is found only in the heart?
options: Cardiac muscles
Skeletal muscles
Smooth muscles
Epithelial tissue
activities.explanation: Cardiac muscles are found only in the heart.

activities.prompt: Epithelial cells have very little space between them. What pattern should a microscope show?
options: Many cells with narrow spaces between them
Many cells with wide empty spaces between them
Few cells spread far apart from each other
Scattered cells with no close-packed pattern

why.Many cells with wide empty spaces betwee: This wrongly treats closely packed cells as widely separated cells.
why.Few cells spread far apart from each oth: This wrongly assumes epithelial tissue contains only a few scattered cells.
why.Scattered cells with no close-packed pat: This wrongly ignores the close-packed pattern of epithelial cells.

activities.explanation: This is right because epithelial cells are closely packed together.

activities.prompt: Blood has a soft watery matrix, while bone has a hard rigid matrix. What difference should a fair test find?
options: The blood sample changes shape; the bone sample does not.
The bone sample keeps its shape; the blood sample does not.
Both samples keep their shape because both are tissues.
Both samples change shape because both have watery matrices.

why.The blood sample changes shape; the bone: This reverses the difference between soft blood and rigid bone.
why.Both samples keep their shape because bo: This wrongly assumes that being a tissue always makes a sample rigid.
why.Both samples change shape because both h: This wrongly gives blood's watery matrix to bone.

activities.explanation: This is right because hard rigid bone keeps its shape, unlike soft blood.

activities.prompt: Haemoglobin is an iron-rich protein that gives blood its red colour. What change should follow if it is removed?
options: The blood should lose its red colour.
The blood should become harder and more rigid.
The blood should stop lining internal organs.
The blood should take over voluntary movements.

why.The blood should become harder and more: This confuses blood with bone's hard rigid matrix.
why.The blood should stop lining internal or: This confuses blood with epithelial tissue's lining role.
why.The blood should take over voluntary mov: This confuses blood with skeletal muscle's voluntary action.

activities.explanation: This is right because haemoglobin gives blood its red colour.

activities.prompt: A student says cardiac muscle helps digestion by moving food slowly. Why is this claim mistaken?
options: Cardiac muscle is found only in the heart.
Cardiac muscle forms the body's control network.
Cardiac muscle lines the mouth and the lungs.
Cardiac muscle is the hard matrix inside bone.

why.Cardiac muscle forms the body's control: This confuses cardiac muscle with nervous tissue.
why.Cardiac muscle lines the mouth and the l: This confuses cardiac muscle with epithelial tissue.
why.Cardiac muscle is the hard matrix inside: This confuses cardiac muscle with bone's hard rigid matrix.

activities.explanation: This is right because cardiac muscle is found only in the heart, not digestion.

lessons.title: Muscles, Joints, Skeleton and Totipotency

activities.prompt: How do our bones, muscles, and joints work together to move us?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Your Musculoskeletal System Works
activities.body: Your musculoskeletal system has working parts. Bones, muscles, joints, cartilage, tendons and ligaments work together. They help you stand, move and maintain posture. A contracting muscle pulls on a bone through its tendon. Joints join bones. The shoulder has a ball and socket joint, while the elbow has a hinge joint. Cartilage discs cushion vertebrae, and fixed joints keep skull bones still.
keyPoints: The system helps you stand, move and maintain posture.
Muscles pull bones through tendons.
Different joints connect bones in different ways.
activities.explanation: The parts work together to support your body and help you move.

activities.prompt: Why does your head turn while your skull bones stay still?
steps: Your skull connects to the backbone through a pivot joint.
This pivot lets your head move against the backbone.
Fixed joints keep the separate bones of your skull still.
So your head moves at the pivot, while the skull bones stay still.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: A contracting muscle pulls on a bone through which part?
options: tendon
ligament
joint
cartilage
activities.explanation: A contracting muscle pulls on a bone through its tendon.

activities.prompt: A joint is a junction between two or more bones.
activities.explanation: A joint is the junction where two or more bones meet.

activities.prompt: The elbow contains a ______ joint.
activities.hint: Think about the joint found in the elbow.
activities.explanation: The elbow contains a hinge joint.

activities.prompt: Which joint is found in the shoulder?
options: ball and socket joint
hinge joint
pivot joint
fixed joint
activities.explanation: The shoulder contains a ball and socket joint.

activities.prompt: Match each body part with its joint or structure.
activities.explanation: The skull and backbone use a pivot joint. Fixed joints keep skull bones still, and ribs form the rib cage.

activities.prompt: Put the muscle-and-bone steps in order.
items: The tendon pulls on a bone
activities.explanation: The muscle contracts first. Its tendon then pulls on the bone.

activities.prompt: A contracting muscle pulls on a bone. Which path shows how the pull travels?
options: Muscle to tendon, then tendon to bone.
Muscle to joint, then joint to bone.
Bone to cartilage, then cartilage to muscle.
Bone to ligament, then ligament to muscle.

This puts the joint in the pull path, but the joint joins bones.
why.Bone to cartilage, then cartilage to mus: This confuses the cushioning discs with the muscle's pull.
why.Bone to ligament, then ligament to muscl: This confuses a ligament with the tendon carrying the pull.

activities.explanation: The muscle's contraction passes through the tendon to pull the bone.

activities.prompt: The elbow has a hinge joint. The shoulder has a ball and socket joint. A child moves only the lower arm. Which joint should move?
options: The shoulder socket should move, while the elbow stays still.
Neither joint should move as the lower arm moves.
The elbow hinge should move, while the shoulder stays still.
Both joints should move equally at the same time.

why.The shoulder socket should move, while t: This links lower-arm movement to the shoulder's ball and socket joint.
why.Neither joint should move as the lower a: This wrongly treats the lower arm as unable to move at the elbow.
why.Both joints should move equally at the s: This wrongly assumes that lower-arm movement must move both joints.

activities.explanation: The elbow's hinge joint is where the lower arm bends.

activities.prompt: The skull connects to the backbone by a pivot joint. Fixed joints keep the skull bones still. What moves when a child turns their head?
options: The ribs moving through the shoulder joint.
One skull bone sliding past another skull bone.
Two fixed skull bones moving farther apart.
The skull moving at its pivot with the backbone.

why.The ribs moving through the shoulder joi: This assigns the work to the shoulder joint instead of the pivot joint.
why.One skull bone sliding past another skul: This confuses the pivot connection with movement between skull bones.
why.Two fixed skull bones moving farther apa: This ignores that fixed joints keep the skull bones from moving.

activities.explanation: The skull moves against the backbone at the pivot connection.

activities.prompt: The skull joins the backbone through a pivot joint. Fixed joints keep the skull bones still. A child says the pivot moves the skull bones. Which correction is fair?
options: The pivot makes every fixed joint in the skull bend freely.
The fixed joints allow the skull bones to slide past each other.
The pivot moves the skull against the backbone, not between skull bones.
The pivot locks each skull bone tightly to its neighbour.

why.The pivot makes every fixed joint in the: This confuses the pivot connection with movement between the skull bones.
why.The fixed joints allow the skull bones t: This reverses the role of fixed joints, which keep skull bones still.
why.The pivot locks each skull bone tightly: This mistakes the pivot connection for fixed joints between skull bones.

activities.explanation: The pivot joins the skull to the backbone, while fixed joints keep skull bones still.

activities.prompt: A child makes an arm model with a strong bone frame. The string acts as a tendon. It joins a muscle piece to a bone piece. Which test best shows a lift?
options: Hold the frame steady; push the bone through the tendon.
Turn the frame into a joint and pull the tendon.
Break the frame; pull the muscle away from the bone.
Hold the frame steady; contract the muscle to pull the bone.

why.Hold the frame steady; push the bone thr: This reverses the pull direction between the muscle and bone.
why.Turn the frame into a joint and pull the: This confuses the tendon with a joint between bones.
why.Break the frame; pull the muscle away fr: This confuses a strong framework with breaking it during a lift.

activities.explanation: Contracting the muscle makes the tendon pull the bone, as shown.
