activities.context: A student compares organisms during a lesson. One uses a single cell for every function of life. In another, repeated division produces cells that form skin, muscles, bones, nerves and organs. Similar cells work together as tissues, different organs form organ systems, and these systems make the organism. Most plants stay fixed and need support; cell walls give rigidity and strength, while animal cells can change shape because they lack a rigid cell wall.
activities.prompt: If work in the second organism were divided more effectively among its tissues, what change would be expected?
options: The organism would become more efficient in carrying out its work.
The organism would lose efficiency because its tissues could no longer work together.
Only one tissue would need to carry out every body function.
The organism would stop forming organ systems because its work would be shared.

why.The organism would lose efficiency becau: Sharing work can improve efficiency rather than stop cooperation.
why.Only one tissue would need to carry out: Concentrating every function in one tissue is the opposite of effective division of labour.
why.The organism would stop forming organ sy: Sharing work does not prevent organs from forming organ systems.

activities.explanation: Division of labour increases the body's efficiency.

activities.context: A student compares organisms during a lesson. One uses a single cell for every function of life. In another, repeated division produces cells that form skin, muscles, bones, nerves and organs. Similar cells work together as tissues, different organs form organ systems, and these systems make the organism. Most plants stay fixed and need support; cell walls give rigidity and strength, while animal cells can change shape because they lack a rigid cell wall.
activities.prompt: If the single cell of a unicellular organism could no longer perform every life function, what would follow?
options: At least one life function could no longer be carried out by that cell.
All life functions would automatically move into newly formed organ systems.
Nothing would change because one cell always handles every function.
Repeated division would immediately create tissues to perform the missing work.

why.All life functions would automatically m: Organ systems do not automatically form when a function is lost.
why.Nothing would change because one cell al: The changed ability means that the cell could no longer handle every function.
why.Repeated division would immediately crea: Repeated division does not guarantee that new cells will perform the missing work.

activities.explanation: The organism depends on one cell for all its life functions.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A tissue is a group of similar cells that works together.
Reason (R): Cells with similar structures and functions group together to form a tissue.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly explains the stated structure and working of a tissue.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Plant tissues help plants use solar energy to make food components.
Reason (R): Plant tissues move the plant from one place to another.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is true, but the reason is false because most plants stay fixed in one place.

activities.prompt: Explain how a unicellular organism is organised differently from an organism made of many cells.
activities.answer: A unicellular organism uses one cell for all the functions of life. In an organism made of many cells, one cell divides repeatedly and produces many cells. These cells form skin, muscles, bones, nerves and organs. Cells with similar structures and functions group together as tissues. Different organs form organ systems, and organ systems form the organism. The key difference is that the first organisation keeps all life functions in one cell, while the other divides work among cells, tissues, organs and organ systems.
points: A unicellular organism uses one cell for all life functions.
Repeated division produces many cells that form body structures.
Similar cells form tissues.
Organs form organ systems, and organ systems form the organism.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A gardener is examining a plant in a school garden. The gardener notices growth zones at the tips of its roots and shoots, a ring of actively dividing cells around the stem, and tissue at the base of an internode. The gardener wonders why these regions differ and what would happen if some of their dividing cells stopped dividing or began to specialise.
activities.prompt: If the cells at the root tips stopped dividing continuously, what would happen next?
options: The root would stop growing longer.
The root would begin growing thicker.
The shoot would stop growing longer.
The root tip would change into permanent tissue.

This confuses growth in length with growth in girth.
The change concerns root-tip cells, not the shoot.
why.The root tip would change into permanent: This confuses differentiation with a停止 in cell division.

activities.explanation: Roots grow only from their tips, where continuous cell division supports growth.

activities.context: A gardener is examining a plant in a school garden. The gardener notices growth zones at the tips of its roots and shoots, a ring of actively dividing cells around the stem, and tissue at the base of an internode. The gardener wonders why these regions differ and what would happen if some of their dividing cells stopped dividing or began to specialise.
activities.prompt: If the cells at the base of an internode begin to specialise, what should the gardener expect next?
options: They would change into specialised permanent tissue.
They would remain actively dividing and stay meristematic.
The stem's girth would increase.
The root would grow longer from its tip.

why.They would remain actively dividing and: The cells are beginning to specialise rather than remain actively dividing.
This is the role of the lateral meristem in the stem.
This is growth at the root tip, not a result of differentiation at an internode.

activities.explanation: Differentiation turns meristematic tissue into specialised permanent tissue.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Actively dividing cells arranged in a ring increase a stem's girth.
Reason (R): The lateral meristem increases a stem's girth.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly identifies the tissue responsible for the increase in girth.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The lateral meristem is located at the base of an internode.
Reason (R): The intercalary meristem is located at the base of an internode.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason is true for the intercalary meristem, but the assertion incorrectly gives that location to the lateral meristem.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between growth in length and growth in girth?
activities.answer: The apical meristem and lateral meristem both involve actively dividing cells, but they produce different kinds of growth. The apical meristem helps a plant grow in length, and plants have growth zones at the tips of their roots and shoots. Since roots grow only from their tips, continuously dividing cells at root tips support root lengthening. By contrast, actively dividing cells arranged in a ring increase a stem's girth. The tissue responsible for this is called lateral meristem.
points: Growth in length is associated with the apical meristem.
Roots and shoots have growth zones at their tips.
A ring of dividing cells increases girth.
Lateral meristem is responsible for increased girth.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A gardener observes an aquatic plant with specialised parenchyma forming air spaces that help its leaves float. Another plant has root hairs that increase the area available for absorbing water and minerals. When the gardener examines the leaves, small pores are visible in their outer covering. The gardener also notes that the inner tissue contains living cells with thin walls, some of which store food, while the outermost layer covers the plant body.
activities.prompt: If the specialised parenchyma stopped forming air spaces, what would most likely happen to the aquatic plant in the case?
options: It would be less able to float.
It would gain a larger area for absorbing minerals through its root hairs.
The pores in its leaf epidermis would disappear.
The thin walls of its parenchyma would become thick walls.

why.It would gain a larger area for absorbin: Air spaces do not increase the area provided by root hairs.
why.The pores in its leaf epidermis would di: A change in parenchyma would not remove stomata from leaves.
why.The thin walls of its parenchyma would b: A change in air-space formation would not make thin walls thick.

activities.explanation: Air spaces help aquatic plants float.

activities.context: A gardener observes an aquatic plant with specialised parenchyma forming air spaces that help its leaves float. Another plant has root hairs that increase the area available for absorbing water and minerals. When the gardener examines the leaves, small pores are visible in their outer covering. The gardener also notes that the inner tissue contains living cells with thin walls, some of which store food, while the outermost layer covers the plant body.
activities.prompt: To help the second plant absorb more water and minerals, what change should the gardener make?
options: Increase the number of stomata in its leaves.
Form more air spaces in its specialised parenchyma.
Grow more root hairs on its roots.
Add more lignin to the walls of its sclerenchyma.

why.Increase the number of stomata in its le: Stomata are pores and are not described as increasing absorption.
why.Form more air spaces in its specialised: Air spaces help aquatic plants float.
why.Add more lignin to the walls of its scle: Lignin makes sclerenchyma walls thick but does not increase root-hair surface area.

activities.explanation: Root hairs increase the surface area for absorbing water and minerals.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Root hairs increase the surface area for absorbing water and minerals.
Reason (R): A larger surface area allows more water and minerals to be absorbed.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly explains how root hairs help in absorption.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Parenchyma can perform photosynthesis in green plant parts.
Reason (R): Parenchyma stores food.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but storing food does not explain the ability to perform photosynthesis.

activities.prompt: Explain how parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma differ.
activities.answer: Parenchyma is made of living cells with thin walls. It stores food and can perform photosynthesis in green plant parts. Specialised parenchyma also forms air spaces that help aquatic plants float. Collenchyma has living cells, but their corners are unevenly thickened. Sclerenchyma cells have thick walls because lignin is deposited in them. Thus, the tissues differ in wall structure and in the functions described.
points: Parenchyma has living cells with thin walls.
Parenchyma stores food and may perform photosynthesis.
Collenchyma has unevenly thickened corners.
Sclerenchyma has thick walls containing deposited lignin.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student is examining a young plant in the school garden. The student notes that xylem and phloem are conducting tissues found together as complex permanent tissues. The outer covering forms one tissue system, while the main body forms another. The student also follows food moving from the leaves through sieve tubes. If sugar movement through these tubes stops, the student must investigate which tissue system and which living cells help control sugar loading and unloading.
activities.prompt: Sugar movement through the plant's sieve tubes has stopped. Which part should the student investigate first?
options: Companion cells
Xylem parenchyma
Sieve tubes
The dermal tissue system

why.Xylem parenchyma: This is xylem's only living component, but it is not identified as controlling sugar movement.
why.Sieve tubes: These tubes transport food, but they do not monitor sugar loading and unloading.
why.The dermal tissue system: This system forms the outer covering rather than controlling sugar movement.

activities.explanation: These cells directly monitor sugar loading and unloading in sieve tubes.

activities.context: A student is examining a young plant in the school garden. The student notes that xylem and phloem are conducting tissues found together as complex permanent tissues. The outer covering forms one tissue system, while the main body forms another. The student also follows food moving from the leaves through sieve tubes. If sugar movement through these tubes stops, the student must investigate which tissue system and which living cells help control sugar loading and unloading.
activities.prompt: The student wants to select the two tissues that jointly form complex permanent tissues. Which choice is correct?
options: The two specialised conducting tissues
Sieve tubes and companion cells
Xylem parenchyma and dermal tissue
Phloem and the ground-tissue system

why.Sieve tubes and companion cells: The passage does not identify these two parts as complex permanent tissues.
why.Xylem parenchyma and dermal tissue: Xylem parenchyma is a component of xylem, and dermal tissue is not one of the pair.
why.Phloem and the ground-tissue system: Phloem is one of the pair, but the ground-tissue system is not.

activities.explanation: Xylem and phloem are the specialised conducting tissues that form this pair.

activities.context: At school, a student learns that the body’s outer covering is made of epithelial tissue. The student also sees that epithelial tissue lines internal organs such as the mouth and lungs. A teacher explains that these cells are closely packed, with very little space between them. The student compares blood and bone and learns that both are connective tissues, although blood has a soft watery matrix and bone has a hard rigid matrix. The lesson also notes that cardiac muscle is found only in the heart.
activities.prompt: If the student has to explain why there is very little space between the cells lining the mouth, which response is correct?
options: Because these are epithelial cells, which are closely packed.
Because these are bone cells supported by a hard, rigid matrix.
Because these are blood cells surrounded by a soft, watery matrix.
Because these are nervous cells forming a control and coordination network.

why.Because these are bone cells supported b: Bone has a hard, rigid matrix, not closely packed lining cells.
why.Because these are blood cells surrounded: Blood has a soft, watery matrix and is not the mouth lining.
why.Because these are nervous cells forming: Nervous tissue forms the body’s control and coordination network.

activities.explanation: Epithelial cells are closely packed with very little space between them.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Tissues in Action

activities.prompt: Which sentence correctly describes a tissue?
options: Similar cells work together as a tissue.
Different organs make one cell.
One cell performs every life function.
Plant cells make an organism.
activities.explanation: Cells with similar structures and functions group together to form a tissue.

activities.prompt: True or false: Division of labour lowers the body's efficiency.
activities.explanation: Division of labour increases the efficiency of the body.

activities.prompt: True or false: A unicellular organism uses one cell for all functions of life.
activities.explanation: A unicellular organism uses one cell for all the functions of life.

activities.prompt: Match each animal tissue with its role.
pairs: Covers the body and lines internal organs
Is found only in the heart
Forms the control and coordination network
activities.explanation: Each pair joins an animal tissue with its stated role.

activities.prompt: Which tissue increases the thickness of a stem?
options: Apical meristem
Lateral meristem
Intercalary meristem
Epidermis
activities.explanation: Lateral meristem increases a stem's girth, which means thickness.

activities.prompt: Tiny pores in the epidermis of leaves are called ______.
activities.hint: These tiny openings occur in leaves.
activities.explanation: Stomata are pores in the epidermis of leaves.

activities.prompt: Which tissue system contains xylem and phloem?
options: Dermal tissue system
Ground tissue system
Vascular tissue system
Meristematic tissue
activities.explanation: The vascular tissue system contains xylem and phloem.

chapters.title: Describing Motion Around Us
chapters.summary: In this chapter: motion in a straight line and describing position; distance travelled and displacement; average speed, average velocity and average acceleration; graphical representation of motion.

lessons.title: Motion in a Straight Line and Describing Position

activities.prompt: How can we tell exactly where something is as it moves?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Understanding Linear Motion
activities.body: Everything in nature is moving, from huge astronomical bodies to tiny particles. Linear motion means movement along a straight line. It is the simplest kind of motion. A swimming race, a falling ball and a train on a straight track show it. To describe motion, state an object's position at different times. An object is at rest when its position does not change with time.
keyPoints: Linear motion means movement along a straight line.
Motion is described using positions at different times.
An object is at rest when its position does not change with time.
activities.explanation: Linear motion is the simplest kind of motion.

activities.prompt: A child watches a ball roll on a straight path and stop. How can the child describe the motion and decide when it is at rest?
steps: The child chooses a fixed point and records positions at different times.
The ball moves along a straight line, so its motion is linear.
Its position changes while rolling, so it is not at rest.
After stopping, its position stays fixed, so it is at rest.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Describing Position and Time
activities.body: You must choose a fixed point as the reference point. An instant of time is one clock reading. A time interval is the time between two instants. On a straight line, an object can move forward or backward. Describe motion by recording an object's position at different times.
keyPoints: A fixed reference point is needed to describe position.
An instant is one clock reading.
A time interval is the duration between two instants.
activities.explanation: A clear description needs a reference point, positions and times.

activities.prompt: Which phrase defines linear motion?
options: Position staying unchanged
A fixed point for reference
Motion along a straight line
Different clock readings
activities.explanation: Linear motion means that an object moves along a straight line.

activities.prompt: An object is at rest when its position does not change with ______.
activities.hint: Think about what passes as we move from one moment to another.
activities.explanation: Rest means that an object's position does not change with time.

activities.prompt: An object at rest has a position that does not change with time.
activities.explanation: An object is at rest when its position does not change with time.

activities.prompt: Match each idea with its meaning.
activities.explanation: Each pair connects an idea with its meaning from the lesson.

activities.prompt: What must you state to describe an object's motion?
options: A fixed point alone
Its position at different times
A single clock reading
A time interval alone
activities.explanation: You must state an object's position at different times.

activities.prompt: Put these steps for describing motion in order.
items: State its position at a different time
activities.explanation: Choose a fixed point, then state the object's positions at different times.

activities.prompt: A toy starts behind a fixed cup. Later, it is beside the cup. What can we say?
options: The toy stayed at rest because both positions are near the cup.
The toy changed position, so it was not at rest.
The toy moved backward because the fixed cup did not move.
The toy moved forward because the fixed cup did not move.

why.The toy stayed at rest because both posi: Nearby places can still be different positions, so rest is not shown.
why.The toy moved backward because the fixed: A fixed cup does not tell us whether the toy moved backward.
why.The toy moved forward because the fixed: A fixed cup does not tell us whether the toy moved forward.

activities.explanation: Its position changed with time, so it was not at rest.

activities.prompt: A child wants to test whether a toy is at rest. Which method is fair?
options: Compare its position with a fixed point at two times.
Compare its position with a moving toy at two times.
Look at the toy once and decide whether it is still.
Watch the toy beside a moving toy at two times.

why.Compare its position with a moving toy a: A moving reference point can hide a change in the toy's position.
why.Look at the toy once and decide whether: One look cannot show whether position changes with time.
why.Watch the toy beside a moving toy at two: Two moving things can hide a change in the toy's position.

activities.explanation: Rest means unchanged position, and a fixed point makes the test fair.

activities.prompt: A child watches a ball roll beside a fixed tree. Which record best shows its motion?
options: The ball's position beside the tree at one time only.
The ball's position beside the tree at different times.
The ball's position beside a moving bicycle at different times.
The tree's position beside the ball at different times.

why.The ball's position beside the tree at o: One position cannot show whether the ball's position changes.
why.The ball's position beside a moving bicy: A moving bicycle can hide the ball's change in position.
why.The tree's position beside the ball at d: Using the moving ball as the point hides its own movement.

activities.explanation: Motion is described by positions from a fixed point at different times.

activities.prompt: A ball rolls right on a straight path, then returns left. How can this motion be described?
options: Forward along the straight line, then backward along it.
Backward along the straight line, then forward along it.
Forward only, because the ball stays on the straight line.
Backward only, because the ball stays on the straight line.

why.Backward along the straight line, then f: The ball first moves in the chosen forward direction.
why.Forward only, because the ball stays on: A straight path can include both forward and backward movement.
why.Backward only, because the ball stays on: A straight path does not remove the ball's backward movement.

activities.explanation: Reversing on a straight line changes the direction of motion.

lessons.title: Distance Travelled and Displacement

activities.prompt: Why might your ending spot differ from the whole path you travelled?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Two Ways to Describe a Journey
activities.body: Total distance is the full length covered during a journey. Displacement is the net change in position between the start and finish. To describe displacement fully, give its direction and number. The magnitude of displacement means its size: the distance between the start and finish positions. In the athlete's example, total distance is 160 m, but displacement is 40 m in the positive direction.
keyPoints: Total distance is 160 m in the athlete's example.
Displacement is the net change in position.
Displacement needs both direction and a number.
activities.explanation: The athlete travelled farther than her final displacement.

activities.prompt: An athlete travels 160 m. She ends 40 m away in the positive direction. Why are the values different?
steps: The route is 160 m, so the total distance is 160 m.
She ends 40 m away, so her displacement magnitude is 40 m.
The positive direction shows where the net change points.
So the values differ: 160 m travelled, but 40 m forward.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Athlete's Total Distance
activities.prompt: Which measurement was 160 m for the athlete?
options: The total distance
The final displacement
A direction only
A numerical value only
activities.explanation: The athlete travelled a total distance of 160 m.

activities.title: Meaning of Displacement
activities.prompt: Displacement means the whole path covered during a journey.
activities.explanation: Displacement is the net change in position, not the whole path covered.

activities.title: The Common Unit
activities.prompt: The SI unit of distance travelled and displacement is the ______.
activities.hint: This unit is used for both measurements.
activities.explanation: Both distance travelled and displacement use the metre as their SI unit.

activities.title: A Complete Description
activities.prompt: Which gives the athlete's displacement fully?
options: Positive direction
40 m in the positive direction
160 m in the positive direction
activities.explanation: A complete displacement needs both a number and a direction.

activities.title: The Athlete's Journey
activities.prompt: Put the athlete's story in the correct order.
items: Start at the athlete's starting position.
State 40 m in the positive direction.
activities.explanation: The athlete's total distance was 160 m, while her displacement was 40 m.

activities.title: Compare the Measurements
activities.prompt: Which statement is always correct about a journey?
options: The displacement magnitude can be greater than total distance.
The displacement magnitude always equals total distance.
The displacement magnitude cannot be greater than total distance.
Total distance needs a direction to be complete.
activities.explanation: The magnitude of displacement cannot be greater than the total distance travelled.

activities.prompt: An athlete travels 160 m in all. Her final position is 40 m from the start. It is in the positive direction. What is her displacement?
options: It is 40 m in the positive direction.
It is 160 m in the positive direction.
It is 40 m without any direction.
It is 160 m without any direction.

This confuses total distance with final displacement.
This gives the right value but leaves out direction.
This uses total distance and also leaves out direction.

activities.explanation: This matches the athlete’s final displacement and its direction.

activities.prompt: A child walks straight to a shop and never turns back. What will the two magnitudes be?
options: Equal, because the child does not turn back.
Different, because the shop is away.
Equal, because both values use metres.
Different, because displacement needs direction.

This assumes going away always makes the magnitudes differ.
This gives equal magnitudes for the wrong reason.
why.Different, because displacement needs di: This thinks direction changes whether magnitudes are equal.

activities.explanation: Without turning back, distance and displacement magnitude are equal.

activities.prompt: A child walks to a friend’s home, then returns home. What happens?
options: Displacement is zero, but total distance is not.
Distance is zero, but displacement is not.
Both are zero, because the child came home.
Both are equal, because the child came home.

why.Distance is zero, but displacement is no: This reverses which quantity becomes zero at the start.
why.Both are zero, because the child came ho: This ignores the path covered during the round trip.
why.Both are equal, because the child came h: This confuses ending at the start with having no travel.

activities.explanation: Returning to the start leaves no net position change.

activities.prompt: A student says, “My displacement is 40 m.” The direction is missing. Is the description complete?
options: No, because displacement also needs direction.
Yes, because the number gives all details.
Yes, because only distance needs direction.
No, because displacement has no numerical value.

why.Yes, because the number gives all detail: This assumes the number alone describes displacement fully.
why.Yes, because only distance needs directi: This uses the rule for total distance.
why.No, because displacement has no numerica: This wrongly says displacement has no numerical value.

activities.explanation: Displacement needs both its numerical value and its direction.

activities.prompt: The gap between the start and end is 160 m. The whole path is 40 m. Can this happen?
options: No, displacement magnitude cannot exceed total distance.
Yes, because the straight gap is always longer.
Yes, because both values use the same unit.
No, because displacement must always be zero.

why.Yes, because the straight gap is always: This wrongly assumes the straight gap can exceed the path.
why.Yes, because both values use the same un: This confuses equal units with equal magnitudes.
why.No, because displacement must always be: This wrongly believes displacement can exceed the whole path.

activities.explanation: Displacement magnitude cannot be greater than total distance.

lessons.title: Average Speed, Average Velocity and Average Acceleration

activities.prompt: What can a journey tell us about speed, velocity, and acceleration?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Three ways to describe motion
activities.body: Average speed tells you the total distance travelled during a time interval. Divide distance by time to find it. It has a value, but no direction. Average velocity divides the change in position by the time interval. Its direction matches displacement, which means change in position. Average acceleration divides change in velocity by the time interval. When speed increases, it acts in the direction of velocity.
keyPoints: Average speed uses distance and time.
Average velocity uses change in position and time.
Average acceleration uses change in velocity and time.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you tell distance, position and velocity changes apart.

activities.title: Race the cars

tasks.say: Make the two cars cover the same distance.
tasks.then: Same speed for the same time means the same distance.

tasks.say: Make the red car cover 200 m.
tasks.then: Speed x time = distance, so this gives 200 m.

activities.explanation: Distance = speed x time.

activities.prompt: A child walks from home to a shop and returns home. Then the child speeds up along a straight road. How do the three averages describe this?
steps: Average speed divides total distance by time, so it measures all travel.
Average speed has no direction, so it cannot show the journey's direction.
Returning home leaves no displacement direction, so average velocity has none.
The child speeds up while moving forward, so average acceleration acts forward.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Average speed is total distance travelled divided by the time interval.
activities.explanation: Yes. You find average speed by dividing total distance by the time interval.

activities.prompt: The direction of average velocity is the same as the direction of ______.
activities.hint: This means the change in position.
activities.explanation: Average velocity points in the direction of displacement.

activities.prompt: Match each quantity with its meaning.
pairs: Total distance divided by time interval
Change in position divided by time interval
Change in velocity divided by time interval
Change in one quantity with a change in time
activities.explanation: Each rate compares a change in one quantity with a change in time.

activities.prompt: A car covers equal distances in equal time intervals on a straight road. What motion is shown?
options: Uniform straight-line motion
Non-uniform straight-line motion
Straight-line motion with no speed
Straight-line motion with no direction
activities.explanation: Equal distances in equal time intervals show uniform motion in a straight line.

activities.prompt: Average velocity has no direction because it has a numerical value.
activities.explanation: Only average speed has no direction. Average velocity points in the direction of displacement.

activities.prompt: Put the parts of the average acceleration calculation in order.
activities.explanation: Divide the change in velocity by the time interval to find average acceleration.

activities.prompt: Average velocity is the change in position divided by the time interval. Its direction is the same as displacement. A child walks from a gate to a shop and back. What is the direction of the child's average velocity?
options: It has no direction, because the child returns to the gate.
It points toward the shop, because the child went there first.
It points toward the gate, because the child returned there.
It points along the path, because the child walked along it.

why.It points toward the shop, because the c: This confuses the first part of the journey with the final displacement.
why.It points toward the gate, because the c: This mistakes the final destination for the final change in position.
why.It points along the path, because the ch: This confuses the travelled path with the direction of displacement.

activities.explanation: Returning to the gate leaves no displacement direction for average velocity.

activities.prompt: Average acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time interval. When speed increases, average acceleration acts in the direction of velocity. A bicycle moves forward and its speed increases. Which direction does average acceleration act?
options: Forward, in the direction of the bicycle's velocity.
Backward, opposite to the bicycle's velocity.
Sideways, across the bicycle's path.
Nowhere, because average acceleration has no direction.

why.Backward, opposite to the bicycle's velo: This mistake treats an increase in speed like a decrease in speed.
This mistake assumes acceleration turns away from the velocity's direction.
why.Nowhere, because average acceleration ha: This mistake confuses average acceleration with directionless average speed.

activities.explanation: Since speed increases, average acceleration acts along the velocity's direction.

activities.prompt: Average speed has no direction. Average velocity follows displacement. Both use metre per second as their SI unit. A child says both averages have the same direction. Is the child correct?
options: No, because only average velocity has a direction.
No, because only average speed has a direction.
Yes, because both use metre per second.
Yes, because both divide by the time interval.

why.No, because only average speed has a dir: This swaps the roles of average speed and average velocity.
A shared unit does not give either average a direction.
why.Yes, because both divide by the time int: A shared time interval does not make their directions the same.

activities.explanation: Average speed has no direction, while average velocity follows displacement.

lessons.title: Graphical Representation of Motion

activities.prompt: How can a graph reveal what a moving object is doing?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Reading Motion Graphs
activities.body: A graph is a picture that shows how an object moves. It can show position, velocity and acceleration changing with time. These are the quantities that graphs can follow. On a position-time graph, time goes along the X-axis and position along the Y-axis. A straight line shows constant velocity, while a curve shows changing velocity. The slope gives the rate of change. Area under a velocity-time graph gives displacement.
keyPoints: A graph visually represents an object's motion.
Time is on the X-axis, while position is on the Y-axis.
A straight line shows constant velocity, while a curve shows changing velocity.
activities.explanation: These graph features help you read motion clearly.

activities.prompt: A child plots a moving toy's position at different times. The points make a curve. What does the curve tell the child about the toy's motion?
steps: Time goes on the X-axis, so change over time is visible.
Position goes on the Y-axis, so points show the toy's place.
The points are curved, so the child joins them with a curve.
A curved graph shows changing velocity, so the motion is non-uniform.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What does a graph give for an object's motion?
options: A spoken description
A written summary
A visual picture
A numerical formula
activities.explanation: A graph gives a visual representation of an object's motion. Good choice!

activities.prompt: The area under a velocity-time graph gives ______.
activities.hint: This is the result shown by the graph's area.
activities.explanation: The area under a velocity-time graph gives displacement. You found the right term!

activities.prompt: Match each graph with what it shows.
activities.explanation: You matched them well. Straight lines show constant velocity, and curves show changing velocity. The graph area gives displacement.

activities.prompt: What does the slope of a graph give?
options: The size of the axis
The kind of graph
The time displayed
The rate of change
activities.explanation: The slope gives the rate of change of the quantity on the Y-axis. Good thinking!

activities.prompt: Which statement about motion graphs is correct?
options: Curved position-time lines show constant velocity.
Velocity-time slopes give displacement.
Straight position-time lines show constant velocity.
Position-time graphs put time on the Y-axis.
activities.explanation: A straight position-time graph shows motion with constant velocity. You spotted the key rule!

activities.prompt: Put these steps for finding displacement in order.
items: Find the area under the graph.
activities.explanation: First use the graph, then find its area. That area gives displacement.

activities.prompt: A cart and a scooter move on paths. Their position-time graphs are straight lines. The cart's line is steeper. Which vehicle has the greater velocity?
options: The cart has a greater constant velocity.
The cart has a smaller constant velocity.
The cart has a changing velocity.
Both vehicles have equal constant velocities.

why.The cart has a smaller constant velocity: A steeper slope gives a greater rate, not a smaller one.
A straight position-time graph shows constant velocity.
why.Both vehicles have equal constant veloci: Different straight slopes show different rates of position change.

activities.explanation: A steeper slope gives a greater rate of position change.

activities.prompt: A blue velocity-time graph has a greater area than an orange one. What can you compare from the areas?
options: The blue trip has greater displacement.
The blue trip has greater velocity.
The blue trip has greater acceleration.
The blue trip has greater final position.

The area gives displacement, not the velocity at each time.
The area gives displacement, not the acceleration.
why.The blue trip has greater final position: The area gives displacement, not the final position.

activities.explanation: The area under a velocity-time graph gives displacement.

activities.prompt: A child's position-time graph is a straight line. A friend says, "The velocity changes because the position changes." Why is this claim wrong?
options: The position changes while the velocity stays constant.
The position changes while the velocity keeps changing.
The position stays fixed while the velocity changes.
The position stays fixed while the velocity stays constant.

why.The position changes while the velocity: This describes a curved position-time graph instead.
why.The position stays fixed while the veloc: The graph shows that the position changes, so it is not fixed.
The graph shows changing position and constant velocity.

activities.explanation: A straight position-time graph shows motion with constant velocity.

lessons.title: Kinematic Equations for Constant Acceleration

activities.prompt: How can we predict an object’s future motion using just a few measurements?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Equations for changing motion
activities.body: Kinematic equations describe changing motion when acceleration is constant. In this case, the acceleration at every moment equals the average acceleration. The equation v = u + at helps us find velocity at any time. On a velocity-time graph, the area enclosed by the graph gives displacement. The signs of u, v, a and s show the directions of these quantities.
keyPoints: Kinematic equations work for motion with constant acceleration.
The area under a velocity-time graph gives displacement.
The signs of u, v, a and s show directions.
activities.explanation: These equations give a mathematical description of changing motion.

activities.prompt: A scooter starts from rest and speeds up forward steadily. Forward is positive. A child predicts its velocity later.
steps: The scooter starts from rest, so its initial velocity u is zero.
Its steady forward acceleration means a does not change.
Because a is constant, v = u + at gives the velocity at any time.
Thus its forward velocity keeps growing because a stays positive and constant.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which statement about constant acceleration is correct?
options: Every velocity must equal the average velocity.
The acceleration at every moment equals the average acceleration.
The displacement at every moment equals the average displacement.
The time at every moment equals the average time.
activities.explanation: With constant acceleration, the acceleration at every moment equals the average acceleration.

activities.prompt: The equation v = u + at lets us calculate ______ at any time.
activities.hint: This quantity is shown by v.
activities.explanation: The equation v = u + at calculates velocity at any time.

activities.prompt: Match each idea with its correct meaning.
pairs: Acceleration at every moment equals average acceleration
activities.explanation: Each pairing shows an important use or meaning from this lesson.

activities.prompt: What does the area enclosed by a velocity-time graph give?
options: The acceleration
The initial velocity
The displacement
The average time
activities.explanation: Displacement is found from the area enclosed by the velocity-time graph.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in order to find displacement from a velocity-time graph.
items: Locate the area enclosed by the graph.
Use that area to find the displacement.
activities.explanation: The displacement comes from the area enclosed by the velocity-time graph.

activities.prompt: A car's acceleration changes during its journey. Which statement is correct?
options: The equations remain valid for the whole journey.
The equations are valid only while acceleration is constant.
The equations replace the velocity-time graph.
The equations show the enclosed area directly.
activities.explanation: Kinematic equations are valid only when acceleration is constant.

activities.prompt: A cart slows down at a constant rate. How does acceleration compare with average acceleration?
options: The accelerations are equal at every instant.
Instantaneous acceleration is always larger than average acceleration.
Average acceleration is always smaller than instantaneous acceleration.
They differ whenever the cart is slowing down.

why.Instantaneous acceleration is always lar: This assumes equality fails even though acceleration is constant.
why.Average acceleration is always smaller t: This reverses the relationship between average and instantaneous acceleration.
why.They differ whenever the cart is slowing: This assumes slowing down breaks equality, but the acceleration remains constant.

activities.explanation: With constant acceleration, both accelerations are equal at every instant.

activities.prompt: One velocity-time graph lies higher than another, but both have equal width. Which graph has more displacement?
options: The taller graph, because it encloses more area.
The shorter graph, because it encloses less time.
Both graphs, because their widths are equal.
The taller graph, because its acceleration must be greater.

why.The shorter graph, because it encloses l: Equal widths do not mean the shorter graph has more area.
why.Both graphs, because their widths are eq: Area depends on height and width, not width alone.
why.The taller graph, because its accelerati: Greater area does not necessarily mean greater acceleration.

activities.explanation: Displacement comes from area, and the taller graph encloses more.

activities.prompt: A skateboarder moves forward and speeds up. Forward is positive. What are the signs of u, v, a and s?
options: u, v, a and s are all positive.
u is positive, while v, a and s are negative.
u, v and s are positive, while a is negative.
u, a and s are positive, while v is negative.

why.u is positive, while v, a and s are nega: This wrongly treats forward motion and acceleration as negative.
why.u, v and s are positive, while a is nega: This wrongly treats forward acceleration as negative.
why.u, a and s are positive, while v is nega: This wrongly treats the final forward velocity as negative.

activities.explanation: All four quantities point in the chosen positive direction.

activities.prompt: v = u + at is used for motion with constant acceleration. Which scooter can use it throughout its ride?
options: A scooter that speeds up at a steady rate.
A scooter that speeds up at a changing rate.
A scooter that slows down at a changing rate.
A scooter whose speed changes unpredictably.

why.A scooter that speeds up at a changing r: Speeding up at a changing rate means acceleration is not constant.
why.A scooter that slows down at a changing: Changing the slowdown rate means acceleration is not constant.
why.A scooter whose speed changes unpredicta: Unpredictable speed changes mean acceleration is not constant.

activities.explanation: Speeding up steadily means the acceleration stays constant.

lessons.title: Motion in a Plane and Uniform Circular Motion

activities.prompt: What makes a merry-go-round rider feel pushed outward while the ride spins?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Understanding Circular Motion
activities.body: Motion in a plane is two-dimensional motion. In circular motion, distance follows the path around a circle. Displacement is the straight line from start to finish. After one complete revolution, displacement and average velocity are zero. Uniform circular motion keeps speed constant, but changes velocity direction. It is accelerated as direction changes continuously. A tangent touches a circle at one point. Velocity points along that tangent.
keyPoints: Motion in a plane has two dimensions.
Uniform circular motion has constant speed.
Velocity changes direction and points along a tangent.
activities.explanation: Circular motion keeps speed constant while changing the direction of velocity.

activities.prompt: A child rides a merry-go-round at constant speed for one turn. What are the distance, displacement, and average velocity?
steps: The distance is the circumference, because one turn covers the whole circle.
The displacement is zero, because the child finishes at the starting point.
The average velocity is zero, because the complete revolution has zero displacement.
This is uniform circular motion, because the speed stays constant.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Recognising Circular Motion
activities.prompt: A child moves around a circular path at constant speed. What motion is this?
options: uniform circular motion
constant-speed still motion
two-dimensional still motion
straight-line circular motion
activities.explanation: Circular motion with constant speed is called uniform circular motion.

activities.title: Distance Around a Circle
activities.prompt: The distance covered in one complete revolution of a circular path is its ______.
activities.hint: Think of the distance around a circle.
activities.explanation: The distance covered during one complete revolution is the circle's circumference.

activities.title: Matching Motion Ideas
activities.prompt: Match each part with its partner.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows an important idea about motion in a circle.

activities.title: Changing Velocity
activities.prompt: Which statement about velocity in uniform circular motion is correct?
options: Only its direction changes.
Its speed always increases.
Its direction stays fixed.
Its speed always decreases.
activities.explanation: The speed stays constant, but the direction of velocity changes.

activities.title: One Complete Revolution
activities.prompt: Put these steps in the correct order.
items: Start at a point on the circle.
activities.explanation: After one complete revolution, displacement and average velocity are both zero.

activities.title: Results After a Revolution
activities.prompt: After one complete revolution, what are the displacement and average velocity?
options: Both are positive
Both are negative
Both are zero
Both are changing
activities.explanation: The displacement and average velocity are both zero after one complete revolution.

activities.prompt: A rider completes one full circle on a merry-go-round. How do the distance and displacement compare after the ride?
options: The distance is the circumference, but the displacement is zero.
The distance is zero, but the displacement is the circumference.
Both distance and displacement equal the circumference of the circle.
Both distance and displacement equal zero for the whole circle.

why.The distance is zero, but the displaceme: This mistake swaps distance and displacement around the circle.
why.Both distance and displacement equal the: This mistake treats the path length as the straight-line displacement.
why.Both distance and displacement equal zer: This mistake thinks a full journey has no distance.

activities.explanation: This is right because one revolution gives circumference distance and zero displacement.

activities.prompt: A toy car moves around a circular track at constant speed. What changes during its journey?
options: Only the speed changes, because the circular path bends.
Only the direction changes, while the speed stays constant.
Both speed and direction change during every part of the turn.
Neither speed nor direction changes during the circular journey.

why.Only the speed changes, because the circ: This mistake thinks a turning path must change speed.
why.Both speed and direction change during e: This mistake thinks constant-speed circular motion changes both values.
why.Neither speed nor direction changes duri: This mistake thinks staying on a circle keeps velocity unchanged.

activities.explanation: This is right because uniform circular motion keeps speed constant but changes direction.

activities.prompt: A child models a real ride that moves around a circle. What should the model show for uniform circular motion?
options: A circular path with constant speed around it.
A circular path with changing speed around it.
A straight path with constant speed along it.
A circular path with constant direction around it.

why.A circular path with changing speed arou: This mistake allows changing speed, but uniform circular motion needs constant speed.
why.A straight path with constant speed alon: This mistake replaces the circular path with a straight path.
why.A circular path with constant direction: This mistake treats uniform speed as unchanged direction.

activities.explanation: It is right: the idealised model keeps constant speed around a circle.

activities.prompt: A child runs around a circular track at constant speed. Which change shows that this motion is accelerated?
options: The speed changes whenever the circular track bends.
The velocity changes direction continuously around the circle.
The child returns to the starting point after one circle.
The distance around the circular track stays the same.

why.The speed changes whenever the circular: This mistake thinks the track's bend must change the runner's speed.
why.The child returns to the starting point: This mistake confuses returning to the start with acceleration.
why.The distance around the circular track s: This mistake thinks constant path length proves that the motion is accelerated.

activities.explanation: This is right because velocity direction changes continuously in circular motion.

activities.prompt: A child completes one full circle around a park at steady speed. What is the average velocity during that circle?
options: Zero, because one full revolution gives zero displacement.
The circumference, because that is the total distance covered.
The constant speed, because speed stays unchanged around the circle.
The total distance, because the child completes one full circle.

why.The circumference, because that is the t: This mistake gives distance instead of average velocity.
why.The constant speed, because speed stays: This mistake gives speed instead of average velocity.
why.The total distance, because the child co: This mistake gives the total distance instead of average velocity.

activities.explanation: This is right because average velocity is zero over one complete circular revolution.

activities.context: During a swimming race, a swimmer moves along a straight lane from the starting side toward the far side. A coach uses the starting side as the fixed reference point. The swimmer's position is checked at different times to describe the motion. When the swimmer stops and remains in one place, the coach says the swimmer is at rest.
activities.prompt: After reaching the far side, what would happen if the swimmer turned around and returned along the same straight lane?
options: The swimmer would continue linear motion, but would now be moving backward from the earlier direction.
The swimmer's motion would become circular because the direction changed.
The swimmer would be at rest because the direction reversed.
The swimmer would no longer be moving because the position changed.

why.The swimmer's motion would become circul: Movement along a straight line remains linear even when the direction reverses.
why.The swimmer would be at rest because the: Rest means that position does not change with time.
why.The swimmer would no longer be moving be: A change in position with time is motion.

activities.explanation: Reversing direction on the same straight line changes forward to backward, not the kind of motion.

activities.context: During a swimming race, a swimmer moves along a straight lane from the starting side toward the far side. A coach uses the starting side as the fixed reference point. The swimmer's position is checked at different times to describe the motion. When the swimmer stops and remains in one place, the coach says the swimmer is at rest.
activities.prompt: What would happen if the coach chose the far side instead of the starting side as the fixed reference point?
options: Descriptions of position would use a different reference point, while the swimmer's motion would remain linear.
The swimmer would be at rest because the reference point changed.
The swimmer would move backward because the reference point changed.
The swimmer's motion would become circular because the reference point changed.

why.The swimmer would be at rest because the: Rest depends on whether position changes with time, not on the reference point.
why.The swimmer would move backward because: Nothing in the case shows that changing the reference point changes the swimmer's direction.
why.The swimmer's motion would become circul: Choosing another fixed point does not turn a straight path into a circular path.

activities.explanation: Changing the reference point changes the description of position, not the straight path of motion.

activities.context: During a swimming race, a swimmer moves along a straight lane from the starting side toward the far side. A coach uses the starting side as the fixed reference point. The swimmer's position is checked at different times to describe the motion. When the swimmer stops and remains in one place, the coach says the swimmer is at rest.
activities.prompt: How should the time from the swimmer's departure to the swimmer's arrival at the far side be described?
options: The duration between two instants of time.
A single clock reading at one moment.
The position of an object relative to a fixed point.
The direction in which an object moves along a straight line.

A single reading is an instant of time, not the duration between readings.
why.The position of an object relative to a: A fixed point is used to describe position rather than time.
why.The direction in which an object moves a: Forward and backward describe direction rather than duration.

activities.explanation: The departure and arrival readings enclose a duration, so they define a time interval.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The swimmer's travel along the straight lane is linear motion.
Reason (R): The swimmer moves along a straight line.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly explains why the swimmer's motion is linear.

activities.prompt: How can the coach describe the swimmer's motion, position, and state of rest?
activities.answer: To describe the swimmer's motion, the coach states the swimmer's position at different times. Each position is understood with respect to the chosen fixed reference point, in this case the starting side. If the swimmer changes position with time, the swimmer is moving; if the position does not change with time, the swimmer is at rest. The coach also states whether the swimmer moves forward or backward along the straight line.
points: Motion is described by giving position at different times.
A fixed reference point is chosen.
Rest means that position does not change with time.
Movement on a straight line may be forward or backward.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: An athlete moves during an event. By the final instant, her total distance travelled is 160 m. Her final position is 40 m from the starting position in the positive direction. A student records both quantities but initially writes down only 160 m when asked for displacement. The student must then compare distance, displacement and direction before giving the full description.
activities.prompt: Why is the student's record of 160 m not a complete description of the athlete's displacement?
options: It identifies total distance, but the directional part of displacement is absent.
It identifies net position change, but the total-distance figure is absent.
It identifies direction, but the numerical part of displacement is absent.
It identifies displacement completely, but the direction is stated incorrectly as negative.

why.It identifies direction, but the numeric: A complete displacement description needs direction.
why.It identifies displacement completely, b: The missing direction is the positive direction.

activities.explanation: The recorded value is the total distance.

activities.context: An athlete moves during an event. By the final instant, her total distance travelled is 160 m. Her final position is 40 m from the starting position in the positive direction. A student records both quantities but initially writes down only 160 m when asked for displacement. The student must then compare distance, displacement and direction before giving the full description.
activities.prompt: If the athlete retraces part of her route, which rule must still apply to her movement?
options: Her displacement magnitude cannot be greater than her total distance.
Her displacement magnitude must be greater than her total distance.
Her displacement magnitude and total distance must always be equal.
Her displacement magnitude cannot be compared with her total distance.

why.Her displacement magnitude must be great: Being greater would violate the stated rule.
why.Her displacement magnitude and total dis: Equality is not required when the athlete turns back.

activities.explanation: Displacement magnitude cannot exceed total distance.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The athlete's total distance and final displacement magnitude are different.
Reason (R): They must be equal because both are measured in metres.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The example gives 160 m and 40 m, so the statement that they must be equal is false.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The athlete's final displacement is 160 m in the positive direction.
Reason (R): A complete description of displacement requires both direction and numerical value.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The direction requirement is true, but the example's displacement is 40 m in the positive direction.

activities.prompt: Explain why writing 160 m does not fully describe the athlete's displacement.
activities.answer: Distance travelled and displacement are different quantities. The athlete travelled a total distance of 160 m, but her displacement describes her net change in position between the starting and final instants. Its magnitude is 40 m because it is the distance between those two positions. A complete description of displacement must also state a direction, and in this example that direction is positive. Therefore, writing only 160 m gives the total distance rather than the full displacement.
points: Total distance travelled is 160 m.
Displacement describes net change in position.
The displacement magnitude is 40 m.
The positive direction must also be included.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A cyclist rides along a straight road. During each equal time interval, the cyclist covers a different distance, so the amount of ground covered changes even though the time allowed does not. A motion sensor records the cyclist’s position at the start and end. Near the end of the ride, the cyclist moves more slowly and then speeds up again without reversing direction.
activities.prompt: What can be concluded about the cyclist’s motion from the different distances covered in equal time intervals?
options: The cyclist is showing non-uniform motion in a straight line.
The cyclist is showing uniform motion in a straight line.
Average speed cannot be calculated because the distance changes.
Average velocity cannot be calculated because the position change is recorded.

why.The cyclist is showing uniform motion in: This mistake treats different distances in equal time intervals as uniform motion.
why.Average speed cannot be calculated becau: Average speed can be calculated using total distance and the time interval.
why.Average velocity cannot be calculated be: The recorded position change and time interval are enough to calculate average velocity.

activities.explanation: Different distances in equal time intervals show non-uniform motion in a straight line.

activities.context: A cyclist rides along a straight road. During each equal time interval, the cyclist covers a different distance, so the amount of ground covered changes even though the time allowed does not. A motion sensor records the cyclist’s position at the start and end. Near the end of the ride, the cyclist moves more slowly and then speeds up again without reversing direction.
activities.prompt: Suppose the cyclist reverses direction during a later ride and returns partway toward the start. Which comparison is then valid?
options: Average speed has the greater numerical value, and only average velocity has a direction.
Average velocity has the greater numerical value, and only average speed has a direction.
Average speed and average velocity have equal numerical values, and neither has a direction.
Average speed and average velocity have equal numerical values, but average velocity has a direction.

why.Average velocity has the greater numeric: This swaps the definitions and incorrectly gives average speed a direction.
why.Average speed and average velocity have: The average values are not equal after the reversal, and average velocity does have a direction.
The average values are unequal after the reversal, although average velocity has a direction.

activities.explanation: Reversing makes the average values unequal, while average velocity retains the direction of displacement.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A cyclist who covers equal distances in equal time intervals on a straight road shows uniform motion.
Reason (R): This happens because equal distances are covered during each equal time interval on a straight road.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly uses the stated condition for uniform motion in a straight line.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): When a cyclist speeds up, average acceleration acts in the direction of velocity.
Reason (R): Average acceleration becomes zero because the cyclist’s speed is changing.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion follows the stated rule, but the reason falsely claims that average acceleration is zero.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between average speed and average velocity.
activities.answer: Average speed is found by dividing total distance travelled by the time interval. It has a numerical value but no direction. Average velocity is found by dividing the change in position by the time interval, and its direction is the same as displacement. Therefore, average speed describes distance covered per unit time, while average velocity also gives the direction of the displacement. Both have metre per second as their SI unit.
points: Average speed uses total distance and time interval.
Average speed has no direction.
Average velocity uses change in position and time interval.
Average velocity has the direction of displacement, and both use metre per second.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A delivery vehicle travels through city streets while a student records its position at different times. The student plots the data with time on the horizontal axis and position on the vertical axis. The recorded points make a straight line. The student also records a second vehicle and wonders whether the two journeys are uniform, how their motion differs, and how displacement can be found.
activities.prompt: If the recorded points had not formed a straight line, what would the student’s graph suggest?
options: The curve would show that the vehicle’s velocity is changing.
The vehicle would still have constant velocity because its position was recorded at different times.
The curve would show that the vehicle’s position did not change with time.
The curve would show that displacement could be found from the area under it.

why.The vehicle would still have constant ve: A curve indicates changing velocity regardless of how many positions were recorded.
why.The curve would show that the vehicle’s: A position-time curve represents changing position with time.
why.The curve would show that displacement c: Displacement is obtained from the area under a velocity-time graph.

activities.explanation: A curved position-time graph shows that velocity is changing.

activities.context: A delivery vehicle travels through city streets while a student records its position at different times. The student plots the data with time on the horizontal axis and position on the vertical axis. The recorded points make a straight line. The student also records a second vehicle and wonders whether the two journeys are uniform, how their motion differs, and how displacement can be found.
activities.prompt: The second vehicle’s points form a curve, while the first vehicle’s points form a straight line. Which comparison is justified?
options: The first vehicle had constant velocity, while the second vehicle’s velocity was changing.
Both vehicles had constant velocity because both sets of points were connected.
Both vehicles had changing velocity because their graphs were compared.
The first vehicle’s velocity was changing, while the second vehicle’s velocity was constant.

why.Both vehicles had constant velocity beca: Connecting plotted points does not make both motions uniform.
why.Both vehicles had changing velocity beca: Comparing graphs does not mean that both vehicles have changing velocity.
why.The first vehicle’s velocity was changin: The straight and curved graphs indicate the opposite velocity patterns.

activities.explanation: A straight line indicates constant velocity, while a curve indicates changing velocity.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The first vehicle’s recorded motion is uniform because its position-time graph is a straight line.
Reason (R): A straight position-time graph shows motion with constant velocity.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The straight line indicates constant velocity, so the reason explains the assertion.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Describing Motion Around Us

activities.title: Linear motion
activities.prompt: Which activity shows linear motion?
options: A rider on a merry-go-round
A swimmer in a race
A stone moving in a circle
A train on a curved track
activities.explanation: A swimmer in a race shows linear motion. Linear motion happens along a straight line.

activities.title: Object at rest
activities.prompt: An object at rest changes its position with time.
activities.explanation: An object is at rest when its position does not change with time.

activities.title: Two times
activities.prompt: A time interval is the duration between two ______ of time.
activities.hint: Think of each clock reading as one moment.
activities.explanation: Two instants mark the start and finish of a time interval.

activities.title: Meaning of key ideas
activities.prompt: Match each idea with its meaning.
pairs: Its position does not change with time
Net change in position between two instants
Change in velocity divided by the time interval
activities.explanation: Each definition matches the key idea from this chapter.

activities.title: Reading a graph
activities.prompt: Put these steps in order to read a position-time graph.
items: Join the points with a line or curve
activities.explanation: Time comes on the X-axis, while position comes on the Y-axis. The points form a line or curve.

activities.title: Distance and displacement
activities.prompt: In the example, what are the athlete's total distance and final displacement?
options: 40 m and 160 m
160 m and 160 m
160 m and 40 m
40 m and 40 m
activities.explanation: The athlete travels 160 m in total. Her final displacement is 40 m in the positive direction.

activities.title: Average velocity
activities.prompt: Average velocity points in the same direction as displacement.
activities.explanation: Average velocity has the same direction as displacement. It is calculated from the change in position.

activities.title: Using a kinematic equation
activities.prompt: The equation v = u + at is valid only when acceleration is ______.
activities.hint: The acceleration must stay the same throughout the motion.
activities.explanation: Kinematic equations work for motion with constant acceleration. They can predict future velocity.

activities.title: Graph clues
activities.prompt: Match each graph clue with what it shows.
pairs: Rate of change of the Y-axis quantity
activities.explanation: The shape, slope and area of a graph provide different information about motion.

chapters.title: Exploring Mixtures and Their Separation
chapters.summary: In this chapter: classifying mixtures; solutions and their concentration; solubility and crystallization; distillation and paper chromatography.

lessons.title: Classifying Mixtures

activities.prompt: Why do some mixtures blend together while others separate into different parts?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What makes a mixture uniform?
activities.body: A mixture can be homogeneous, meaning its parts are uniform throughout. A homogeneous mixture is also called a solution. Solutions always stay homogeneous. Vinegar is an example. A stirred mixture of sand and water is not uniform. Its sand particles are visible and settle with time. Most mixtures of gases are homogeneous. Most solid-solid mixtures are heterogeneous, so they are not uniform. Blood is neither a solution nor a true suspension.
keyPoints: Homogeneous means uniform throughout.
A homogeneous mixture is also called a solution.
Visible, settling particles show that a mixture is not uniform.
activities.explanation: These clues help you classify mixtures by how their parts look.

activities.prompt: Why does stirred sand in water not stay like a solution?
steps: Sand particles in water are visible and settle with time.
The stirred sand-and-water mixture is not uniform.
A solution always stays homogeneous, so this mixture is not a solution.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Treasure Map Test
activities.prompt: Which statement describes a well-stirred sugar solution?
options: It has the same sweetness at every sip.
It becomes sweeter after the first sip.
It is sweeter at the bottom only.
It changes sweetness during the sip.
activities.explanation: Good spot! The sweetness stays the same from the first sip to the last.

activities.title: Kitchen Example
activities.prompt: Vinegar is an example of a heterogeneous mixture.
activities.explanation: Vinegar is an example of a homogeneous mixture, so this statement is false.

activities.title: Another Name
activities.prompt: A homogeneous mixture is also called a ______.
activities.hint: Think of the other name used for a homogeneous mixture.
activities.explanation: You have it! A homogeneous mixture is also called a solution.

activities.title: Match the Mixture Clues
activities.prompt: Match each mixture with its property.
activities.explanation: Each clue shows whether the mixture stays uniform or changes with time.

activities.title: At the Market
activities.prompt: Why is stirred sand and water not a homogeneous mixture?
options: Sand particles stay visible and settle.
Sand particles dissolve and disappear.
Sand particles rise and stay spread.
Sand particles join into one layer.
activities.explanation: Visible sand that settles with time shows that the mixture is not uniform.

activities.title: Gas Mixtures
activities.prompt: Most mixtures of gases are homogeneous.
activities.explanation: Yes! Most mixtures of gases are homogeneous, meaning they are uniform throughout.

activities.title: Watch the Sand Settle
activities.prompt: Put these observations in the order they happen.
activities.explanation: Stirring comes first. The visible particles then settle as time passes.

activities.title: The Blood Challenge
activities.prompt: How should blood be classified in this lesson?
options: only a solution
only a true suspension
both a solution and suspension
neither solution nor suspension
activities.explanation: You have it right! Blood is neither a solution nor a true suspension.

activities.prompt: A child stirs sugar into water and drinks it slowly. What happens?
options: The first sip will be sweeter than the last.
Every sip will taste equally sweet.
The first sip will be less sweet than the last.
The sweetness will change from one sip to another.

why.The first sip will be sweeter than the l: It wrongly predicts that sweetness changes during drinking.
why.The first sip will be less sweet than th: It reverses the expected sweetness of the first and last sips.
why.The sweetness will change from one sip t: It wrongly predicts that sweetness changes between sips.

activities.explanation: A well-stirred sugar solution tastes the same from first sip to last.

activities.prompt: A child mixes two dry solids together. What is most likely?
options: The mixture will be homogeneous and uniform.
The mixture will be heterogeneous and non-uniform.
The mixture will remain a clear solution.
The mixture will become a true suspension.

why.The mixture will be homogeneous and unif: Most solid-solid mixtures are heterogeneous, not homogeneous.
why.The mixture will remain a clear solution: It wrongly treats a solid-solid mixture as a solution.
why.The mixture will become a true suspensio: It wrongly treats a solid-solid mixture as a true suspension.

activities.explanation: Most solid-solid mixtures are heterogeneous and not uniform.
