lessons.title: Solutions and Their Concentration

activities.prompt: How can we discover how much solute is in a solution?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What is a solution?
activities.body: Mix a solute with a solvent to make a solution. In sugar and water, sugar is the solute and water is the solvent. Concentration can use percentage forms. Mass by mass gives solute grams in 100 grams of solution. Mass by volume gives solute grams in 100 millilitres of solution. Volume by volume gives solute millilitres in 100 millilitres of solution. A mass by volume example is 5% glucose solution.
keyPoints: A solution forms by mixing a solute with a solvent.
Sugar is the solute and water is the solvent.
Different percentage forms describe solute amounts.
activities.explanation: A solution contains a solute mixed with a solvent.

activities.prompt: For 100 millilitres of 5% glucose solution, how much glucose is needed?
steps: Use mass by volume, because the example is a 5% glucose solution.
The volume is 100 millilitres, so this amount defines the percentage.
Five percent gives 5 grams, because this percentage measures grams of solute.
Therefore, the solution should contain 5 grams of glucose.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Solute and solvent
activities.prompt: In sugar and water, which statement is correct?
options: Sugar is the solute.
Water is the solute.
Sugar is the solvent.
Water is the mixture.
activities.explanation: Sugar is the solute. Water is the solvent.

activities.title: Match each part
activities.prompt: Match each item with its correct description.
pairs: needs specified amounts of salt and sugar
activities.explanation: Each pair shows the correct role or requirement described in the lesson.

activities.title: Find the example
activities.prompt: Which is a common example of mass by volume percentage?
options: 5% glucose solution
salt and sugar mixture
pesticide and water mixture
water by itself
activities.explanation: A common mass by volume example is 5% glucose solution.

activities.title: Complete the definition
activities.prompt: Mass by volume percentage gives grams of solute in ______ millilitres of solution.
activities.hint: Think of the amount of solution used in this definition.
activities.explanation: Mass by volume percentage uses 100 millilitres of solution.

activities.title: Make a sugar and water solution
activities.prompt: Put these steps in the correct order.
activities.explanation: Sugar is the solute, water is the solvent, and mixing them makes a solution.

activities.title: Oral Rehydration Solution
activities.prompt: Which statement about Oral Rehydration Solution is correct?
options: It needs specified amounts of salt and sugar.
It needs any amount of salt and sugar.
It needs only sugar, with no salt.
It needs more sugar than salt.
activities.explanation: Oral Rehydration Solution needs specified amounts of salt and sugar.

activities.prompt: A farmer adds extra pesticide to protect crops. What may happen next?
options: The crops may suffer damage.
The crops may gain extra protection.
The crops may receive no benefit.
The crops may need more pesticide.

This mistake assumes more pesticide always gives more protection.
This mistake assumes extra pesticide cannot help the crops.
This mistake ignores that adding even more can damage crops.

activities.explanation: This is right because too much pesticide can damage crops.

activities.prompt: For 100 grams of 5% mass-by-mass solution, how much solute is there?
options: 100 grams
5 grams
5 millilitres
100 millilitres

why.100 grams: This mistake treats all the solution as solute.
why.5 millilitres: This mistake uses millilitres where grams are required.
why.100 millilitres: This mistake uses the wrong unit and solution amount.

activities.explanation: This is right: 5% means 5 grams in 100 grams of solution.

activities.prompt: In 100 millilitres of 5% volume-by-volume solution, how much solute is there?
options: 100 grams
100 millilitres
5 grams
5 millilitres

why.100 grams: This mistake uses grams for a volume-by-volume percentage.
why.100 millilitres: This mistake treats all the solution as liquid solute.
why.5 grams: This mistake uses grams instead of millilitres.

activities.explanation: This is right: 5% means 5 millilitres in 100 millilitres of solution.

activities.prompt: Two 5% solutions use mass-by-mass and mass-by-volume. Why may amounts differ?
options: Their 100-gram and 100-millilitre solution bases differ.
They must contain the same grams of solute.
They must contain the same millilitres of solute.
Their labels always describe the same solution.

why.They must contain the same grams of solu: This mistake assumes equal percentages always mean equal solute amounts.
why.They must contain the same millilitres o: This mistake treats both percentages as measurements of volume.
why.Their labels always describe the same so: This mistake ignores the different units used by each percentage.

activities.explanation: Mass by mass uses 100 grams; mass by volume uses 100 millilitres.

lessons.title: Solubility and Crystallization

activities.prompt: What makes crystals grow when a warm solution slowly cools?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What is solubility?
activities.body: Solubility tells you the maximum amount of a solute. It dissolves in a fixed quantity of solvent. A solute is the dissolving substance. A solvent is what holds it. A saturated solution cannot dissolve any more solute at its temperature. A solid usually dissolves better in warmer liquid. A gas usually becomes less soluble as temperature rises. A solubility curve shows solubility against temperature.
keyPoints: Solubility is the maximum amount that dissolves.
A saturated solution cannot dissolve more solute.
Temperature affects solid and gas solubility differently.
activities.explanation: Learn how temperature changes what can dissolve.

activities.prompt: A glass holds a warm, saturated solution. You move it somewhere cool. What forms, and why?
steps: The solution was saturated, so no more solid could dissolve.
Less solid can stay dissolved, because solid solubility falls as temperature falls.
The extra solid therefore separates out as pure crystals.
Slow cooling then gives larger, shiny, and well-shaped crystals.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: How crystals form
activities.body: Crystallization is the laboratory formation of crystals from a saturated solution. It depends on differences in solubility at different temperatures. Slow cooling gives larger, shiny and well-shaped crystals. Crystals have particles in a regular geometric pattern. Their particles sit in an orderly pattern. Crystallization separates pure crystals from mixtures.
keyPoints: Crystallization forms crystals from a saturated solution.
Slow cooling gives larger, shiny, well-shaped crystals.
Crystals have an orderly particle pattern.
activities.explanation: These ideas explain how crystals form and grow.

activities.prompt: What does solubility measure?
options: Time needed for complete solid dissolution
Total gas found above a liquid sample
Maximum solute in a fixed solvent amount
Minimum solvent needed for a saturated solution
activities.explanation: It is the greatest amount that can dissolve in a fixed quantity of solvent.

activities.prompt: A saturated solution can dissolve any extra solute at the same temperature.
activities.explanation: At that temperature, it cannot dissolve any more solute.

activities.prompt: The solubility of a gas in a liquid generally decreases as temperature rises.
activities.explanation: As temperature rises, a gas generally becomes less soluble in a liquid.

activities.prompt: Match each item with its correct statement.
pairs: Solubility usually falls as temperature rises
activities.explanation: The pairs show temperature effects, graph meaning and solid separation.

activities.prompt: Put these events in order during slow cooling.
items: Solid solubility is higher at the warmer temperature.
Solid solubility is lower at the cooler temperature.
Extra compound separates as a pure solid.
activities.explanation: Cooling lowers solid solubility. Extra compound can then separate as a pure solid.

activities.prompt: Crystallization separates pure ______ from mixtures.
activities.hint: Think about the solid structures formed in the lesson.
activities.explanation: Pure crystals are separated from mixtures by crystallization.

activities.prompt: A saturated solution is cooled slowly. What is most likely to happen?
options: Extra solid separates as crystals, because less can dissolve when cooled.
All the water disappears, leaving only dry crystals behind.
More solid stays dissolved, because cooling always raises solubility.
Nothing changes, because saturation fixes the amount at all temperatures.

why.All the water disappears, leaving only d: This mistake thinks cooling removes all water from the solution.
why.More solid stays dissolved, because cool: This mistake confuses cooling with heating.
why.Nothing changes, because saturation fixe: This mistake assumes saturation prevents any temperature effect.

activities.explanation: This is right: extra solid separates as crystals when cooled.

activities.prompt: A student heats a saturated solution of a solid. What generally happens?
options: Less solid can dissolve, because solid solubility falls with temperature.
Crystals form at once, because heating always lowers the temperature.
More solid can dissolve, because solid solubility rises with temperature.
No extra solid can dissolve, because saturation means no change.

why.Less solid can dissolve, because solid s: This mistake reverses the usual change in solid solubility.
why.Crystals form at once, because heating a: This mistake confuses heating with cooling.
why.No extra solid can dissolve, because sat: This mistake thinks saturation fixes how much can dissolve.

activities.explanation: This is right because solid solubility rises with temperature.

activities.prompt: A gas is dissolved in a liquid. The liquid is warmed. What happens to the gas?
options: More gas stays dissolved, because gas solubility rises with temperature rises.
Less gas stays dissolved, because gas solubility falls as temperature rises.
The same gas stays dissolved, because liquids always hold every gas.
The gas becomes solid, because heating always causes crystallization.

why.More gas stays dissolved, because gas so: This mistake reverses the usual change in gas solubility.
why.The same gas stays dissolved, because li: This mistake thinks dissolved gas cannot leave the liquid.
why.The gas becomes solid, because heating a: This mistake confuses a dissolved gas with a forming crystal.

activities.explanation: This is right because gas solubility falls as temperature rises.

activities.prompt: Two samples of the same saturated solution are cooled at different speeds. Which has larger crystals?
options: The quickly cooled sample, because quick cooling gives larger crystals.
Neither sample, because crystal size does not depend on cooling speed.
Both samples equally, because saturation fixes the size of crystals.
The slowly cooled sample, because slow cooling gives larger crystals.

why.The quickly cooled sample, because quick: This mistake swaps slow cooling for quick cooling.
why.Neither sample, because crystal size doe: This mistake thinks crystal size is unrelated to cooling speed.
why.Both samples equally, because saturation: This mistake thinks saturation fixes the size of crystals.

activities.explanation: This is right because slow cooling gives larger, shiny, well-shaped crystals.

activities.prompt: A student claims crystallization cannot separate a homogeneous mixture. What observation proves the claim wrong?
options: The mixture stays one liquid, because crystallization cannot separate it.
Only the liquid appears, because crystals contain no dissolved compound.
Pure crystals appear and separate from the homogeneous mixture.
More mixed liquid appears, because crystallization always adds to the mixture.

why.The mixture stays one liquid, because cr: This mistake thinks crystallization cannot separate a homogeneous mixture.
why.Only the liquid appears, because crystal: This mistake treats crystals as if they contain only solvent.
why.More mixed liquid appears, because cryst: This mistake thinks crystallization adds more mixed liquid.

activities.explanation: This is right because crystallization separates pure crystals from the mixture.

activities.prompt: At 40 °C, compound B can remain dissolved. The amount is 241 grams per 100 grams of water. What happens when this solution cools?
options: All compound stays dissolved, because saturation never changes with temperature.
Extra compound separates as crystals with a regular particle pattern.
The water disappears, leaving compound particles in a random pattern.
More compound dissolves, because cooling always raises solid solubility.

why.All compound stays dissolved, because sa: This mistake thinks saturation never changes with temperature.
why.The water disappears, leaving compound p: This mistake assumes crystallization removes the solvent.
why.More compound dissolves, because cooling: This mistake reverses how solid solubility changes with temperature.

activities.explanation: This is right because less compound stays dissolved and extra solid separates.

lessons.title: Distillation and Paper Chromatography

activities.prompt: What happens when a mixture heats up and cools down again?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How distillation works
activities.body: Distillation heats a liquid mixture until the liquid with the lower boiling point vaporises. The vapour is then cooled, and it turns back into a liquid. A condenser does the cooling. Distillation works well when boiling points differ by at least about 25 °C. Paper chromatography uses a solvent, which carries substances up paper at different speeds.
keyPoints: The lower-boiling liquid vaporises first
Cooled vapour becomes a liquid
Boiling points should differ by about 25 °C
activities.explanation: Different boiling points help during distillation. Cooling collects the vapour as a liquid.

activities.prompt: A student must collect acetone from a mixture with water.
steps: Acetone boils at about 56 °C, while water boils at 100 °C.
So acetone, the lower-boiling liquid, vaporises first when heated.
Its vapour enters the condenser, where it is cooled.
It turns back into liquid, so acetone is collected first.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: How paper chromatography works
activities.body: Paper chromatography can separate pigments from spinach leaves. Different colours from black sketch-pen ink may spread out. The solvent carries the substances up the paper at different speeds. This movement helps the pigments separate from one another on the paper.
keyPoints: Spinach pigments can separate
Ink colours may spread out
The solvent moves substances at different speeds
activities.explanation: The solvent carries pigments at different speeds. This helps them separate on the paper.

activities.title: The first step
activities.prompt: What happens during distillation first?
options: The mixture is heated
The vapour is cooled
The liquid turns to vapour
The solvent moves up paper
activities.explanation: Heating starts the process. The liquid with the lower boiling point then vaporises.

activities.title: Comparing boiling points
activities.prompt: About how much lower is acetone's boiling point than water's?
options: About 25 °C
About 44 °C
About 56 °C
About 100 °C
activities.explanation: Acetone boils at about 56 °C. Water boils at 100 °C, giving a difference of 44 °C.

activities.title: Match each term to its job
activities.prompt: Match each term to its job.
activities.explanation: Each term matches its action. The condenser cools vapour, while the solvent carries substances.

activities.title: Order the distillation steps
activities.prompt: Put the distillation steps in order.
items: Cool the vapour in the condenser
Turn the vapour back into a liquid
activities.explanation: Heating forms the vapour. The condenser cools it, and it becomes liquid again.

activities.title: Why pigments separate
activities.prompt: Why do different pigments separate on chromatography paper?
options: The paper heats the pigments equally
The solvent carries them at different speeds
The pigments all move at one speed
The condenser cools each pigment
activities.explanation: The solvent carries the substances up the paper at different speeds. Different colours may spread out.

activities.title: Name the cooling part
activities.prompt: In distillation, a ______ cools the vapour of the lower-boiling liquid.
activities.hint: Name the part that cools vapour.
activities.explanation: The condenser cools the vapour. The cooled vapour then turns back into a liquid.

activities.prompt: A student heats a mixture of acetone and water. What should enter the condenser first?
options: Acetone vapour, because acetone has the lower boiling point.
Water vapour, because water has the lower boiling point.
Both vapours together, because their boiling points are equal.
No vapour, because a liquid cannot become vapour.

why.Water vapour, because water has the lowe: This reverses the given boiling points: water boils at 100 °C.
why.Both vapours together, because their boi: This mistakes different boiling points for the same boiling point.
why.No vapour, because a liquid cannot becom: This wrongly thinks heating cannot turn a liquid into vapour.

activities.explanation: Acetone boils at about 56 °C, lower than water at 100 °C.

activities.prompt: Two liquids boil at temperatures less than 25 °C apart. Will distillation work well?
options: No, because the boiling points are not far enough apart.
No, because equal boiling points are needed for separation.
Yes, because any small difference is enough for separation.
Yes, because cooling can separate every different liquid.

why.No, because equal boiling points are nee: This wrongly says equal boiling points are needed for distillation.
why.Yes, because any small difference is eno: This assumes every small boiling-point difference is large enough.
why.Yes, because cooling can separate every: This mistakes cooling for the rule about boiling-point differences.

activities.explanation: Distillation works when boiling points differ by at least about 25 °C.

activities.prompt: Black ink contains different colours. The solvent carries ink substances up paper at different speeds. If one moves faster, where will it be later?
options: Farther up the paper than the slower-moving substance.
Lower down the paper than the slower-moving substance.
At the same place as the slower-moving substance.
Still where it first started, because only the solvent moves.

why.Lower down the paper than the slower-mov: This reverses the meaning of moving at a faster speed.
why.At the same place as the slower-moving s: This ignores that the substances travel at different speeds.
why.Still where it first started, because on: This wrongly assumes that the ink substances do not move.

activities.explanation: A faster substance is carried farther up the paper by the solvent.

activities.prompt: Ink colours can spread out on paper at different speeds. A student says the paper moved them. What is wrong?
options: The solvent moves the colours, and their speeds can differ.
The condenser moves the colours, and their speeds can differ.
Heating moves the colours, and their speeds can differ.
Boiling moves the colours, and their speeds can differ.

why.The condenser moves the colours, and the: This confuses the condenser with the solvent that moves colours.
why.Heating moves the colours, and their spe: This confuses paper chromatography with heating a mixture for distillation.
why.Boiling moves the colours, and their spe: This confuses the boiling step with the solvent in chromatography.

activities.explanation: The solvent carries the substances up the paper at different speeds.

lessons.title: Separating Immiscible Liquids and Sublimable Solids

activities.prompt: How can you separate oil and water, and make a solid disappear?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Different ways to separate materials
activities.body: Oil and water are immiscible liquids. They do not mix and form separate layers. Sublimation changes a solid directly into vapour, without becoming liquid. A magnet can separate iron nails from sawdust. An alloy can contain metals, or a metal and a non-metal. Physical methods cannot separate an alloy's components.
keyPoints: Immiscible liquids form separate layers.
Sublimation changes a solid directly into vapour.
Physical methods cannot separate an alloy's components.
activities.explanation: Each method depends on how the materials behave.

activities.prompt: A child mixes oil and water, then heats a solid that can sublime. What happens in each case?
steps: Oil and water do not mix, because they are immiscible liquids.
Leave them standing, because immiscible liquids form separate layers.
Heat the solid, because sublimation changes it directly into vapour.
The liquids separate into layers, while the solid changes into vapour.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What do oil and water do?
options: They mix evenly
They form separate layers
They become gases
They form an alloy
activities.explanation: Oil and water do not mix, so they form separate layers.

activities.prompt: Oil and water mix evenly.
activities.explanation: Oil and water do not mix. They form separate layers.

activities.prompt: Sublimation changes a solid directly into ______, without becoming liquid.
activities.hint: The solid changes into this without passing through liquid.
activities.explanation: Sublimation changes a solid directly into vapour.

activities.prompt: Match each material or process with its correct result.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a separation method and its correct result.

activities.prompt: Which option correctly describes something an alloy can contain?
options: Two metals or two non-metals
A metal and a non-metal
Oil, water and sawdust
Iron nails and magnets
activities.explanation: An alloy can contain a metal and a non-metal.

activities.prompt: Arrange these words to show the path of sublimation.
activities.explanation: The solid changes directly into vapour. It does not become liquid.

activities.prompt: Oil and water are shaken together. What happens after they settle?
options: They will form two separate layers.
They will remain one mixed liquid.
The oil will dissolve fully in the water.
They will both turn into gases.

This wrongly assumes shaking makes the liquids mix completely.
why.The oil will dissolve fully in the water: This wrongly confuses not mixing with dissolving.
This wrongly assumes the liquids change into gases.

activities.explanation: This is right because immiscible liquids form separate layers.

activities.prompt: Two gases meet in a room. What should you expect next?
options: They will mix easily and uniformly.
They will form two separate layers.
They will refuse to mix at all.
They will both become liquids.

This wrongly treats gases like immiscible liquids.
This wrongly assumes gas particles stay apart.
This wrongly assumes mixing gases makes them liquid.

activities.explanation: This is right because gas particles mix easily and uniformly.

activities.prompt: Iron nails and sawdust are mixed. Which action tests separation best?
options: Move a magnet through the whole mixture.
Move a magnet through only half the mixture.
Add water and wait for layers.
Shake the closed mixture for longer.

why.Move a magnet through only half the mixt: Testing only half may miss what happens in the whole mixture.
Water is used for immiscible liquids, not this mixture.
Shaking alone cannot show that a magnet caused the separation.

activities.explanation: A magnet can separate iron nails from sawdust.

activities.prompt: A heated solid changes directly into vapour. What happened during the change?
options: It sublimated without becoming liquid.
It melted before becoming vapour.
It dissolved in the surrounding air.
It split into two solid layers.

This wrongly assumes every heated solid melts first.
This wrongly treats a direct change into vapour as dissolving.
This wrongly treats sublimation as forming separate solid layers.

activities.explanation: Sublimation changes a solid directly into vapour without becoming liquid.

activities.prompt: A claim says alloys need two metals. Why is it wrong?
options: An alloy may contain a metal and a non-metal.
An alloy must contain two different gases.
An alloy must contain one pure metal only.
An alloy cannot contain any non-metal.

why.An alloy must contain two different gase: This wrongly treats gases as possible alloy components.
why.An alloy must contain one pure metal onl: This wrongly assumes every alloy contains only one pure metal.
This wrongly assumes an alloy cannot contain a non-metal.

activities.explanation: This is right because an alloy may contain a metal and a non-metal.

lessons.title: Suspensions, Centrifugation and Colloids

activities.prompt: Could we separate tiny particles and blood components, and help muddy water become clear?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Particles in mixtures
activities.body: A suspension contains solid particles that remain in a liquid without dissolving. Heavier mud can settle, while tiny particles may pass through filtration. Centrifugation spins a mixture in a tube, moving heavier particles outwards to settle. Alum makes fine particles clump through coagulation. Blood is a colloid. Light scattering by particles is called the Tyndall effect.
keyPoints: Suspension particles do not dissolve.
Centrifugation moves heavier particles outwards.
Alum causes particles to clump together.
Blood is a colloid.
The Tyndall effect is light scattering.
activities.explanation: These ideas describe what particles do in mixtures.

activities.prompt: Tiny mud particles remain after muddy water is filtered. What will centrifugation do?
steps: The mud stays mixed because solid particles remain suspended without dissolving.
Some tiny particles remain because filtration is not always enough.
A tube is spun at high speed because this creates centrifugal force on heavier particles.
Heavier particles move outwards and settle, so centrifugation can separate the mud.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Ways to study particles
activities.body: Centrifugation spins a mixture in a tube at high speed. Its force moves heavier particles outwards, where they settle. Alum makes fine suspended particles clump together, and this action is called coagulation. Blood is a colloid, not a solution or a true suspension. Light scattering by particles has a special name: the Tyndall effect.
keyPoints: Centrifugation uses spinning and outward movement.
Alum causes fine particles to clump.
Blood is a colloid.
The Tyndall effect is light scattering.
activities.explanation: These clues identify separation methods and special mixtures.

activities.prompt: Which sentence describes a suspension?
options: Solid particles stay without dissolving
Solid particles dissolve in the liquid
Solid particles become a new liquid
Solid particles rise and disappear
activities.explanation: In a suspension, solid particles remain suspended without dissolving.

activities.prompt: Heavier mud particles settle at the bottom of muddy water.
activities.explanation: Heavier mud particles settle at the bottom of muddy water.

activities.prompt: Centrifugation ______ a mixture in a tube at high speed.
activities.hint: It moves the mixture very quickly.
activities.explanation: Centrifugation spins a mixture in a tube at high speed.

activities.prompt: During centrifugation, what happens to heavier particles?
options: They dissolve in the liquid.
They move inwards and vanish.
They move outwards and settle.
They stay at the tube's centre.
activities.explanation: Centrifugal force moves heavier particles outwards, where they settle.

activities.prompt: Match each clue with its result or name.
activities.explanation: Each pair joins a particle clue with its correct result or name.

activities.prompt: Which statement is correct about blood and light scattering?
options: Blood is a solution; scattering is coagulation.
Blood is a suspension; scattering is centrifugation.
Blood is a colloid; scattering is Tyndall effect.
Blood is a colloid; scattering is filtration.
activities.explanation: Blood is a colloid, and light scattering by particles is the Tyndall effect.

activities.prompt: Put these centrifugation steps in order.
items: Mixture spins in a tube at high speed
Centrifugal force moves heavier particles outwards
activities.explanation: The mixture spins first, then heavier particles move outwards and settle.

activities.prompt: Muddy water is poured through a filter. Tiny particles remain in the water. Why?
options: The filter cannot remove any particles from muddy water.
The filter can miss tiny particles, so filtration is not always enough.
The tiny particles dissolve while passing through the filter.
The filter changes tiny particles into heavier mud particles.

why.The filter cannot remove any particles f: This overstates the filter; filtration is not always enough to remove tiny particles.
why.The tiny particles dissolve while passin: This wrongly says the solid particles dissolve.
why.The filter changes tiny particles into h: This wrongly says filtering changes the particles instead of missing some.

activities.explanation: Tiny particles can remain because filtration is not always enough.

activities.prompt: A laboratory needs to separate the components of blood. Which method fits this job?
options: Use centrifugation, because it spins blood at high speed.
Use alum, because coagulation separates blood in laboratories.
Use filtration alone, because it always removes every tiny particle.
Use settling alone, because blood is a true suspension.

why.Use alum, because coagulation separates: This confuses coagulation with laboratory centrifugation.
why.Use filtration alone, because it always: This wrongly assumes filtration always removes every tiny particle.
why.Use settling alone, because blood is a t: This wrongly calls blood a true suspension; blood is a colloid.

activities.explanation: Centrifugation is used in laboratories to separate components of blood.

lessons.sceneAlt: A spoon slowly drops sugar into a glass of water to show how a solution is made.
lessons.sceneCaption: A spoon slowly drops sugar into a glass of water to show making a solution.

activities.context: In a kitchen, a student stirred sugar into a glass of water until the sweetness was the same from the first sip to the last. Sand particles were visible in the glass and settled with time. The student also used vinegar while cooking. In a later lesson, the teacher said that blood is neither a solution nor a true suspension.
activities.prompt: If the glass is left standing for a while, what should the student expect?
options: The visible sand will have settled, while the sugar solution itself remains equally sweet.
The visible sand will dissolve, making the whole mixture uniform.
The sugar will form separate visible grains at the bottom of the glass.
Both the sand and the sugar will remain evenly spread throughout the water.

why.The visible sand will dissolve, making t: Visible sand does not become part of the sweet solution merely by standing.
why.The sugar will form separate visible gra: The facts describe the sugar staying in solution rather than forming separate grains.
why.Both the sand and the sugar will remain: Settling with time shows that the sand does not remain evenly mixed.

activities.explanation: Settling particles make the mixture non-uniform, while the solution stays homogeneous.

activities.context: In a kitchen, a student stirred sugar into a glass of water until the sweetness was the same from the first sip to the last. Sand particles were visible in the glass and settled with time. The student also used vinegar while cooking. In a later lesson, the teacher said that blood is neither a solution nor a true suspension.
activities.prompt: Why can vinegar be classified as a solution?
options: Because vinegar is homogeneous, and a homogeneous mixture is another name for a solution.
Because vinegar contains visible particles that settle into separate parts with time.
Because vinegar forms visibly different layers and is therefore heterogeneous.
Because vinegar is a true suspension whose parts remain visibly separate.

why.Because vinegar contains visible particl: Visible settling particles indicate a non-uniform mixture, not vinegar.
why.Because vinegar forms visibly different: Different visible layers would indicate heterogeneity, which does not apply to vinegar.
why.Because vinegar is a true suspension who: Vinegar is not described as a true suspension.

activities.explanation: Vinegar is given as a homogeneous mixture, which is also called a solution.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A stirred sand-and-water mixture is heterogeneous.
Reason (R): Sand particles are visible and settle with time.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The visible particles and their settling show that the mixture is not uniform.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Most mixtures of gases are homogeneous.
Reason (R): A homogeneous mixture is also called a solution.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but the alternative name does not explain why most gas mixtures are homogeneous.

activities.prompt: Explain how a well-stirred sugar solution differs from a stirred mixture of sand and water.
activities.answer: The well-stirred sugar solution is homogeneous because its sweetness is the same from the first sip to the last. A homogeneous mixture is also called a solution, and a solution always remains homogeneous. The stirred sand-and-water mixture is not uniform. Its sand particles are visible and settle with time. Therefore, the sugar solution is a solution, whereas the sand-and-water mixture is heterogeneous rather than a solution.
points: The sugar solution has the same sweetness throughout.
A homogeneous mixture is also called a solution.
The sand-and-water mixture is not uniform.
The sand particles are visible and settle with time.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student is asked to prepare oral rehydration solution. The student must use the specified amounts of salt and sugar. In another part of the task, the student labels a container holding 5% glucose solution, where 5% is a mass by volume percentage. The student also explains that a pesticide must be used in a suitable amount because too little may fail to protect crops, while too much can damage them.
activities.prompt: If the student changes one of the specified amounts of salt or sugar, what should be expected?
options: The solution would no longer be prepared with the amounts that are required.
The solution would still be acceptable because salt and sugar are both present.
The solution would still be acceptable because the solvent is water.
The solution would still be acceptable because the solution contains some solute.

why.The solution would still be acceptable b: Having both ingredients present does not show that their amounts are correct.
Water is the solvent, but this does not replace the required quantities of salt and sugar.
Containing some solute does not ensure that the specified amounts have been used.

activities.explanation: Oral rehydration solution needs the specified amounts.

activities.context: A student is asked to prepare oral rehydration solution. The student must use the specified amounts of salt and sugar. In another part of the task, the student labels a container holding 5% glucose solution, where 5% is a mass by volume percentage. The student also explains that a pesticide must be used in a suitable amount because too little may fail to protect crops, while too much can damage them.
activities.prompt: If too much pesticide is used, which outcome should the farmer expect?
options: Possible damage to the crops is expected.
Stronger protection of the crops is expected.
Less protection of the crops is expected.
No protection of the crops is expected.

why.Stronger protection of the crops is expe: The given information does not say that too much pesticide gives stronger protection.
why.Less protection of the crops is expected: The given information links too much pesticide with damage, not reduced protection.
The given information does not say that too much pesticide gives no protection.

activities.explanation: Too much pesticide can damage crops.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A 5% glucose solution contains 5 grams of glucose in 100 millilitres of solution.
Reason (R): Mass by volume percentage gives the grams of solute in 100 millilitres of solution.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly explains how the percentage of the glucose solution is expressed.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Using too much pesticide can damage crops.
Reason (R): Using too little pesticide may fail to protect crops.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but the reason does not explain why too much pesticide can damage crops.

activities.prompt: Why should the student use only the specified amounts of salt and sugar when preparing oral rehydration solution, and why should pesticide not be used in excess?
activities.answer: Oral rehydration solution needs specified amounts of salt and sugar, so changing those amounts would not meet the preparation requirement given for it. A pesticide also needs a suitable amount. Too little may fail to protect crops, whereas too much can damage them. Therefore, the student should follow the required amounts for the solution and avoid using excessive pesticide.
points: Oral rehydration solution needs specified amounts of salt and sugar.
Changing the amounts would not meet the given preparation requirement.
Too little pesticide may fail to protect crops.
Too much pesticide can damage crops.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student has a saturated solution of compound B at 40 °C, where 241 grams of B can remain in solution per 100 grams of water. The student cools the solution, and extra compound B separates from the liquid as a pure solid. The student wants large, shiny, well-shaped crystals and wonders whether the cooling should be slow or rapid.
activities.prompt: Why did extra compound B separate from the solution as a pure solid after cooling?
options: The lower temperature reduced the amount of solid B that could remain dissolved.
The lower temperature increased the amount of solid B that could remain dissolved.
The solution had become more suitable for dissolving a gas.
A saturated solution cannot lose dissolved solute when its temperature changes.

why.The lower temperature increased the amou: This reverses the stated temperature-solubility trend.
why.The solution had become more suitable fo: The presence of compound B makes this gas-solubility rule irrelevant.
why.A saturated solution cannot lose dissolv: Saturation applies at the stated temperature and does not prevent temperature effects.

activities.explanation: Cooling generally lowers the solubility of a solid in a liquid.

activities.context: A student has a saturated solution of compound B at 40 °C, where 241 grams of B can remain in solution per 100 grams of water. The student cools the solution, and extra compound B separates from the liquid as a pure solid. The student wants large, shiny, well-shaped crystals and wonders whether the cooling should be slow or rapid.
activities.prompt: What would happen if the saturated solution were warmed before being cooled back to 40 °C?
options: More compound B could dissolve because the solubility of a solid generally rises with temperature.
Extra compound B would immediately form crystals because warming lowers solid solubility.
Less compound B could dissolve because all solutes become less soluble when warmed.
Nothing could happen because a saturated solution cannot change at any temperature.

why.Extra compound B would immediately form: This incorrectly treats warming as if it lowers solid solubility.
why.Less compound B could dissolve because a: The decreasing-solubility trend applies to gases, not the solid described here.
why.Nothing could happen because a saturated: Saturation is stated for a particular temperature and does not rule out changes at other temperatures.

activities.explanation: Warming generally increases the solubility of a solid in a liquid.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Extra compound B can separate as pure crystals when the saturated solution is cooled.
Reason (R): The solubility of a solid in a liquid generally decreases as temperature falls.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason directly explains why cooling can leave extra compound B undissolved.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Slow cooling is a suitable way to obtain larger, shiny and well-shaped crystals.
Reason (R): The solubility of a gas in a liquid generally decreases as temperature rises.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but the gas-solubility rule does not explain the quality of crystals formed by slow cooling.

activities.prompt: Explain why a saturated solution cannot dissolve more solute and what can happen when its temperature changes.
activities.answer: A saturated solution contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve in the fixed quantity of solvent at its temperature. Therefore, no more solute can dissolve there unless the temperature changes in a way that increases the solubility of the solid. For a solid in a liquid, solubility generally increases when temperature rises and decreases when temperature falls. Thus, cooling the compound B solution from 40 °C reduces its capacity to hold dissolved B. The extra B can then separate from the liquid as a pure solid, often as crystals. This separation is crystallization.
points: A saturated solution holds the maximum amount of solute at its temperature.
The solubility of a solid generally increases with temperature.
Cooling generally reduces the amount of solid that can remain dissolved.
Extra solute can separate as a pure solid, often as crystals.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student wants to recover acetone from a mixture of acetone and water. The mixture is heated, and the acetone vapour enters a condenser, where it is cooled and becomes liquid. The student then places black sketch-pen ink on paper and lets a solvent move up it. Several colours spread through the ink. The student also uses spinach leaves to test whether their pigments can be separated.
activities.prompt: After the acetone has vaporised, what should happen next in the student's apparatus?
options: It should change from vapour to liquid as it cools.
It should remain vapour because the condenser cannot cool it.
It should be carried up chromatography paper by the solvent.
It should be heated again before it enters the condenser.

why.It should remain vapour because the cond: The condenser is used to cool the lower-boiling liquid's vapour.
why.It should be carried up chromatography p: Paper and a moving solvent are used in chromatography.
why.It should be heated again before it ente: The vapour should be cooled after it has formed, not heated again.

activities.explanation: Cooling turns the acetone vapour back into liquid.

activities.context: A student wants to recover acetone from a mixture of acetone and water. The mixture is heated, and the acetone vapour enters a condenser, where it is cooled and becomes liquid. The student then places black sketch-pen ink on paper and lets a solvent move up it. Several colours spread through the ink. The student also uses spinach leaves to test whether their pigments can be separated.
activities.prompt: Why do different colours appear from the black sketch-pen ink on the paper?
options: The solvent carries the ink's substances up the paper at different speeds.
The condenser cools each colour and gives it a different boiling point.
All the ink substances travel together because the ink has one colour.
The paper heats the ink until the colours become separate liquids.

why.The condenser cools each colour and give: The condenser cools vapour and does not give colours boiling points.
why.All the ink substances travel together b: One ink colour can contain substances that travel at different speeds.
why.The paper heats the ink until the colour: The separation here is caused by movement with the solvent, not heating.

activities.explanation: Substances carried by the solvent can move at different speeds.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Acetone will vaporise before water when the student's mixture is heated.
Reason (R): Acetone boils at about 56 °C, while water boils at 100 °C.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Acetone's lower boiling point explains why it vaporises first.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Exploring Mixtures and Their Separation

activities.prompt: Which one is a homogeneous mixture, also called a solution?
options: Vinegar
Stirred sand and water
Blood
Oil and water
activities.explanation: Vinegar is a homogeneous mixture. A homogeneous mixture is also called a solution.

activities.prompt: A well-stirred sugar solution tastes equally sweet from the first sip to the last.
activities.explanation: A well-stirred sugar solution has the same sweetness throughout.

activities.prompt: In sugar and water, sugar is the ______ and water is the solvent.
activities.hint: Name the part that dissolves.
activities.explanation: In sugar and water, sugar is the solute and water is the solvent.

activities.prompt: What does mass by mass percentage give?
options: Grams of solute in 100 grams of solution
Grams of solute in 100 millilitres of solution
Millilitres of solute in 100 millilitres of solution
Grams of solvent in 100 grams of solution
activities.explanation: Mass by mass percentage gives the grams of solute in 100 grams of solution.

activities.prompt: Match each method with the mixture or material it can separate.
pairs: Pure crystals from a homogeneous mixture
activities.explanation: A magnet separates iron nails from sawdust. Centrifugation separates blood components in laboratories.

activities.prompt: Put the distillation steps in the correct order.
activities.explanation: The lower-boiling liquid vaporises first. The condenser cools its vapour, which becomes a liquid.

activities.prompt: Which statement about crystallization is correct?
options: Slow cooling gives smaller, dull, uneven crystals.
Slow cooling removes the need for solubility differences.
Slow cooling gives larger, shiny, well-shaped crystals.
Slow cooling can separate components of an alloy.
activities.explanation: Slow cooling gives larger, shiny and well-shaped crystals. Crystallization depends on solubility differences at different temperatures.

activities.prompt: Blood is a true suspension.
activities.explanation: Blood is a colloid, not a solution or a true suspension.

activities.prompt: In chromatography, the solvent carries substances up the paper at different ______.
activities.hint: Some substances move faster than others.
activities.explanation: The solvent carries the substances up the paper at different speeds.

activities.prompt: What happens when a solution has dissolved all the solute it can at its temperature?
options: It becomes unsaturated after shaking.
It is saturated and cannot dissolve more.
It must form separate solid layers.
It changes into a true suspension.
activities.explanation: A saturated solution cannot dissolve any more solute at its temperature. It remains a solution.

chapters.title: How Forces Affect Motion
chapters.summary: In this chapter: what is force?; balanced and unbalanced forces; the force of friction; newton's first law of motion.

lessons.title: What Is Force?

activities.prompt: What can a push or pull do to the world around you?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Force Has Effects
activities.body: A force can move an object from rest. It can change a moving object's speed and direction. It can even change an object's shape. Force direction must be clear. Magnitude means how strong a force is. The SI unit of force is the newton. Weight is Earth's gravitational pull on an object. A spring balance measures force magnitude. People directly feel millinewton forces. Scientists measure forces as small as yoctonewtons.
keyPoints: A force can cause movement or change motion.
Direction and magnitude affect a force's effect.
Force is measured in newtons.
activities.explanation: These are the main effects and details of force.

activities.prompt: A toy car is at rest. You push it, then push a moving toy car from the side. What happens?
steps: The first push makes the car move because a force can move an object from rest.
The sideways push changes the car's direction because a force can change a moving object's direction.
If the push is stronger, its magnitude changes, and the effect changes too.
So direction and magnitude both matter when describing a force's effect.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: A Force at Work
activities.prompt: What can a force change in a moving object?
options: Its speed
Its colour
Its taste
Its smell
activities.explanation: A force can change the speed and direction of a moving object.

activities.title: Turning While Moving
activities.prompt: A force can change both the speed and direction of a moving object.
activities.explanation: Both speed and direction can change when a force acts.

activities.title: The Force Unit
activities.prompt: The SI unit of force is the ______.
activities.hint: Use the unit named in your lesson.
activities.explanation: The SI unit of force is the newton.

activities.title: Force Words and Meanings
activities.prompt: Match each force word with its meaning.
pairs: Earth's gravitational pull on an object
activities.explanation: Each pair connects a force word with its correct meaning.

activities.title: Measuring Force
activities.prompt: Which tool can measure the magnitude of a force?
options: A spring balance
A direction card
A speed counter
A shape tray
activities.explanation: A spring balance measures the magnitude of a force.

activities.title: Feeling Tiny Forces
activities.prompt: The smallest forces people can directly feel are in the yoctonewton range.
activities.explanation: People directly feel forces in the millinewton range. Scientists measure yoctonewton forces.

activities.title: Two Changes
activities.prompt: Changing a force's magnitude or ______ changes the effect of that force.
activities.hint: This must be stated clearly for a force.
activities.explanation: Changing magnitude or direction changes the effect of a force.

activities.prompt: A toy car is still on the floor. You push it. What happens next?
options: The car moves because the push is a force.
The car stays still because its weight holds it.
The car moves only because its weight pulls it.
The car stays still because force cannot move it.

why.The car stays still because its weight h: This mistake thinks weight prevents a force from moving an object.
why.The car moves only because its weight pu: This mistake thinks weight, rather than the push, causes the movement.
why.The car stays still because force cannot: This mistake thinks forces cannot change an object's rest.

activities.explanation: A force can make an object move from rest.

activities.prompt: A toy car rolls forward. The same forward push is made twice. The second push is stronger. What is different?
options: The force's magnitude is greater, so its effect changes.
The force's direction is different, so its effect changes.
The car's weight is greater, so its effect changes.
The car's shape is different, so its effect changes.

why.The force's direction is different, so i: The direction stays the same because both pushes act forward.
why.The car's weight is greater, so its effe: This mistake confuses a stronger force with a heavier car.
why.The car's shape is different, so its eff: This mistake confuses the effect of a push with a shape change.

activities.explanation: A stronger force has a greater magnitude, which changes its effect.

lessons.title: Balanced and Unbalanced Forces

activities.prompt: Why do some objects stay still while others start to move?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Forces Acting Together
activities.body: More than one force usually acts on an object. Friction acts opposite a push. Earth pulls a floating ball downwards, while the liquid pushes it upwards. Equal forces in opposite directions are balanced forces. Unbalanced forces make a non-zero net force, meaning a net force that is not zero. A net force is the force left after combining all forces. Magnitude means the size of a force.
keyPoints: Balanced forces are equal and opposite.
Unbalanced forces produce a non-zero net force.
Net force points towards the larger force.
activities.explanation: Opposite forces can balance, but unequal forces leave a net force.

activities.prompt: A floating ball is pulled downwards by Earth and pushed upwards by liquid. The two forces are equal and opposite. What happens to the net force?
steps: The liquid pushes the ball upwards because the liquid pushes it upwards.
The Earth pulls the ball downwards because the Earth pulls it downwards.
The forces are balanced because they are equal and act in opposite directions.
The net force is zero because balanced forces leave no unbalanced force.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Friction acts in the same direction as a push on a box.
activities.explanation: Friction acts against the push, not in the same direction.

activities.prompt: Equal forces acting in ______ directions are called balanced forces.
activities.hint: Think about two pushes facing each other.
activities.explanation: Balanced forces have equal sizes and opposite directions.

activities.prompt: Match each force situation with its net-force rule.
pairs: Forces producing a non-zero net force
Net force equals their magnitude difference
Net force equals the sum of their magnitudes
activities.explanation: Each pair uses the net-force rule given in the lesson.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in order for opposite, unequal forces.
items: Compare the sizes of the two forces.
Find the difference between their magnitudes.
Point the net force towards the larger force.
activities.explanation: The net force equals the difference and points towards the larger force.

activities.prompt: A rope has opposite, unequal forces. Which statement is correct?
options: It moves towards the larger force.
It moves towards the smaller force.
It stays still because the forces balance.
It moves in the same direction as both forces.
activities.explanation: Unbalanced forces make a rope move towards the larger force.

activities.prompt: Two forces act in the same direction. What is their net force?
options: The sum of their magnitudes.
The difference of their magnitudes.
The smaller magnitude alone.
The larger magnitude alone.
activities.explanation: Their magnitudes add together, and the net force acts in their direction.

activities.prompt: A floating ball is pulled down by Earth. The liquid pushes it upwards. The pulls are equal and opposite. What is the net force?
options: It is zero.
It points upward.
It points downward.
It equals their sum.

This mistake chooses the direction of the liquid's push.
This mistake chooses the direction of the Earth's pull.
This mistake uses the rule for forces in the same direction.

activities.explanation: This is right because equal opposite forces are balanced, so the net force is zero.

activities.prompt: Two people push the same cart in the same direction. Their pushes are unequal. What is the net force?
options: It is the sum, in the same direction.
It is the difference, in the same direction.
It is zero, with no direction.
It is the sum, in the opposite direction.

why.It is the difference, in the same direct: This mistake uses the rule for opposite unequal forces.
This mistake assumes that opposite forces are balanced.
why.It is the sum, in the opposite direction: This mistake reverses the direction of the net force.

activities.explanation: This is right because same-direction forces add and keep their direction.

activities.prompt: A floating ball is pulled down by Earth. The liquid pushes it upwards with a larger force. In which direction is the net force?
options: Upwards, towards the larger force.
Downwards, towards the larger force.
Downwards, towards the smaller force.
Upwards, towards the smaller force.

This mistake chooses the smaller force's direction.
This mistake chooses the smaller force's direction.
This mistake chooses the smaller force's direction.

activities.explanation: This is right because the net force points towards the larger force.

activities.prompt: A box is pushed across a floor. Friction acts opposite the push. The push is larger than friction. In which direction is the net force?
options: In the push direction.
In the friction direction.
There is no net force.
In both directions at once.

This mistake chooses the smaller force's direction.
This mistake treats the unequal forces as balanced.
This mistake thinks the net force can point in two directions.

activities.explanation: This is right because the net force points towards the larger force.

activities.prompt: A child claims, 'Any two opposite forces are balanced.' Which test would check this claim fairly?
options: Use two equal pulls in opposite directions.
Use one pull in only one direction.
Use two unequal pulls in opposite directions.
Use two pulls in the same direction.

why.Use two equal pulls in opposite directio: This is right because unequal opposite forces are not balanced.
This misses the claim because it uses equal forces.
This misses the claim because it does not use opposite forces.

activities.explanation: This misses the claim because it does not use opposite forces.

activities.prompt: Two forces act in opposite directions, but their magnitudes differ. What can be said about the net force?
options: A non-zero force towards the larger force.
A zero force towards the larger force.
A non-zero force towards the smaller force.
A zero force towards the smaller force.

This mistake treats opposite unequal forces as balanced.
why.A non-zero force towards the smaller for: This mistake points towards the smaller force instead of the larger one.
This mistake treats opposite unequal forces as balanced and chooses the smaller force.

activities.explanation: This is right because unequal opposite forces give a non-zero net force towards the larger force.

lessons.title: The Force of Friction

activities.prompt: What makes a sliding box slow down and stop?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Forces on a pushed box
activities.body: Friction is a force that acts opposite to the applied force on a pushed box. A box starts moving when the applied force is greater than friction. Its motion depends only on its net force. This means the combined effect of forces acting together. Weight pulls down, while the normal force pushes up. These two forces can balance each other.
keyPoints: Friction acts opposite to the applied force.
A box moves when the applied force is greater than friction.
Motion depends only on net force.
activities.explanation: Opposing forces can balance or help an object move.

activities.prompt: A child pushes a box, then stops. Why does the box stop?
steps: Friction acts opposite the applied force, so it changes the net force.
The box starts moving because the applied force is greater than friction.
Without a force to counter it, friction slows the moving box.
Therefore, the box stops without needing another push.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: More about friction
activities.body: Air also exerts friction on a moving box. This air friction is often small enough to neglect. A spring balance gives an approximate measure of friction. Different surfaces have different amounts of friction. Less friction lets a coin stack travel farther before stopping.
keyPoints: Air also exerts friction on a moving box.
Air friction is often small enough to neglect.
Less friction helps a coin stack travel farther.
activities.explanation: Air friction may be small, while a spring balance can measure friction approximately.

activities.title: Push a box
activities.prompt: A child pushes a box across the floor. Which statement is correct?
options: Friction acts in the same direction as the push.
Friction acts opposite to the push.
Friction acts in an upward direction.
Friction does not act on the box.
activities.explanation: Friction on a pushed box acts opposite to the applied force.

activities.prompt: A box starts moving when the applied force is greater than ______.
activities.hint: This force acts opposite to the applied force.
activities.explanation: The applied force overcomes friction, so the box starts moving.

activities.title: Match the forces
activities.prompt: Match each force or idea with its correct description.
pairs: Friction acts opposite to the applied force
Needs a force to counter friction
activities.explanation: Each pair matches the direction or role given in the lesson.

activities.title: Air friction
activities.prompt: Which statement about air friction is correct?
options: It acts only on a stationary box.
It is always greater than surface friction.
It is often small enough to neglect.
It makes a box move without any push.
activities.explanation: Air friction often has a small effect, so it may be neglected.

activities.title: The journey of a box
activities.prompt: Put these events in the correct order.
items: The applied force becomes greater than friction.
The box slows down and stops.
activities.explanation: The box starts when the push beats friction. Without the push, it slows and stops.

activities.title: Forces and motion
activities.prompt: Which statement about a box and its forces is correct?
options: Weight acts up; normal force acts down.
Friction acts with the push; motion depends on weight.
Air friction never acts; the push stops at once.
Weight and normal force balance; motion depends on net force.
activities.explanation: Weight and normal force balance. The motion of an object depends only on its net force.

activities.prompt: A child pushes a box harder than friction pushes back. What happens?
options: It starts moving because the push beats friction.
It stays still because weight holds it down.
It stays still because normal force helps the push.
It moves backward because friction pulls it forward.

why.It stays still because weight holds it d: This mistake thinks weight prevents a box from moving.
why.It stays still because normal force help: This mistake treats the upward normal force as a forward force.
why.It moves backward because friction pulls: This mistake reverses the direction of friction.

activities.explanation: The push is greater than friction, so the box starts moving.

activities.prompt: A moving box loses its applied force. What will happen to it?
options: It keeps moving because no force acts on it.
It speeds up because weight pulls it backward.
It stops at once because friction removes its motion.
It slows down and stops because friction still acts.

why.It keeps moving because no force acts on: This mistake ignores friction, which remains after the push.
why.It speeds up because weight pulls it bac: This mistake treats downward weight as a backward speeding force.
why.It stops at once because friction remove: Friction slows the box gradually; it does not remove motion at once.

activities.explanation: Friction slows and stops it because no force counters it.

activities.prompt: A coin stack slides on two different surfaces. Which travels farther?
options: The stack on the surface with more friction.
The stack on the surface with less friction.
Both coin stacks travel the same distance always.
Neither stack travels because air friction stops it.

why.The stack on the surface with more frict: More friction makes the coin stack stop sooner.
why.Both coin stacks travel the same distanc: This forgets that different surfaces have different friction amounts.
why.Neither stack travels because air fricti: This mistake thinks air friction always stops the coin stack.

activities.explanation: Less friction lets the coin stack travel farther before stopping.

lessons.title: Newton's First Law of Motion

activities.prompt: Why does a skateboard keep gliding even when nobody pushes it?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Motion and Inertia
activities.body: Galileo argued that a moving object would keep moving if nothing blocked its movement. Newton used inertia for an object's resistance to change in motion. An object at rest stays at rest. A moving object keeps constant velocity. Constant velocity means its size and direction do not change. A net force is needed to change this motion. With zero net force, acceleration is zero.
keyPoints: Objects resist changes in motion.
A net force is needed to change motion.
Constant velocity keeps the same size and direction.
activities.explanation: Inertia helps an object keep resting or moving steadily.

activities.prompt: A child pushes a toy car. Then no force acts. What happens?
steps: The push makes it begin moving because a net force is needed.
After the push ends, the net force is zero.
The car keeps moving because zero net force cannot change its velocity.
Its speed and direction stay unchanged because its velocity is constant.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: An object is at rest. What happens when the net force is zero?
options: Remains at rest
Starts moving slowly
Changes direction
Begins to rotate
activities.explanation: With zero net force, the object cannot begin moving.

activities.prompt: Galileo argued that an object would stop moving if all impediments were removed.
activities.explanation: Galileo argued that the object would keep moving if all impediments were removed.

activities.prompt: Newton used ______ to describe an object's resistance to change in motion.
activities.hint: This is Newton's word for resistance to change.
activities.explanation: Inertia describes an object's resistance to change in motion.

activities.prompt: Match each idea with its correct meaning.
pairs: Force needed to stop a moving object
activities.explanation: Each pair connects an idea from the lesson with its meaning.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in order when a moving object is stopped.
activities.explanation: A force changes the object's velocity before the object stops.

activities.prompt: Which statement correctly describes constant velocity?
options: Neither size nor direction changes
Only the size changes
Only the direction changes
Both size and direction change
activities.explanation: Constant velocity means that neither magnitude nor direction changes.

activities.prompt: A moving object can stop without any force changing its velocity.
activities.explanation: Stopping a moving object requires a force to change its velocity.

activities.prompt: A box moves forward. Equal forward and backward forces act. What happens?
options: It continues at constant velocity.
It slows down and stops.
It moves forward faster.
It begins moving backward.

This mistake assumes a backward force must reduce forward motion.
This mistake treats the backward force as a forward push.
This mistake assumes equal backward force must reverse the motion.

activities.explanation: This is right because equal forces cancel, so velocity stays constant.

activities.prompt: A moving box has equal opposite forces. What is its acceleration?
options: It stays zero.
It grows forward.
It grows backward.
It keeps changing.

This mistake assumes one forward force must cause acceleration.
This mistake assumes one backward force must cause acceleration.
This mistake thinks balanced forces can cause changing velocity.

activities.explanation: This is right because zero net force means zero acceleration.

lessons.title: Newton's Second Law of Motion

activities.prompt: What happens when the same push meets a heavier object?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Force Changes Motion
activities.body: A net force makes an object accelerate in its own direction. The acceleration points in the direction of the net force. Greater net force gives greater acceleration. Greater mass gives smaller acceleration. The equation F = ma links force, mass and acceleration. Momentum is an object's mass multiplied by its velocity.
keyPoints: Force produces acceleration.
More net force gives more acceleration.
More mass gives less acceleration.
activities.explanation: The equation joins force, mass and acceleration.

activities.prompt: Two toy cars receive the same net force. One car has less mass. Which car accelerates more?
steps: The same net force pushes both toy cars.
The car with less mass has a smaller mass.
For the same force, smaller mass gives greater acceleration.
So, the lighter toy car accelerates more.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: The equation F = ___ links force, mass and acceleration.
activities.hint: Write the two symbols on the right.
activities.explanation: The equation F = ma links force, mass and acceleration.

activities.prompt: Match each cause or object with its result.
pairs: Larger acceleration for the same object
Larger acceleration at the same force
Acceleration of 1 m s–2 for a 1 kg mass
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a relationship stated in the lesson.

activities.prompt: A net force acts on a ball. Which statement is correct?
options: The ball accelerates opposite the force's direction.
The ball stays still despite the force.
The ball accelerates in the force's direction.
The ball's acceleration ignores the force.
activities.explanation: The acceleration points in the direction of the net force.

activities.prompt: Momentum is the product of an object's mass and ______.
activities.hint: Think about what tells you how fast an object moves.
activities.explanation: Momentum equals mass multiplied by velocity.

activities.prompt: An airbag reduces the force on a person by decreasing stopping time.
activities.explanation: An airbag increases stopping time, so the force is reduced.

activities.prompt: Why does a fielder increase stopping time while catching a ball?
options: To increase the momentum of the ball.
To reduce the force on their hands.
To increase the mass of the ball.
To increase the force on their hands.
activities.explanation: Increasing stopping time reduces the force on the fielder's hands.

activities.prompt: Two children push the same empty box in the same direction. One pushes alone, while both push together. How does the acceleration change?
options: It increases because the net force is larger.
It decreases because more pushers mean more force.
It stays the same because the box's mass is unchanged.
It becomes zero because two pushes make no net force.

why.It decreases because more pushers mean m: This wrongly treats a larger force as giving less acceleration.
why.It stays the same because the box's mass: This ignores that a larger force gives greater acceleration.
why.It becomes zero because two pushes make: This wrongly assumes two same-direction pushes cancel.

activities.explanation: A larger force on the same box gives greater acceleration.

activities.prompt: Two toy carts receive the same net force. One is empty, and one is full. Which accelerates more?
options: The empty cart, because it has less mass.
The full cart, because it has more mass.
Neither cart, because the same force gives no acceleration.
Both carts, because the same force gives equal acceleration.

This confuses more mass with greater acceleration.
why.Neither cart, because the same force giv: This wrongly believes force cannot produce acceleration.
why.Both carts, because the same force gives: This ignores that different masses have different accelerations.

activities.explanation: For the same force, the cart with less mass accelerates more.

activities.prompt: A toy car is pushed right and pulled left. The rightward net force is larger. Which way does the car accelerate?
options: It accelerates right, in the direction of the net force.
It accelerates left, in the direction of the left push.
It stays still, because two pushes cancel the acceleration.
It turns around, because the right push acts longer.

why.It accelerates left, in the direction of: This follows the smaller push instead of the net force.
why.It stays still, because two pushes cance: This wrongly assumes that any two pushes cancel acceleration.
why.It turns around, because the right push: This wrongly uses push time instead of net force.

activities.explanation: The acceleration points in the direction of the larger net force.

activities.prompt: A heavy trolley and a light toy car move together. They have the same velocity. Which object has more momentum?
options: The heavy trolley, because its mass is larger.
The light toy car, because its mass is smaller.
Both have the same momentum, because their velocities are equal.
Neither has momentum, because momentum needs acceleration.

why.The light toy car, because its mass is s: This confuses smaller mass with greater momentum.
why.Both have the same momentum, because the: This ignores mass and wrongly thinks velocity alone fixes momentum.
why.Neither has momentum, because momentum n: This wrongly believes momentum needs acceleration instead of mass and velocity.

activities.explanation: Momentum is mass times velocity, so the larger mass gives more momentum.
