lessons.title: Newton's Third Law and Systems

activities.prompt: Why do you feel pushed when you push something?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Forces Come in Pairs
activities.body: A force appears when at least two objects interact. In every interaction, one object exerts an equal and opposite force on another. These paired forces have equal magnitudes, but they act on different objects. This is Newton's third law. Walking and paddling show this rule when the ground or water pushes forwards.
keyPoints: Forces appear when objects interact.
The paired forces are equal and opposite.
Each paired force acts on a different object.
activities.explanation: Every interaction contains a pair of equal and opposite forces acting on different objects.

activities.prompt: Why do you feel pushed back when you kick a ball?
steps: Kicking means your foot and the ball interact.
Your foot pushes the ball, so the ball pushes your foot.
These paired forces have equal magnitudes but opposite directions.
That push from the ball is why your foot feels pushed back.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Analysing a System
activities.body: To analyse a system, focus only on forces from outside it. For a system with two boxes, its acceleration uses the boxes' combined mass. Equal and opposite forces need not produce equal accelerations. Remember that paired forces act on different objects. This helps you analyse the system without judging each force by one object alone.
keyPoints: Only outside forces matter in a system.
A two-box system uses combined mass.
Equal and opposite forces can give unequal accelerations.
activities.explanation: Outside forces matter, and a two-box system's acceleration uses combined mass.

activities.title: A Force from the Ball
activities.prompt: In the ball-kicking example, which object exerts a force on you?
options: The ball
The ground
The paddle
The water
activities.explanation: Kicking a ball makes you feel a force from the ball.

activities.title: Match Each Action
activities.prompt: Match each action to the partner force described in the lesson.
pairs: The ground pushes our feet forwards
The water pushes its paddle forwards
activities.explanation: Each pair connects an action with its paired force.

activities.prompt: The paired forces in an interaction act on the same object.
activities.explanation: Paired forces act on two different objects.

activities.title: Equal Strength
activities.prompt: The two forces in an interaction have equal ______.
activities.hint: Think about how strong each force is.
activities.explanation: The two forces in an interaction have equal magnitudes.

activities.title: Choosing the Right Forces
activities.prompt: When analysing a system, which forces should you use?
options: Only forces from outside
Only forces from inside
Forces from every part
No forces at all
activities.explanation: Only forces from outside the system matter during its analysis.

activities.title: Mass of a Two-Box System
activities.prompt: The acceleration of a two-box system uses their ______ mass.
activities.hint: Add the masses of both boxes.
activities.explanation: The acceleration of a two-box system uses their combined mass.

activities.prompt: You kick a ball. What will your foot feel, and why?
options: The ball pushes your foot with an equal force.
The ball pulls your foot with an equal force.
The ball pushes your foot with a stronger force.
The ball does not push your foot at all.

why.The ball pulls your foot with an equal f: The ball's force on your foot is a push, not a pull.
why.The ball pushes your foot with a stronge: The ball's force has the same magnitude as your foot's force.
Kicking the ball makes you feel a force from the ball.

activities.explanation: The ball pushes your foot with an equal, opposite force.

activities.prompt: A moving toy car bumps a wall. What should happen to the forces?
options: The car and wall push each other with equal, opposite forces.
The car pushes the wall, but the wall only receives the force.
The wall pushes the car, but the car only receives the force.
Both forces act on the car, so neither acts on the wall.

why.The car pushes the wall, but the wall on: This forgets the wall's equal, opposite push on the car.
why.The wall pushes the car, but the car onl: This forgets the car's equal, opposite push on the wall.
why.Both forces act on the car, so neither a: Paired forces must act on two different objects.

activities.explanation: Both objects interact, so each receives an equal, opposite force.

activities.prompt: A child walks forwards on the ground. What makes the child move forwards?
options: The ground pushes the child's feet forwards.
The child's feet push the ground forwards.
The ground pulls the child's feet forwards.
The child's shoes pull the ground backwards.

why.The child's feet push the ground forward: This is the other force, not the push moving the child.
why.The ground pulls the child's feet forwar: Walking uses the ground's push, not a pull on the feet.
why.The child's shoes pull the ground backwa: This reverses the paired forces and their directions.

activities.explanation: Walking forwards happens because the ground pushes our feet forwards.

activities.prompt: A canoe and paddler form a system. Which outside push moves it forwards?
options: The water pushes the paddle forwards.
The paddle pushes the water forwards only.
The paddler pulls the canoe forwards.
The canoe pushes the paddle backwards.

why.The paddle pushes the water forwards onl: This leaves out the water's equal, opposite push on the paddle.
The forward push comes from the water acting on the paddle.
This reverses which object receives the forward push.

activities.explanation: The water's push on the paddle moves the canoe forwards.

activities.prompt: One box and two tied boxes get equal outside pulls. Which prediction is fair?
options: Their accelerations can differ because their combined masses differ.
Their accelerations must match because the outside pulls match.
Only the one-box system can have an acceleration.
Their accelerations depend only on how many boxes are tied.

why.Their accelerations must match because t: This mistakes equal forces for equal accelerations.
why.Only the one-box system can have an acce: Both systems can accelerate when an outside pull acts.
why.Their accelerations depend only on how m: Acceleration uses the boxes' mass, not only their number.

activities.explanation: Equal forces need not give equal accelerations, and mass is combined.

activities.prompt: A magnet moves a paperclip without contact. Which force claim is fair?
options: The paired forces are equal and opposite on different objects.
Only contact interactions can have equal and opposite forces.
Non-contact forces can have different magnitudes during an interaction.
The magnet can push without any paired force acting back.

why.Only contact interactions can have equal: This wrongly limits Newton's third law to touching objects.
why.Non-contact forces can have different ma: The two forces in this interaction still have equal magnitudes.
why.The magnet can push without any paired f: An interacting magnet and paperclip still have a paired force.

activities.explanation: Newton's third law also applies to this non-contact interaction.

activities.context: A child places a model cart on the floor and pulls it with a force toward the left. The cart was at rest, but it begins moving when the force acts. The child then pulls with less force, so the cart slows, and later pulls toward the right, so its direction of motion changes. The child uses a spring balance to measure how strong the pull is. The cart's weight is the gravitational force with which Earth pulls it.
activities.prompt: Why did the cart begin moving?
options: The child's applied pull caused the resting cart to start moving.
The spring balance acted as the pull on the cart.
The cart's weight was the same as the child's pull.
Measuring the pull removed the cart's weight.

why.The spring balance acted as the pull on: A spring balance measures force rather than pulling the cart.
why.The cart's weight was the same as the ch: Weight is Earth's gravitational pull, not the child's applied pull.
why.Measuring the pull removed the cart's we: Measuring a force's magnitude does not remove the object's weight.

activities.explanation: A force can make an object move from rest.

activities.context: A child places a model cart on the floor and pulls it with a force toward the left. The cart was at rest, but it begins moving when the force acts. The child then pulls with less force, so the cart slows, and later pulls toward the right, so its direction of motion changes. The child uses a spring balance to measure how strong the pull is. The cart's weight is the gravitational force with which Earth pulls it.
activities.prompt: What happens if the child increases the magnitude of the pull while keeping its direction unchanged?
options: The pull would become a stronger force.
The pull would automatically point in the opposite direction.
The spring balance would no longer be able to measure it.
The cart's weight would become greater.

why.The pull would automatically point in th: Changing magnitude does not automatically reverse direction.
why.The spring balance would no longer be ab: A spring balance can measure the magnitude of a force.
A stronger applied pull does not increase the object's weight.

activities.explanation: Magnitude tells us how strong a force is.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Changing the magnitude of a force changes its effect.
Reason (R): The magnitude of a force tells us how strong it is.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason explains why changing magnitude changes the force's effect.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A spring balance can measure the direction of a force.
Reason (R): The direction of a force must be stated clearly.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false, while the reason is true but does not explain it.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between the magnitude and direction of a force, and state how each can be checked.
activities.answer: Magnitude tells us how strong a force is, while direction tells us which way it acts. Both parts must be clear when a force is described. A spring balance can be used to measure the magnitude of a force, but the direction must still be stated clearly. Changing either the magnitude or the direction changes the effect of the force. The SI unit used for the magnitude of force is the newton.
points: Magnitude means how strong the force is.
Direction means which way the force acts.
A spring balance measures magnitude.
Magnitude is measured in newtons.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A boy pushes a box across a floor. Friction acts in the direction opposite to his push. He pulls a rope attached to the box, while another boy pulls the other end in the opposite direction. Their pulls are unequal, so the rope moves toward the stronger pull. On a nearby table, a floating ball is pulled downwards by the Earth and pushed upwards by the liquid.
activities.prompt: Which statement describes the net force on the box if the boy’s push becomes larger than friction?
options: It will be non-zero and point in the direction of the push.
It will be non-zero and point in the direction of friction.
It will be zero because the two forces act in opposite directions.
It will point in the direction in which the rope is being pulled.

why.It will be non-zero and point in the dir: The net force equals the difference between their magnitudes.
why.It will be zero because the two forces a: Since the push is larger, the net force points toward the push.
why.It will point in the direction in which: The rope’s direction does not determine the forces on the box.

activities.explanation: The push and friction are opposite but unequal forces.

activities.context: A boy pushes a box across a floor. Friction acts in the direction opposite to his push. He pulls a rope attached to the box, while another boy pulls the other end in the opposite direction. Their pulls are unequal, so the rope moves toward the stronger pull. On a nearby table, a floating ball is pulled downwards by the Earth and pushed upwards by the liquid.
activities.prompt: If the second boy increases his pull until his force is larger than the first boy’s force, what will happen next?
options: The rope will move in the second boy’s direction.
The rope will move toward the first boy.
The rope will stay still because both boys are pulling.
The rope will move in the direction of the smaller force.

The net force is the difference between their magnitudes.
why.The rope will stay still because both bo: The net force points toward the larger pull.
why.The rope will move in the direction of t: A rope moves toward the larger force when the forces are unbalanced.

activities.explanation: The two pulls act in opposite directions.

activities.context: A boy pushes a box across a floor. Friction acts in the direction opposite to his push. He pulls a rope attached to the box, while another boy pulls the other end in the opposite direction. Their pulls are unequal, so the rope moves toward the stronger pull. On a nearby table, a floating ball is pulled downwards by the Earth and pushed upwards by the liquid.
activities.prompt: Why does the floating ball have a non-zero net force if the Earth’s pull is larger than the liquid’s push?
options: The forces are opposite but unequal, so their difference is non-zero.
The forces are equal and opposite, so they cancel completely.
The forces act in the same direction, so their magnitudes are added.
The Earth does not pull the ball, so only the liquid’s force acts.

why.The forces act in the same direction, so: The net force equals the difference between opposite unequal forces.
why.The Earth does not pull the ball, so onl: That difference is non-zero when the forces are unequal.

activities.explanation: The Earth’s pull and the liquid’s push act in opposite directions.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): If a box is pushed with a force larger than friction, the net force points in the direction of the push.
Reason (R): For opposite unequal forces, the net force equals the difference between their magnitudes and points toward the larger force.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason gives the rule that directly explains the direction of the net force.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A floating ball has a non-zero net force when the Earth’s downward pull is larger than the liquid’s upward push.
Reason (R): The Earth pulls the floating ball downwards.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but the reason does not explain that the two opposite forces are unequal.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between balanced and unbalanced forces?
activities.answer: Balanced forces are equal forces acting in opposite directions, such as the Earth’s downward pull on a floating ball and an equal upward push from the liquid. Unbalanced forces include opposite forces of unequal size and forces acting in the same direction. They produce a non-zero net force. For opposite unequal forces, the net force equals the difference between their magnitudes and points toward the larger force. For forces in the same direction, the net force equals their sum and acts in that same direction.
points: Balanced forces are equal and opposite.
Balanced forces have a zero net force.
Unbalanced forces have a non-zero net force.
Opposite unequal forces have a net force equal to their difference.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student pushes a box across a surface with a spring balance attached. The box begins to move when the push becomes greater than friction. While the box moves, the push acts in one direction and friction acts in the opposite direction. Air also exerts friction, although this air friction is often small enough to neglect. The box slows and stops after the push is removed. Later, the student tests a coin stack on a surface with less friction.
activities.prompt: What would happen if the push were only equal to friction?
options: The box would remain at rest.
The box would move faster in the direction of the push.
The box would move in the direction opposite to the push.
The box would move at the same speed in the direction of the push.

why.The box would move faster in the directi: A push equal to friction does not make the box move faster.
why.The box would move in the direction oppo: The motion cannot begin opposite the push when the forces balance.
why.The box would move at the same speed in: An equal push does not create motion at the same speed.

activities.explanation: The box starts moving only when the push is greater than friction.

activities.context: A student pushes a box across a surface with a spring balance attached. The box begins to move when the push becomes greater than friction. While the box moves, the push acts in one direction and friction acts in the opposite direction. Air also exerts friction, although this air friction is often small enough to neglect. The box slows and stops after the push is removed. Later, the student tests a coin stack on a surface with less friction.
activities.prompt: What should the student expect when the coin stack is placed on a surface with less friction?
options: The stack will travel a greater distance before coming to rest.
The stack will stop sooner after being placed down.
The stack will travel the same distance as on a surface with more friction.
The stack will move farther only if the surface has more friction.

why.The stack will stop sooner after being p: Less friction does not cause the stack to stop sooner.
why.The stack will travel the same distance: Different amounts of friction affect how far the stack travels.
why.The stack will move farther only if the: More friction does not produce the greater travel described.

activities.explanation: Less friction allows the coin stack to travel farther before stopping.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Friction on a pushed box acts opposite to the applied force.
Reason (R): Friction acts in the same direction as the applied force.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is true, but the reason is false because friction acts opposite the applied force.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A box slows down and stops after the applied force is removed.
Reason (R): A moving object needs a force to counter friction.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the reason explains why the box slows down when the applied force is removed.

activities.prompt: Explain why a moving box slows down and stops after the applied force is removed.
activities.answer: When the push is removed, friction still acts opposite the box's motion. Because the box is moving, a force is needed to counter that friction. With the push gone, there is no applied force to balance the friction, so the net force acts in the direction of friction. Since an object's motion depends only on its net force, the box slows down and stops. The weight and normal force do not change this result: weight acts downward, the normal force acts upward, and they balance each other.
points: Friction acts opposite the motion.
A moving object needs a force to counter friction.
Without the push, the net force acts through friction.
Weight and normal force balance each other.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A child gives a toy box one forward push across a floor where no other force acts. The box is then moving forward while two children pull it with equal forward and backward forces. The child wonders whether the box needs another push to stay in motion, and whether it could suddenly change speed or direction without a net force.
activities.prompt: What will happen to the box while the two pulls remain equal?
options: It will move faster because the forward pull keeps acting.
It will stop because the backward pull cancels its motion.
It will continue moving with unchanged speed and direction.
It will begin moving in the backward direction.

why.It will move faster because the forward: Equal pulls produce zero net force, so the box cannot change its velocity.
why.It will stop because the backward pull c: Equal pulls do not stop the box; it continues with constant velocity.
why.It will begin moving in the backward dir: Zero net force cannot stop the forward motion or reverse the box.

activities.explanation: This correctly states that the box maintains constant velocity.

activities.context: A child gives a toy box one forward push across a floor where no other force acts. The box is then moving forward while two children pull it with equal forward and backward forces. The child wonders whether the box needs another push to stay in motion, and whether it could suddenly change speed or direction without a net force.
activities.prompt: What happens if one child pulls forward more strongly while the other pulls backward with the same force?
options: Its velocity stays unchanged because both children are still pulling.
Its velocity changes because a nonzero net force now acts.
Its velocity changes only after the box first comes to rest.
Its acceleration remains zero because the box is already moving.

why.Its velocity stays unchanged because bot: A nonzero net force is needed to change the box's velocity.
why.Its velocity changes only after the box: The box's velocity can change while it is moving.
why.Its acceleration remains zero because th: A net force is present, so its acceleration is not zero.

activities.explanation: The stronger forward pull creates a nonzero net force.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: How Forces Affect Motion

activities.prompt: Which statement about forces is true?
options: They can change an object's shape.
They only make resting objects move.
They never change an object's speed.
They always keep an object's shape.
activities.explanation: A force can move an object, change its motion, or change its shape.

activities.prompt: Friction on a pushed box acts in the same direction as the push.
activities.explanation: Friction acts opposite to the push, not in the same direction.

activities.prompt: A spring balance can measure the ______ of a force.
activities.hint: This tells you how strong the force is.
activities.explanation: A spring balance gives the magnitude of a force.

activities.prompt: Match each force term with its correct meaning.
pairs: Tells how strong a force is
activities.explanation: Each pair matches the meaning given in your book.

activities.prompt: Put the box's movement steps in correct order.
items: The applied force is greater than friction.
The box slows down and stops.
activities.explanation: The box moves when the push overcomes friction, then stops after the push is removed.

activities.prompt: Which statement about interaction forces is correct?
options: They act on two different objects.
They act on one shared object.
They always act in one direction.
They can have different magnitudes.
activities.explanation: Interaction forces have equal magnitudes and opposite directions, but act on different objects.

activities.prompt: Equal and opposite interaction forces always produce equal accelerations.
activities.explanation: Equal and opposite forces do not always produce equal accelerations.

activities.prompt: The equation F = ma links force, ______ and acceleration.
activities.hint: A smaller mass gives a larger acceleration for the same force.
activities.explanation: The equation links force, mass and acceleration.

activities.prompt: Match each item with its lesson link.
pairs: Gives larger acceleration for the same force
activities.explanation: These pairs show how forces, acceleration, momentum and stopping time are linked.

activities.prompt: The same force acts on two objects. Which object has the larger acceleration?
options: The object with smaller mass.
The object with larger mass.
Both objects equally.
Neither object accelerates.
activities.explanation: For the same force, a smaller mass gives a larger acceleration.

chapters.title: Work, Energy, and Simple Machines
chapters.summary: In this chapter: work done by a constant force; work, energy and forms of energy; kinetic energy and potential energy; gravitational potential energy and conservation.

lessons.title: Work Done by a Constant Force

activities.prompt: How can we discover what makes lifting a bag feel like more work?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Understanding Work
activities.body: A constant force stays the same while it acts. Displacement means how far an object moves in the force’s direction. Work equals force multiplied by displacement in that direction. A larger force over the same distance does more work. Zero force means zero work. No displacement in the force’s direction also means zero work. The sign depends on how force and displacement point. The SI unit is the joule.
keyPoints: Work = force multiplied by displacement in the force’s direction.
A larger force over the same distance means more work.
The sign depends on force and displacement directions; the unit is the joule.
activities.explanation: Force, displacement and their directions help you decide the work done.

activities.prompt: A child pulls a bag forward, then pushes harder over the same distance. Which action does more work?
steps: The first force and the bag's displacement point the same way.
This direction matters because work uses displacement along the force.
The stronger force acts through the same distance because the path is unchanged.
So the stronger push does more work because a larger force acts over that distance.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which calculation gives the work done by a constant force?
options: Force multiplied by displacement in the force’s direction.
Force divided by displacement in the force’s direction.
Force added to displacement in the force’s direction.
Force subtracted from displacement in the force’s direction.
activities.explanation: Exactly! Multiply force by displacement in the force’s direction.

activities.prompt: Work equals force multiplied by ______ in the force’s direction.
activities.hint: This means how far the object moves in the force’s direction.
activities.explanation: Exactly! Displacement is how far the object moves in that direction.

activities.prompt: What happens when a larger force acts over the same distance?
options: It does more work in proportion.
It does the same amount of work.
It does less work than before.
It does no work at all.
activities.explanation: Correct! A larger force over the same distance does proportionally more work.

activities.prompt: Match each work condition with its correct result.
pairs: Three bags at the same height
activities.explanation: Each pair links a condition with the work result it produces.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in the correct order for finding work.
items: Find displacement in the force’s direction.
activities.explanation: Multiply force by its displacement in the force’s direction, then use joules.

activities.prompt: Which information determines the sign of work?
options: The relative directions of force and displacement.
The values of force and displacement used.
The SI unit used for work done.
The number of bags that were lifted.
activities.explanation: Compare the directions of force and displacement to determine the sign.

activities.prompt: A child pulls a suitcase forward while it moves forward. What is the sign of the work?
options: The force and displacement point the same way, so work is positive.
The force and displacement point opposite ways, so work is positive.
The force and displacement point opposite ways, so work is zero.
The force and displacement point the same way, so work is zero.

why.The force and displacement point opposit: It treats opposite directions as if force and displacement matched.
It treats opposite directions as if there were no displacement.
why.The force and displacement point the sam: It assumes matching directions make the displacement count as zero.

activities.explanation: This is right because matching directions make the work positive.

activities.prompt: A suitcase slides while nobody pushes it. How much work does the applied force do?
options: No work, because the applied force is zero.
More work, because the suitcase still moves.
Some work, because the suitcase has a displacement.
No work can be done because the suitcase is moving.

why.More work, because the suitcase still mo: It mistakes movement for an applied force.
why.Some work, because the suitcase has a di: It mistakes displacement alone for work.
why.No work can be done because the suitcase: It assumes a moving object must still have an applied force.

activities.explanation: This is right because zero applied force means zero work.

activities.prompt: A child holds a bag still for a moment, so it does not move. How much work does the holding force do?
options: Zero work, because the bag has no displacement during holding.
Full work, because the child holds the bag upward.
More work, because the child's arm gets tired.
Some work, because the bag stays above the floor.

why.Full work, because the child holds the b: It confuses holding a force with doing work through movement.
why.More work, because the child's arm gets: It confuses tiredness with displacement in the force's direction.
why.Some work, because the bag stays above t: It mistakes staying above the floor for displacement.

activities.explanation: This is right because no displacement means no work by the holding force.

activities.prompt: Two children push separate carts the same distance. One child pushes with a larger force. What happens to the work?
options: The stronger push does more work over that distance.
The weaker push does more work over that distance.
Both pushes do equal work over that distance.
Neither push does any work over that distance.

why.The weaker push does more work over that: It reverses the effect of using a larger force.
why.Both pushes do equal work over that dist: It ignores that the larger force changes the work.
why.Neither push does any work over that dis: It assumes any push produces no work.

activities.explanation: This is right because a larger force gives more work over the same distance.

activities.prompt: Three shopping bags must be lifted to the same height. How much work is needed?
options: Three times as much work as lifting one bag.
One third as much work as lifting one bag.
The same work as lifting one bag.
No work, because every bag reaches one height.

why.One third as much work as lifting one ba: It reverses the comparison between three bags and one bag.
It ignores that lifting three bags needs more work.
why.No work, because every bag reaches one h: It confuses reaching the same height with doing no work.

activities.explanation: This is right because lifting three bags needs three times as much work.

activities.prompt: A child pulls a toy wagon forward while it slides backward. What is the sign of the work?
options: Negative, because the force and displacement point opposite ways.
Positive, because the force and displacement point opposite ways.
Zero, because the force and displacement point opposite ways.
Positive, because the wagon moved through some distance.

why.Positive, because the force and displace: It ignores that opposing directions make the work negative.
why.Zero, because the force and displacement: It mistakes backward displacement for displacement with the force.
why.Positive, because the wagon moved throug: It treats opposite directions as if the displacement were absent.

activities.explanation: This is right because opposing directions make the work negative.

lessons.title: Work, Energy and Forms of Energy

activities.prompt: What happens to energy when a moving object slows down?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Energy and Work
activities.body: Energy is the capacity to do work. Work done on an object is closely related to its energy. The work-energy theorem says that work done equals the change in energy. Energy can change from one form into another. Mechanical energy comes from motion or position, while kinetic energy comes from motion.
keyPoints: Work done equals the change in energy.
Energy can change from one form into another.
Kinetic energy comes from motion.
activities.explanation: These are the main ideas about work and energy.

activities.prompt: A battery-powered toy car pushes a block. How does energy move from the circuit to the block?
steps: The circuit transfers energy to the toy car.
The car changes that energy into kinetic energy because it moves.
This mechanical energy lets the car do work on the block.
Work done on the block equals the block's energy change.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: How Energy Moves
activities.body: Energy can move between objects as heat. The Sun sends energy to Earth through radiation. Electric circuits also transfer energy. The work-energy theorem holds for a group of objects. It also holds when acting forces are not constant. These ideas connect work, transfers, and changes of energy form.
keyPoints: Heat transfers energy between objects.
The Sun's energy reaches Earth by radiation.
Electric circuits transfer energy.
activities.explanation: These examples show that energy can move and change.

activities.title: What Is Energy?
activities.prompt: What does an object possess when it can do work?
options: Heat
Motion
Work
Energy
activities.explanation: Great choice. Energy is the capacity to do work.

activities.title: Work and Energy
activities.prompt: Work done on an object and the object's energy are closely related.
activities.explanation: Correct. Work done equals the change in an object's energy.

activities.title: Energy from Motion
activities.prompt: What is the energy possessed by an object because of its motion called?
options: Heat energy
Radiated energy
Kinetic energy
Electric energy
activities.explanation: Yes. Kinetic energy is the energy possessed because of motion.

activities.title: Motion and Position
activities.prompt: Energy possessed because of motion or position is called ______ energy.
activities.hint: Think about an object's motion and position.
activities.explanation: Yes. This form is called mechanical energy.

activities.title: Energy Transfer
activities.prompt: Match each energy-transfer situation with its description.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows an energy transfer described in the lesson.

activities.title: Changing Forces
activities.prompt: The work-energy theorem holds even when forces acting on an object are not constant.
activities.explanation: Correct. The theorem also holds when the acting forces are not constant.

activities.prompt: A rolling ball knocks over a paper cup. What does this show about the ball's mechanical energy?
options: Its motion gives it energy, so it can do work.
It has energy only while touching the paper cup.
The paper cup must transfer energy to the ball first.
Its energy comes only from the ball's final position.

why.It has energy only while touching the pa: This wrongly limits energy to the moment of contact.
why.The paper cup must transfer energy to th: This confuses the object doing work with the object affected.
why.Its energy comes only from the ball's fi: This wrongly says motion energy comes only from position.

activities.explanation: Motion gives the ball kinetic energy, so it can do work.

activities.prompt: A child pushes a toy cart. The push does work, and the cart gains energy. What should the child conclude about this change?
options: Work done on the cart equals the cart's energy change.
Work done on the cart equals the energy of other objects.
The cart's energy changes only when it stops moving.
Work and energy change are always completely separate.

why.Work done on the cart equals the energy: This confuses the cart's energy change with other objects' energy.
why.The cart's energy changes only when it s: This wrongly waits until stopping for the energy change.
why.Work and energy change are always comple: This denies the close link between work and energy.

activities.explanation: Work done on the cart equals the cart's energy change.

activities.prompt: Two children push a box. We treat the children and box as one system. An outside push does work on this system. What should the student find?
options: Its energy change equals the work done on it.
Each child's energy change equals the whole system's change.
The box's energy change alone equals the system's change.
Its energy stays unchanged because the work was done inside.

why.Each child's energy change equals the wh: This mixes an individual child's work with the whole system's change.
why.The box's energy change alone equals the: This mixes the box alone with the energy of the whole system.
why.Its energy stays unchanged because the w: This wrongly ignores the work done from outside the system.

activities.explanation: The theorem applies to systems, so work equals their energy change.

activities.prompt: A toy car moves while its push changes strength. How should the student apply the work-energy theorem?
options: Find work done, then find the car's energy change.
Ignore the theorem because the push is not constant.
Find the energy change only after the car stops.
Use one force strength for the whole motion.

why.Ignore the theorem because the push is n: This wrongly assumes that constant forces are required.
why.Find the energy change only after the ca: This wrongly delays the energy change until stopping.
why.Use one force strength for the whole mot: This wrongly treats changing forces as one constant force.

activities.explanation: The work done still equals the car's energy change.

activities.prompt: Two spoons touch. One is warm, and the other is cool. The cool spoon becomes warm. How should the child explain this?
options: Energy moved to the cool spoon as heat.
The cool spoon made energy appear by becoming warm.
Heat moved from the cool spoon to the warm spoon.
No energy moved because the spoons only touched.

why.The cool spoon made energy appear by bec: This wrongly treats energy as something made from nothing.
why.Heat moved from the cool spoon to the wa: This reverses the heat transfer shown by the warming spoon.
why.No energy moved because the spoons only: This wrongly thinks touching cannot transfer energy.

activities.explanation: Energy can transfer from one object to another as heat.

activities.prompt: The Sun's energy reaches Earth by radiation. An electric circuit then runs a moving fan. Which energy story fits the facts?
options: Radiation brings Sun energy, and circuit energy becomes kinetic energy.
Radiation makes Sun energy, and circuit energy stays unchanged.
Heat carries Sun energy, and circuit energy becomes position energy.
Radiation brings Sun energy, but circuits cannot transfer energy.

why.Radiation makes Sun energy, and circuit: This mistakes radiation for making energy and misses its change.
why.Heat carries Sun energy, and circuit ene: This wrongly uses heat for Sun energy and position for motion.
why.Radiation brings Sun energy, but circuit: This denies that energy can be transferred in electric circuits.

activities.explanation: Sun energy arrives by radiation, and circuit energy can change form.

lessons.title: Kinetic Energy and Potential Energy

activities.prompt: What helps moving objects and stretched springs hold onto energy?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Energy in motion and storage
activities.body: Kinetic energy is the energy of movement. An object that does not move has zero kinetic energy. Kinetic energy depends on mass and velocity. Its SI unit is the joule, and it has no direction. Positive work can increase velocity and kinetic energy. Negative work can decrease both. Potential energy is stored through deformation. A deformed spring stores energy. A group of objects can store energy due to relative positions.
keyPoints: Moving objects have kinetic energy.
Mass and velocity affect kinetic energy.
Potential energy can be stored in deformation.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you connect movement, work, and stored energy.

activities.prompt: A ball changes speed, and its velocity doubles. How does its kinetic energy change?
steps: The moving ball has kinetic energy because all moving objects possess it.
Kinetic energy depends on mass and velocity, so a speed change matters.
After doubling velocity, the ball has four times its first kinetic energy.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Spot the moving object
activities.prompt: Which example shows an object with kinetic energy?
options: A bicycle parked in a garage
A bicycle moving along a road
A book lying on a shelf
A stone resting beside a path
activities.explanation: All moving objects possess kinetic energy. The bicycle on the road is moving.

activities.title: An object at rest
activities.prompt: An object that does not move has zero kinetic energy.
activities.explanation: An object that does not move is defined to have zero kinetic energy.

activities.title: Name the unit
activities.prompt: The SI unit of kinetic energy is the ______.
activities.hint: Use the unit given for kinetic energy.
activities.explanation: The SI unit of kinetic energy is the joule.

activities.title: What affects kinetic energy?
activities.prompt: What two things does kinetic energy depend on?
options: mass and direction
mass and deformation
mass and velocity
mass and work
activities.explanation: Kinetic energy depends on an object's mass and velocity.

activities.title: Negative work
activities.prompt: When negative work decreases velocity, kinetic energy increases.
activities.explanation: When negative work decreases velocity, kinetic energy decreases.

activities.title: Energy and its descriptions
activities.prompt: Match each energy idea with its description.
pairs: Stores energy and can do work
Can allow objects to store energy
activities.explanation: Movement gives kinetic energy. Deformation and relative positions can store energy.

activities.title: Positive work and energy
activities.prompt: Put this positive-work sequence in order.
activities.explanation: When positive work increases velocity, kinetic energy increases.

activities.title: Double the velocity
activities.prompt: When velocity doubles, kinetic energy becomes ______ times its previous value.
activities.hint: Compare the new kinetic energy with the previous value.
activities.explanation: If velocity doubles, kinetic energy becomes four times its previous value.

activities.prompt: One toy car has more mass and greater velocity than another. Which car has more kinetic energy?
options: The car with more mass and velocity has more kinetic energy.
The car with more mass has more kinetic energy because mass matters.
The car with greater velocity has more kinetic energy because velocity matters.
Neither car has kinetic energy because their masses are different.

why.The car with more mass has more kinetic: This forgets that the other car also has the greater velocity.
why.The car with greater velocity has more k: This forgets that the other car also has the greater mass.
why.Neither car has kinetic energy because t: Both cars move, so both have kinetic energy despite different masses.

activities.explanation: Kinetic energy depends on both mass and velocity, and this car has more of both.

activities.prompt: A push first speeds up a toy car. A backward pull then slows it. How does the car's kinetic energy change?
options: It first increases, then decreases as velocity changes.
It first decreases, then increases as velocity changes.
It stays the same because both pushes change its motion.
It becomes zero after either push changes its motion.

why.It first decreases, then increases as ve: This reverses the effects of positive and negative work.
why.It stays the same because both pushes ch: Changing velocity changes kinetic energy, so it does not stay constant.
why.It becomes zero after either push change: The car still moves after slowing, so its energy is not zero.

activities.explanation: Positive work raises velocity and energy, while negative work lowers both.

lessons.title: Gravitational Potential Energy and Conservation

activities.prompt: Why does a falling ball trade height for speed?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What is gravitational potential energy?
activities.body: Gravitational potential energy is the stored energy of the Earth-ball system. A ball higher above Earth’s surface has more potential energy. You can set potential energy to zero when the object lies on the ground. Raising an object needs force against its gravitational force, equal to its weight. The SI unit is the joule. During a fall, potential energy decreases as kinetic energy increases. Mechanical energy is their sum.
keyPoints: Mechanical energy is the sum of kinetic and potential energy.
The near-Earth relation is valid only near Earth’s surface.
Real pendulums lose energy through friction at the support and air resistance.
activities.explanation: These ideas connect height, falling energy, and energy losses.

activities.prompt: A ball falls toward Earth. Why do its two energies change?
steps: At first, the Earth-ball system stores potential energy.
As the ball falls, its height decreases, so potential energy decreases.
Lost potential energy becomes kinetic energy during the fall.
So the falling ball gains kinetic energy while losing potential energy.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Stored energy
activities.prompt: What is the stored energy of the Earth-ball system called?
options: gravitational potential energy
kinetic potential energy
mechanical potential energy
sound potential energy
activities.explanation: The stored energy of the Earth-ball system is called gravitational potential energy.

activities.title: The energy unit
activities.prompt: The SI unit of potential energy is ______.
activities.hint: Use the unit given in the lesson.
activities.explanation: The SI unit of potential energy is the joule.

activities.title: Energy during a fall
activities.prompt: During a fall, what happens to the ball’s energies?
options: Potential falls; kinetic grows
Potential grows; kinetic falls
Both energies grow together
Both energies shrink together
activities.explanation: As an object falls, its potential energy decreases while its kinetic energy increases.

activities.title: Energy meanings
activities.prompt: Match each energy idea to its meaning.
pairs: stored energy of the Earth-ball system
sum of kinetic and potential energy
activities.explanation: Each pair matches an energy idea with the meaning given in the lesson.

activities.title: Where the relation works
activities.prompt: The near-Earth gravitational potential energy relation is valid only:
options: only close to Earth’s surface
only far from Earth’s surface
only below Earth’s surface
at every distance from Earth
activities.explanation: The near-Earth gravitational potential energy relation is valid only near Earth’s surface.

activities.title: Energy losses in a pendulum
activities.prompt: Which losses occur in a real pendulum?
options: support friction and air resistance
support heat and water resistance
support sound and wind pressure
support light and magnetic pull
activities.explanation: Real pendulums lose energy through friction at the support and air resistance.

activities.prompt: A ball falls from a height. What happens to its potential and kinetic energies?
options: Potential energy decreases, while kinetic energy increases.
Potential energy increases, while kinetic energy decreases.
Both energies stay the same throughout the fall.
Potential energy becomes zero, while kinetic energy stays zero.

why.Potential energy increases, while kineti: This reverses the energy changes during a fall.
why.Both energies stay the same throughout t: This wrongly says that falling changes neither energy.
why.Potential energy becomes zero, while kin: This wrongly says that the falling ball has no kinetic energy.

activities.explanation: This correctly describes the energy changes during a fall.

activities.prompt: A ball and Earth form one system. A student wants to test how height changes stored energy. Which setup is fairest?
options: Compare two identical balls placed at different heights.
Compare two different balls placed at the same height.
Compare one ball’s weight with its height above ground.
Compare one ball’s motion with another ball’s motion.

why.Compare two different balls placed at th: It keeps height the same, so height cannot be tested.
why.Compare one ball’s weight with its heigh: It changes the balls and height together, so the test is mixed.
why.Compare one ball’s motion with another b: It compares motion instead of stored potential energy.

activities.explanation: It changes height while keeping the balls identical.

activities.prompt: A real pendulum swings many times. Why does its swinging eventually weaken?
options: Friction at the support and air resistance remove energy.
The ball loses all energy only at its highest point.
The pendulum gains energy whenever it moves downward.
The ground sets the pendulum’s potential energy to zero.

why.The ball loses all energy only at its hi: This puts energy loss at the highest point instead of resistance.
why.The pendulum gains energy whenever it mo: This wrongly says the pendulum gains energy while swinging.
why.The ground sets the pendulum’s potential: This wrongly uses the ground as the cause of energy loss.

activities.explanation: This names both ways the real pendulum loses energy.

activities.prompt: A ball is far above Earth’s surface. Can the student use the near-Earth potential energy relation?
options: No, because it works only near Earth’s surface.
Yes, because the relation works at every height.
Yes, because potential energy always uses joules.
No, because joules apply only near Earth.

why.Yes, because the relation works at every: This wrongly assumes the relation works at every height.
why.Yes, because potential energy always use: Joules give the unit, but not where the relation works.
why.No, because joules apply only near Earth: This wrongly treats the unit as a limit on where relation works.

activities.explanation: The relation is valid only near Earth’s surface.

lessons.title: Power

activities.prompt: How could we compare how quickly two athletes do the same job?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What is power?
activities.body: Power tells you how quickly work gets done. More work in the same time needs more power. Average power is work divided by time. Power is measured in watts. One watt means one joule of work each second. One horsepower equals 746 watts. The unit watt honours James Watt.
keyPoints: Power is the rate at which work is done.
Average power is work done divided by time taken.
The SI unit of power is the watt.
activities.explanation: Power shows how quickly work gets done.

activities.prompt: Two children move equal boxes in 5 seconds. One moves more. Who has more power?
steps: Power tells us how quickly work gets done, so time matters.
Moving more equal boxes means doing more work in the same time.
Both children use equal time, so more work means a greater rate.
Therefore, the child moving more boxes has more power.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Power in everyday life
activities.prompt: What does power tell you?
options: The rate of work
The amount of work
The time for work
The mass being moved
activities.explanation: Power is the rate at which work is done.

activities.title: Match power ideas
activities.prompt: Match each power idea to its meaning.
pairs: rate at which work is done
work done divided by time taken
activities.explanation: Each pair connects a power idea with its meaning.

activities.title: Finding average power
activities.prompt: How do you find average power?
options: Work divided by time
Time divided by work
Work added to time
Work multiplied by time
activities.explanation: Average power equals the work done divided by the time taken.

activities.title: Complete the definition
activities.prompt: Power is the rate at which ______ is done.
activities.hint: Think about what gets done quickly.
activities.explanation: Power measures how quickly work is done.

activities.title: Find average power
activities.prompt: Put these steps in order to find average power.
activities.explanation: Average power comes from dividing the work done by the time taken.

activities.title: A weightlifter's power
activities.prompt: The weightlifter lifts a 75 kg mass by 2 m in 5 seconds. Which power is needed?
options: 1 W
5 W
activities.explanation: The weightlifter needs 300 W for this lift.

activities.prompt: Power is the rate at which work is done. Sam and Lee each carry equal boxes up one flight. Sam finishes in 5 seconds, while Lee takes longer. Who has more power?
options: Sam has more power because he does the same work sooner.
Lee has more power because he takes more time.
Both have equal power because the work is equal.
Neither can be compared because power depends on mass.

why.Lee has more power because he takes more: This mistake treats taking longer as evidence of more power.
why.Both have equal power because the work i: This mistake thinks equal work alone makes power equal.
why.Neither can be compared because power de: This mistake confuses the mass carried with the rate of work.

activities.explanation: This is right because the same work is done sooner.

activities.prompt: Power is the rate at which work is done. Two helpers each have 5 seconds to move equal boxes. One helper moves more boxes than the other. Which helper uses more power?
options: The helper who moves more boxes uses more power.
The helper who moves fewer boxes uses more power.
Both helpers use equal power because their times match.
Power cannot be compared because the boxes look equal.

why.The helper who moves fewer boxes uses mo: This mistake reverses the link between more work and power.
why.Both helpers use equal power because the: This mistake ignores the different amounts of work done.
why.Power cannot be compared because the box: This mistake thinks equal-looking boxes make the powers equal.

activities.explanation: This is right because more work is done in the same time.

activities.prompt: Average power equals work divided by time taken. Two carts will do the same work. What should be measured to compare their power?
options: The time each cart takes to finish the same work
The mass of each cart before the work starts
The distance each cart rolls during the test
The colour of each cart before the work starts

why.The mass of each cart before the work st: This mistake assumes a heavier cart must have more power.
why.The distance each cart rolls during the: This mistake assumes distance measures power without using time.
why.The colour of each cart before the work: This mistake assumes colour can show the rate of work.

activities.explanation: This is right because average power uses the time taken.

activities.prompt: A weightlifter needs 300 W to lift a 75 kg mass by 2 m. The lift takes 5 seconds. What happens if the same lift is done in less time?
options: More power is needed because the same work is done sooner.
Less power is needed because the work is now smaller.
The same power is needed because the mass stays 75 kg.
No power can be compared because time does not matter.

why.Less power is needed because the work is: This mistake assumes the amount of work changes with time.
why.The same power is needed because the mas: This mistake assumes unchanged mass means unchanged power.
why.No power can be compared because time do: This mistake ignores time when finding average power.

activities.explanation: This is right because the same work in less time needs more power.

lessons.title: Simple Machines

activities.prompt: How can simple machines make a tough job feel easier?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What simple machines do
activities.body: Simple machines make work easier by changing the size or direction of the applied force. They cannot reduce the total work needed. The applied force is the effort. The force to overcome is the load. Mechanical advantage is the load divided by the effort. A pulley is a grooved wheel with a rope.
keyPoints: Simple machines change the size or direction of force.
The effort is applied force, and the load is the force overcome.
Mechanical advantage compares the load with the effort.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you compare different simple machines.

activities.prompt: A child uses a fixed pulley to raise a box. What changes?
steps: The child applies an effort to the rope.
The fixed pulley guides the rope and changes the effort's direction.
The effort's magnitude stays the same because fixed pulleys do not reduce it.
Therefore, the pull changes direction, but not magnitude.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Changing your pulling direction
activities.prompt: What does a fixed pulley change about the effort?
options: The effort's magnitude
The direction of effort
The total work required
The mechanical advantage
activities.explanation: A fixed pulley changes the effort's direction without reducing its magnitude.

activities.title: The force you apply
activities.prompt: The force applied to a machine is called the ______.
activities.hint: This is the force that you apply.
activities.explanation: The applied force is called the effort.

activities.title: Fixed pulley advantage
activities.prompt: A fixed pulley has a mechanical advantage of ______.
activities.hint: Its mechanical advantage is equal to one.
activities.explanation: A fixed pulley has a mechanical advantage of 1.

activities.title: Match the machine words
activities.prompt: Match each description with its correct word.
pairs: Rigid bar rotating about a fixed point
activities.explanation: Each description gives the meaning of a machine word.

activities.title: Finding mechanical advantage
activities.prompt: Which ratio gives the mechanical advantage of a machine?
options: Load divided by effort
Effort divided by load
Effort plus the load
Load minus effort
activities.explanation: Mechanical advantage is the ratio of the load to the effort.

activities.title: A movable pulley system
activities.prompt: Which statement about a movable pulley system is correct?
options: It can have mechanical advantage above 1.
It always has mechanical advantage equal to 1.
It always reduces the total work needed.
It always has no mechanical advantage.
activities.explanation: A movable pulley system can have a mechanical advantage greater than 1.

activities.prompt: A movable pulley system can have a mechanical advantage greater than 1. Its load is larger than its effort. What is its mechanical advantage?
options: One, because the load and effort are equal.
Less than one, because the load is larger than effort.
One, because every pulley system has the same advantage.
Greater than one, because the load is larger than effort.

why.One, because the load and effort are equ: This is wrong because the load and effort are not equal.
why.One, because every pulley system has the: This wrongly assumes every pulley system has advantage one.

activities.explanation: Correct: a larger load than effort gives an advantage above one.

activities.prompt: An inclined plane helps move a heavy load to a higher level. Simple machines cannot reduce the total work required for a task. A child says moving the box feels easier. Which explanation fits both facts?
options: It reduces the total work while the load stays unchanged.
It changes the force needed, but total work stays the same.
It removes all effort even though the load still rises.
It increases the total work because moving feels easier.

why.It reduces the total work while the load: This mistake confuses easier movement with less work.
why.It removes all effort even though the lo: This mistake thinks easier movement means no effort.
why.It increases the total work because movi: This mistake thinks feeling easier means more work.

activities.explanation: Correct: easier movement does not reduce total work.

activities.prompt: A fixed pulley has a mechanical advantage of 1. A design claims it can make the load twice the effort. What does this show about the design's claim?
options: The claim is wrong because load and effort must be equal.
The claim is possible because fixed pulleys increase force.
The claim is wrong because load must be lighter than effort.
The claim is possible because fixed pulleys reduce work.

why.The claim is possible because fixed pull: This wrongly treats a fixed pulley as a force increaser.
why.The claim is wrong because load must be: This wrongly expects a fixed pulley to have advantage below one.
why.The claim is possible because fixed pull: This wrongly assumes a fixed pulley can reduce work.

activities.explanation: Correct: mechanical advantage one means load equals effort.

activities.prompt: A longer effort arm reduces the effort needed to move the same load. A child wants to test this using levers. Which test is fair?
options: Keep the effort arm and change only the load.
Use different loads and change only the effort arm.
Use the same load and change only the effort arm.
Use different loads and different effort arms together.

why.Keep the effort arm and change only the: Changing the load does not test the effort arm alone.
why.Use different loads and change only the: Different loads would change more than the effort arm.
why.Use different loads and different effort: Changing both hides which change caused the result.

activities.explanation: Correct: changing only effort arm gives a fair test.
