activities.context: A student lifts a school bag through a vertical path, applying an upward force while the bag’s displacement is also upward. At first, one bag is raised to a chosen height. The student then raises three separate bags to that same height, using an upward applied force, and later repeats the lift with a stronger upward force over the same distance.
activities.prompt: If the student stops applying any upward force while holding the bag at the same position, what will happen to the work done on the bag?
options: No work will be done on the bag.
Work will still be done because the bag has changed position.
Work will be done because the upward displacement remains.
Work will increase if the bag is lifted farther.

why.Work will still be done because the bag: Movement alone does not produce work when the applied force is zero.
why.Work will be done because the upward dis: Displacement matters only in relation to the applied force.
why.Work will increase if the bag is lifted: Increasing displacement cannot produce work when the applied force remains zero.

activities.explanation: A zero applied force means that no work is done.

activities.context: A student lifts a school bag through a vertical path, applying an upward force while the bag’s displacement is also upward. At first, one bag is raised to a chosen height. The student then raises three separate bags to that same height, using an upward applied force, and later repeats the lift with a stronger upward force over the same distance.
activities.prompt: If the student uses a larger upward force over the same distance, how will the work done change?
options: It will increase in direct proportion to the applied force.
It will remain unchanged because the distance is unchanged.
It will increase by a fixed amount regardless of the force.
It will decrease as the applied force becomes larger.

why.It will remain unchanged because the dis: An unchanged distance does not cancel a larger force when finding the product.
why.It will increase by a fixed amount regar: The change is proportional to the force, not a fixed increase.
why.It will decrease as the applied force be: A larger force over the same distance produces proportionally more work.

activities.explanation: Work equals force multiplied by displacement in the force’s direction.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Lifting three bags to the same height requires three times as much work as lifting one bag.
Reason (R): With the same force and displacement for each bag, adding the work calculation for three lifts gives three times the work for one lift.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason applies the work formula to each of the three equal lifts and explains the threefold total.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): When there is no displacement in the direction of the force, the work done is zero.
Reason (R): The work is zero because the applied force is zero.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: A zero force is not required for zero work when there is no displacement in the force’s direction.

activities.prompt: Explain why using a larger force over the same distance results in more work.
activities.answer: Work done by a constant force is found by multiplying the force by the displacement in the direction of that force. When the force becomes larger but the displacement stays the same, the product becomes proportionally larger. The applied force also acts in the same direction as the displacement, so the work is positive. Therefore, increasing the force over the same distance increases the work in the same proportion as the force.
points: States that work equals force multiplied by displacement in the force’s direction.
Explains that the distance remains unchanged.
States that the increase in work is proportional to the increase in force.
Mentions that the force and displacement act in the same direction.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student places a small electric fan near a sunny window. The Sun’s energy reaches Earth by radiation. Energy from the solar source is transferred through an electric circuit to the fan, where it changes into energy associated with the motion of the blades. The moving blades possess mechanical energy, and the energy they possess because of motion is kinetic energy. The student wonders what would happen if the circuit stopped transferring energy.
activities.prompt: If the circuit stopped transferring energy to the fan, which statement best describes the energy situation?
options: The blades can no longer gain kinetic energy from the circuit.
The blades will immediately gain more kinetic energy from radiation at the window.
The blades’ mechanical energy will change into kinetic energy.
The circuit will continue transferring energy even though it has stopped.

why.The blades will immediately gain more ki: Radiation alone does not make the blades gain kinetic energy.
why.The blades’ mechanical energy will chang: A form of energy cannot create motion energy without motion.
why.The circuit will continue transferring e: Energy transfer cannot continue after the transfer has stopped.

activities.explanation: The circuit transfers energy to the fan.

activities.context: A student places a small electric fan near a sunny window. The Sun’s energy reaches Earth by radiation. Energy from the solar source is transferred through an electric circuit to the fan, where it changes into energy associated with the motion of the blades. The moving blades possess mechanical energy, and the energy they possess because of motion is kinetic energy. The student wonders what would happen if the circuit stopped transferring energy.
activities.prompt: What should the student do first if the fan blades stop moving?
options: Check whether energy is actually being transferred through the electric circuit.
Use radiation reaching Earth as proof that the blades are moving.
Replace the circuit’s energy transfer with heat transfer to another object.
Assume that the Sun has stopped sending energy by radiation.

why.Use radiation reaching Earth as proof th: Radiation reaching Earth does not prove that the blades move.
why.Replace the circuit’s energy transfer wi: Heat transfer to another object does not check the fan’s circuit.
why.Assume that the Sun has stopped sending: The blades may stop even while radiation continues reaching Earth.

activities.explanation: Energy transfer through the circuit supplies energy for blade movement.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Work done on an object equals the change in that object’s energy.
Reason (R): The theorem is based on the close relationship between work done and an object’s energy.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The stated relationship between work and energy explains the theorem.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Energy can be transferred from one object to another as heat.
Reason (R): Energy cannot change from one form into another.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is true, but the reason is false because energy can change forms.

activities.prompt: Explain how the work-energy theorem connects work done on an object with energy, including when forces are not constant.
activities.answer: When work is done on an object, its energy changes. This close connection is expressed by the work-energy theorem, which states that the work done equals the change in energy. The theorem is not restricted to situations in which forces remain constant, because it also holds when the forces acting on an object are not constant. The same principle can be applied to a system of objects rather than being limited to one object.
points: Work done on an object changes its energy.
Work done equals the change in energy.
The theorem applies to systems of objects.
The theorem also applies when forces are not constant.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a school activity, a student pushes a football across the floor. The football moves faster after the push, so the student says its kinetic energy has increased. The student then stops the football and watches it remain still, saying its kinetic energy is now zero. Nearby, a spring is compressed and released, making the spring able to do work. The student also arranges several blocks at different relative positions and says their arrangement can store energy.
activities.prompt: If the student gives the already moving football another push that increases its velocity, what will happen to its kinetic energy?
options: It will increase because the velocity increased.
It will decrease because the football is moving.
It will remain unchanged because the football was already moving.
It will become four times larger because the velocity changed.

why.It will decrease because the football is: Being moving alone does not make kinetic energy fall.
why.It will remain unchanged because the foo: An unchanged mass does not cancel a velocity increase.
why.It will become four times larger because: Four times applies when velocity doubles, not whenever it changes.

activities.explanation: Positive work raises velocity, so kinetic energy rises.

activities.context: During a school activity, a student pushes a football across the floor. The football moves faster after the push, so the student says its kinetic energy has increased. The student then stops the football and watches it remain still, saying its kinetic energy is now zero. Nearby, a spring is compressed and released, making the spring able to do work. The student also arranges several blocks at different relative positions and says their arrangement can store energy.
activities.prompt: Why is the deformed spring able to do work?
options: Its deformation has stored energy within it.
Its motion has given it kinetic energy.
Its unchanged relative positions prevent energy storage.
Negative work has removed its energy.

The spring's energy storage comes from deformation, not motion.
why.Its unchanged relative positions prevent: The case identifies deformation as the source of the spring's stored energy.
The spring is not described as losing energy through negative work.

activities.explanation: Deformation stores energy, allowing the spring to do work.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): If velocity doubles, the kinetic energy becomes four times its previous value.
Reason (R): Kinetic energy has no direction.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but having no direction does not explain the change in kinetic energy.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A deformed spring stores energy and gains a capacity to do work.
Reason (R): A deformed spring stores this energy only when it is moving.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is true, but the reason is false because the energy is stored through deformation.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between kinetic energy and potential energy.
activities.answer: Kinetic energy is the energy possessed by a moving object. An object that does not move is defined to have zero kinetic energy, and kinetic energy depends on the object's mass and velocity. Its SI unit is the joule, and it has no direction. Potential energy is energy stored through an object's deformation. For example, a deformed spring stores energy and gains a capacity to do work. A system can also store energy because of the relative positions of its objects. Thus, kinetic energy is connected with motion, while potential energy is connected with stored energy.
points: Kinetic energy is possessed by moving objects.
A non-moving object is defined as having zero kinetic energy.
Kinetic energy depends on mass and velocity.
Potential energy is stored through deformation or relative positions.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A ball at a greater height above Earth’s surface has greater gravitational potential energy.
Reason (R): The ball must be raised against a gravitational force equal to its weight.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and raising the ball against its weight explains the increase in potential energy.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A real pendulum continues to have the same mechanical energy despite friction and air resistance.
Reason (R): The pendulum loses energy through friction at the support and air resistance.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false, while the reason correctly states that the pendulum loses energy.

activities.prompt: Explain how the energy of the ball changes when it is raised from the ground and then released near Earth’s surface.
activities.answer: When the ball lies on the ground, its potential energy can be defined as zero. Raising it against a gravitational force equal to its weight increases its height above Earth’s surface, so its gravitational potential energy becomes greater. When the ball is released, its potential energy decreases while its kinetic energy increases. The lost potential energy is converted into kinetic energy during the fall. Mechanical energy is the sum of the ball’s kinetic and potential energy. The near-Earth potential-energy relation is valid only near Earth’s surface.
points: Potential energy is set to zero at ground level.
Raising the ball increases its height and potential energy.
Potential energy is converted into kinetic energy during the fall.
Mechanical energy is the sum of kinetic and potential energy.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Work, Energy, and Simple Machines

activities.title: Force and movement
activities.prompt: Which statement about the applied force is correct?
options: It acts with the bag’s displacement.
It acts against the bag’s displacement.
It acts in a different direction from the bag.
It changes while the bag stays still.
activities.explanation: The applied force acts in the same direction as the bag’s displacement.

activities.title: The unit of work
activities.prompt: The SI unit of work done is the joule.
activities.explanation: The joule is the SI unit used to measure work done.

activities.title: Calculate the work
activities.prompt: For a constant force, work equals force multiplied by ______.
activities.hint: Choose the distance moved in the force’s direction.
activities.explanation: This calculation uses displacement in the force’s direction.

activities.title: The work-energy theorem
activities.prompt: What does the work-energy theorem state?
options: Work done equals the change in energy.
Energy change equals the time taken.
Power equals the change in energy.
Work done equals the force applied.
activities.explanation: The theorem connects work done with the change in an object’s energy.

activities.title: Match each idea
activities.prompt: Match each energy or machine idea with its correct description.
activities.explanation: These pairs connect each idea with its unit, meaning, or formula.

activities.title: Energy from the Sun
activities.prompt: Put the Sun’s energy-transfer steps in order.
items: The Sun’s energy is transferred by radiation.
activities.explanation: The Sun’s energy travels through space as radiation and reaches Earth.

activities.title: Power and time
activities.prompt: A worker does more work in the same time. What happens to power?
options: It increases.
It decreases.
It stays the same.
It becomes zero.
activities.explanation: Doing more work in the same time requires more power.

activities.title: Double the velocity
activities.prompt: If velocity doubles, kinetic energy becomes ______ times its previous value.
activities.hint: Remember the lesson’s doubling rule for kinetic energy.
activities.explanation: Doubling velocity makes kinetic energy four times its previous value.

activities.title: Energy during a fall
activities.prompt: As a ball falls, its potential energy increases.
activities.explanation: As the ball falls, its potential energy decreases while its kinetic energy increases.

activities.title: A fixed pulley
activities.prompt: What does a fixed pulley do to the effort?
options: Changes its direction.
Reduces its magnitude.
Increases its magnitude.
Removes the load.
activities.explanation: It changes the direction of the effort without reducing its magnitude.

chapters.title: Journey Inside the Atom
chapters.summary: In this chapter: roots of atomic theory; thomson’s atomic model; rutherford and the gold foil experiment; bohr’s model and the proton.

lessons.title: Roots of Atomic Theory

activities.prompt: What is the tiniest piece our world could possibly have?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Matter and tiny particles
activities.body: Matter is everything we can see, observe or feel. It consists of tiny particles called atoms. These atoms are too small to see with the naked eye. Acharya Kanada thought that repeated division would reveal matter’s smallest particles. He called them parmanus. John Dalton proposed that all matter is made of indivisible atoms.
keyPoints: Matter consists of tiny particles called atoms.
Atoms are too small to see with the naked eye.
Dalton proposed that matter is made of indivisible atoms.
activities.explanation: This lesson begins with matter, atoms and early ideas about the smallest particles.

activities.prompt: If you keep dividing chalk, where should the dividing stop?
steps: Chalk is matter, so it contains tiny atoms.
Kanada thought repeated division would reveal matter's smallest particles.
These particles were called parmanus and could not be divided further.
So division should stop at indivisible parmanus, which the senses cannot perceive.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Kanada’s smallest particles
activities.body: Kanada’s parmanus were imagined as infinitely small. They could not be perceived through the senses. He thought that repeatedly dividing matter would reveal these particles. Parmanus combine in groups of two or three. These groups are called dyads and triads.
keyPoints: Parmanus were imagined as infinitely small.
Kanada thought division would reveal the smallest particles.
Parmanus form dyads and triads.
activities.explanation: Kanada’s idea helped early thinkers imagine the smallest possible particles.

activities.prompt: Atoms are too small to see with the naked eye.
activities.explanation: Atoms are far too small to be seen with the naked eye.

activities.prompt: Match each thinker with their contribution.
activities.explanation: Kanada called the smallest particles parmanus. Leucippus and Democritus used atomos. Dalton proposed atomic theory.

activities.prompt: What did Acharya Kanada call the smallest particles?
options: Parmanus
Atomos
Dyads
Triads
activities.explanation: Acharya Kanada called the smallest particles parmanus. Atomos was the Greek word used by Leucippus and Democritus.

activities.prompt: A parmanu was described as ______ small and impossible to perceive through the senses.
activities.hint: Use the word meaning without any limit.
activities.explanation: A parmanu was described as infinitely small. It was also impossible to perceive through the senses.

activities.prompt: Which statement about the idea of the atom is correct?
options: The atom began as an imaginary idea.
The atom began as an experimental discovery.
Atoms could be seen with the naked eye.
Matter had no smallest particles.
activities.explanation: The idea of the atom began as an imaginary idea rather than an experimental discovery.

activities.prompt: Put the steps in the order described by Kanada’s thought.
items: Find that they cannot be divided further
activities.explanation: Kanada thought that repeated division would reveal the smallest particles. These particles could not be divided further.

activities.prompt: A child looks at salt with naked eyes. What should they expect?
options: They may see the grain, but not its atoms.
They will see atoms as tiny separate dots.
They will see each atom if they look longer.
They will see nothing because all matter is invisible.

why.They will see atoms as tiny separate dot: This wrongly treats atoms as visible dots.
why.They will see each atom if they look lon: Looking longer does not overcome their tiny size.
why.They will see nothing because all matter: This wrongly says visible matter is also invisible.

activities.explanation: Atoms are too small to see with naked eyes.

activities.prompt: A learner rejects Dalton’s theory because atoms are unseen. What reply fits?
options: Dalton’s 1808 idea began as an imagined explanation of matter.
Dalton’s 1808 idea fails unless its atoms are visible.
Dalton’s 1808 idea applies only where naked eyes see.
Dalton’s 1808 idea says visible objects have no atoms.

why.Dalton’s 1808 idea fails unless its atom: This wrongly makes direct sight necessary for Dalton’s idea.
why.Dalton’s 1808 idea applies only where na: This wrongly limits matter to what naked eyes can see.
why.Dalton’s 1808 idea says visible objects: This wrongly says visible objects contain no atoms.

activities.explanation: Dalton proposed atoms as an imagined idea in 1808.

activities.prompt: A spoon is filed smaller. Does filing make its atoms divisible?
options: No. The pieces still contain indivisible atoms.
Yes. Each new piece has smaller, divisible atoms.
Yes. Enough filing turns atoms into visible grains.
No. Atoms disappear whenever matter is filed.

why.Yes. Each new piece has smaller, divisib: This wrongly treats smaller matter pieces as smaller atoms.
why.Yes. Enough filing turns atoms into visi: This wrongly thinks atoms can become visible grains.
why.No. Atoms disappear whenever matter is f: This wrongly thinks dividing matter removes its atoms.

activities.explanation: Filing makes smaller matter pieces, but atoms stay indivisible.

lessons.title: Thomson’s Atomic Model

activities.prompt: What secrets might invisible particles reveal about the tiny building blocks of everything?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Thomson’s Picture of the Atom
activities.body: Radioactivity showed that atoms contain smaller particles, so they are not indivisible. Thomson studied current through gases at low pressure. He found cathode rays moving from the negative cathode towards the positive anode. These rays were streams of negatively charged particles with much smaller mass than atoms. The particles were later called electrons. Thomson proposed a sphere of positive charge for the atom. He called this the plum pudding model.
keyPoints: Atoms contain smaller particles and are not indivisible.
Cathode rays contain negatively charged particles called electrons.
Thomson pictured the atom as a sphere of positive charge.
activities.explanation: You now know how Thomson’s experiments led to his atomic model.

activities.prompt: Two tubes use different gases and cathode materials. Why do both make the same rays?
steps: He studied current through a gas at low pressure.
Electrons moved from the negative cathode towards the positive anode.
Their nature stayed the same with different cathodes and gases.
So electrons were a fundamental part of every atom.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Thomson’s Atomic Model
activities.prompt: What did Thomson propose an atom looked like?
options: a sphere of positive charge
a solid sphere of negative charge
a small empty ring
a flat positive disc
activities.explanation: Thomson pictured the atom as a sphere of positive charge. He called this the plum pudding model.

activities.title: The Name of the Particles
activities.prompt: The negatively charged particles in cathode rays were later called ______.
activities.hint: They were fundamental components of every atom.
activities.explanation: These negatively charged particles were later called electrons.

activities.title: Match Each Finding
activities.prompt: Match each finding with its correct name.
pairs: rays moving towards the positive anode
particles with much smaller mass than atoms
invisible energy and particles emitted by some elements
activities.explanation: Each pair connects a finding with the correct scientific name.

activities.title: Thomson’s Discoveries in Time Order
activities.prompt: Put Thomson’s discoveries in time order.
items: Thomson studied current through gases at low pressure.
Thomson observed rays moving towards the positive anode.
He found streams of negatively charged particles.
The particles were later called electrons.
activities.explanation: The study led to an observation, a finding about the particles, and their later name.

activities.title: Changing the Tube
activities.prompt: Suppose you changed both the cathode material and the gas. The nature of the rays would...
options: stay the same
always become positive
always become weaker
change with each material
activities.explanation: The nature of cathode rays did not depend on the cathode material or the gas. Their nature stayed the same.

activities.title: What Radioactivity Revealed
activities.prompt: Radioactivity showed that atoms were...
options: divisible into smaller particles
indivisible and unchanging
empty, with no particles inside
made only of positive charge
activities.explanation: Radioactivity showed that atoms contain smaller particles. This meant that atoms were not indivisible.

activities.prompt: An atom releases radiation. What does this reveal about the idea that atoms cannot be divided?
options: Atoms contain smaller particles inside them.
Atoms are made of positive charge only.
Atoms are always spheres of pure energy.
Atoms stop containing any smaller particles.

This confuses positive charge with the particles revealed by radiation.
This treats energy as the only part of every atom.
why.Atoms stop containing any smaller partic: This reverses the finding that smaller particles exist inside atoms.

activities.explanation: Right, because radioactivity showed that atoms contain smaller particles.

activities.prompt: You want to test whether cathode ray particles depend on cathode material. Which test is fairest?
options: Repeat with different cathodes but the same gas.
Repeat with different gases but the same cathode.
Change only the tube length during the test.
Use one tube and make no measurements.

why.Repeat with different gases but the same: This changes the gas instead of testing the cathode material.
why.Change only the tube length during the t: This changes the tube instead of testing the cathode material.
This gives no comparison, so no test of the cathode material.

activities.explanation: Right, because changing only the cathode tests whether its material matters.

activities.prompt: Cathode rays had the same nature with different gases and cathode materials. What does this show?
options: Electrons are a basic part of every atom.
Electrons come only from one metal.
Each gas has its own tiny particles.
Electrons exist only inside cathode rays.

This assumes electrons belong to only one metal.
This assumes each gas creates its own separate particles.
why.Electrons exist only inside cathode rays: This assumes electrons exist only inside the moving rays.

activities.explanation: Right, because the same electrons appear with every cathode material and gas.

lessons.title: Rutherford and the Gold Foil Experiment

activities.prompt: What surprised the scientists when alpha particles met a whisper-thin sheet of gold?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Gold Foil Experiment
activities.body: In 1911, Geiger and Marsden tested Thomson’s model. They aimed alpha particles at an extremely thin gold foil. Most particles passed through undeflected. Some bent sharply, and a few bounced back. This scattering showed that positive charge was concentrated in a tiny region called the nucleus. Rutherford then pictured electrons revolving around it, like planets around the Sun.
keyPoints: Most alpha particles passed through undeflected.
Some were sharply deflected, and a few bounced back.
Positive charge was concentrated in a tiny nucleus.
activities.explanation: Sharp bends and rebounds revealed a tiny centre of positive charge.

activities.prompt: Why did some alpha particles bounce back from thin gold foil?
steps: Most particles passed through because most of each atom is empty space.
Sharp deflections and backward bounces showed strong effects inside some atoms.
Those results led Rutherford to place positive charge in a tiny nucleus.
Thomson’s model failed because it could not explain these results.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Rutherford’s Atomic Picture
activities.body: Rutherford’s atomic picture helps us imagine the atom’s structure. Positive charge was concentrated in a tiny nucleus. Most of an atom is empty space. Electrons revolve around the nucleus, somewhat like planets orbiting the Sun. To picture the scale, imagine a cricket ground sized atom. Its nucleus would be like a tiny pepper grain.
keyPoints: Positive charge was concentrated in a tiny nucleus.
Most of an atom is empty space.
Electrons revolve around the nucleus.
activities.explanation: The nucleus is tiny, while most of the atom is empty space.

activities.title: The Experiment Beam
activities.prompt: What did Geiger and Marsden direct towards the gold foil?
options: A narrow beam of alpha particles
A beam of gold atoms
A beam of electrons
A beam of light rays
activities.explanation: They directed a narrow beam of alpha particles towards the foil.

activities.title: Thomson’s Prediction
activities.prompt: Thomson’s model predicted that alpha particles would sharply bounce back.
activities.explanation: It predicted straight passage or only slight bending, not sharp rebounds.

activities.title: What Is Scattering?
activities.prompt: The bending of particles away from their straight path is called ______.
activities.hint: This word names the bending away from a straight path.
activities.explanation: Sharp bending and bouncing back show scattering.

activities.title: The Main Result
activities.prompt: What did most alpha particles do after meeting the gold foil?
options: They passed through undeflected
They bounced straight back
They stopped inside the foil
They bent sharply away
activities.explanation: Most particles passed through undeflected, just as the lesson shows.

activities.title: Match the Observed Results
activities.prompt: Match each particle group with its observed result.
activities.explanation: Each particle group had a different observed path through the foil.

activities.title: Rutherford’s Conclusion
activities.prompt: Which statement is Rutherford’s conclusion from these results?
options: Positive charge is concentrated in a tiny nucleus.
Most alpha particles became electrons.
The gold foil was mostly empty space.
Electrons stopped moving around the nucleus.
activities.explanation: Rutherford concluded that positive charge was concentrated in a tiny region called the nucleus.

activities.prompt: Scattering means bending from a straight path. What causes sharp bending in gold foil?
options: Positive charge concentrated inside a tiny nucleus
Positive charge spread evenly through each gold atom
Electrons revolving closely around every nucleus
Empty space filling each entire gold atom

why.Positive charge spread evenly through ea: This wrongly spreads positive charge instead of concentrating it.
why.Electrons revolving closely around every: This confuses orbiting electrons with the concentrated positive nucleus.
why.Empty space filling each entire gold ato: Empty space explains straight passage, not sharp bending.

activities.explanation: The nucleus concentrates the positive charge that produces sharp bending.

activities.prompt: Which observation most clearly showed that Thomson’s model was wrong?
options: Most passed through, but a few bounced back.
Most bounced back, but a few passed through.
All passed through without any bending.
All stopped inside the very thin foil.

why.Most bounced back, but a few passed thro: This reverses the observed numbers of passing and returning particles.
This fits Thomson’s prediction and does not show its failure.
This was not observed and does not show a model failure.

activities.explanation: The model allowed only straight or slight bending, not bouncing back.

activities.prompt: Which plan gives the fair test of Thomson’s prediction?
options: Use a narrow beam and an extremely thin gold foil.
Use a wide beam and a very thick sheet of gold.
Use a narrow beam and a solid block of gold.
Use a wide beam and a thin sheet of paper.

why.Use a wide beam and a very thick sheet o: It changes both the beam and foil from the planned test.
why.Use a narrow beam and a solid block of g: A solid block cannot test passage through an extremely thin foil.
why.Use a wide beam and a thin sheet of pape: Paper is not the gold foil used to test Thomson’s model.

activities.explanation: It uses a narrow beam and the extremely thin gold foil.

lessons.title: Bohr’s Model and the Proton

activities.prompt: How do tiny electrons stay in their shells without losing energy?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Shells, Energy and Protons
activities.body: Bohr proposed a new atomic model in 1913. In his model, electrons follow fixed circular paths called stationary states, orbits or shells. Each electron has a definite energy in a shell. Electrons can move between shells only by absorbing or releasing a fixed amount of energy. Farther shells have higher energy. Rutherford showed that protons provide the nucleus’s positive charge. A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons.
keyPoints: Electrons occupy fixed circular paths called shells.
Moving between shells needs a fixed energy change.
Protons give the nucleus its positive charge.
activities.explanation: This card shows the main ideas about shells, energy and protons.

activities.prompt: An electron moves from one shell to a farther shell. How does its energy change?
steps: An electron can move only between allowed shells.
Moving to a farther shell gives the electron higher energy.
The change between levels is a fixed amount of energy.
So the electron absorbs that fixed amount to move farther.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which model did Bohr propose?
options: An atomic model with fixed shells
A model without an atomic nucleus
A model with electrons between shells
A model without any electron energy
activities.explanation: This matches Bohr’s atomic model, proposed in 1913.

activities.prompt: Bohr proposed his atomic model in ______.
activities.hint: Give the year from the lesson.
activities.explanation: Bohr proposed this model in 1913.

activities.prompt: An electron can move between shells without absorbing or releasing energy.
activities.explanation: Electrons change shells by absorbing or releasing a fixed amount of energy.

activities.prompt: Match each idea with its partner.
pairs: Equal numbers in a neutral atom
activities.explanation: A shell has a fixed path and limited capacity. Protons supply the nucleus’s positive charge.

activities.prompt: Put these locations in order from nearest the nucleus to farthest.
activities.explanation: The proton is in the nucleus. The fixed shells lie at different distances around it.

activities.prompt: What must happen when an electron moves from a nearer shell to a farther shell?
options: It releases a fixed amount of energy
It keeps exactly the same energy
It absorbs a fixed amount of energy
It loses energy within the nearer shell
activities.explanation: The farther shell has higher energy. Moving there requires absorbing a fixed amount of energy.

activities.prompt: An electron moves inside one stationary state. What happens to its energy?
options: It stays the same.
It slowly falls to zero.
It changes every moment.
It doubles with every circle.

This mistakes movement inside a shell for energy loss.
This assumes energy must change during every movement.
This invents a rule that energy grows during each circle.

activities.explanation: Energy is not lost within one fixed shell.

activities.prompt: An electron moves from a nearer shell to a farther shell. How does its energy change?
options: It increases by a fixed amount.
It decreases by a fixed amount.
It stays exactly the same.
It changes by any amount.

This reverses the energy order of the shells.
This ignores that farther shells have higher energy.
This misses the fixed amount needed for a change.

activities.explanation: A farther shell has higher energy, with a fixed change.

activities.prompt: Protons are much heavier than electrons. Rutherford found their nuclear role. What correction is correct?
options: Protons provide positive charge despite being heavier.
Electrons provide positive charge despite being heavier.
Electron paths provide the nucleus's positive charge.
Shell energy provides the nucleus's positive charge.

why.Electrons provide positive charge despit: This wrongly gives electrons the role of protons.
why.Electron paths provide the nucleus's pos: This wrongly treats electron paths as the source of charge.
why.Shell energy provides the nucleus's posi: This wrongly treats shell energy as the source of charge.

activities.explanation: Protons provide the positive charge even though they are heavier.

activities.prompt: A neutral atom has protons and electrons. What counts must match?
options: Protons and electrons must have the same count.
Protons and shells must have the same count.
Electrons and shells must have the same count.
Protons and fixed paths must have the same count.

why.Protons and shells must have the same co: This confuses particle counts with shell counts.
why.Electrons and shells must have the same: This confuses particle counts with shell counts.
why.Protons and fixed paths must have the sa: This confuses moving paths with particles in the atom.

activities.explanation: A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons.

lessons.title: Neutrons and Element Symbols

activities.prompt: Why do atoms have different symbols, and what invisible particle helps explain their mass?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Missing Particle
activities.body: James Chadwick solved the mass puzzle in 1932. A helium atom has about four times a hydrogen atom’s mass. He found a particle with nearly a proton’s mass, but no electrical charge. This neutral particle was named the neutron. Neutrons sit in the nucleus of every atom except hydrogen. Most atomic mass comes from protons and neutrons in the nucleus. Neutrons reduce repulsion between positive protons.
keyPoints: Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932.
A neutron has nearly a proton’s mass but no charge.
Neutrons reduce repulsion between positive protons.
activities.explanation: Neutrons help explain an atom’s mass and keep its nucleus stable.

activities.prompt: At school, a child compares helium and hydrogen atoms. Helium has about four times the mass. What explains the extra mass without adding charge?
steps: Hydrogen has no neutron, while helium has neutrons inside its nucleus.
Chadwick found a neutral particle nearly as heavy as a proton.
He named it the neutron, and it explains the extra mass.
Neutrons also reduce repulsion between positive protons inside the nucleus.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: How Element Symbols Developed
activities.body: Dalton introduced the first pictorial symbols for known elements. In 1813, Berzelius suggested changing these symbols. He said that symbol letters should come from Latin names. The International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry approves element names and symbols. The first letter of a chemical symbol is capital. The second letter is small.
keyPoints: Dalton introduced pictorial symbols for known elements.
Berzelius suggested letters from Latin names.
The first symbol letter is capital and the second is small.
activities.explanation: Element symbols developed through Dalton, Berzelius and an approving chemistry group.

activities.prompt: What did Chadwick discover in 1932?
options: A particle with nearly a proton’s mass and positive charge
A particle with nearly a proton’s mass and no charge
A particle with nearly a hydrogen atom’s mass and no charge
A particle with nearly a proton’s mass and negative charge
activities.explanation: Chadwick found a particle with nearly a proton’s mass but no electrical charge.

activities.prompt: Neutrons are found in the nucleus of every atom, including hydrogen.
activities.explanation: Neutrons are found in every atom’s nucleus except hydrogen.

activities.prompt: The first letter of a chemical symbol is ______, while the second letter is small.
activities.hint: Use the rule for writing element symbols.
activities.explanation: Element symbols begin with a capital letter. Their second letter is small.

activities.prompt: Match each person or group with the correct contribution or rule.
pairs: International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry
activities.explanation: Each pair connects a symbol rule or contributor with the correct contribution.

activities.prompt: Put these milestones in time order.
items: Chadwick solves the mass puzzle in 1932
activities.explanation: Dalton’s symbols came first. Berzelius followed in 1813. Chadwick came later in 1932.

activities.prompt: Why do neutrons help reduce repulsion inside an atom’s nucleus?
options: They add positive charge to the nucleus.
They replace most protons in the nucleus.
They reduce repulsion between positive protons.
They make hydrogen atoms contain neutrons.
activities.explanation: Neutral neutrons help reduce the repulsion between positively charged protons.

activities.prompt: Helium has about four times the mass of hydrogen. Chadwick found a particle nearly as heavy as a proton but neutral. What helps explain the extra mass?
options: A charged particle much lighter than a proton.
A neutral particle far lighter than a proton.
A neutral particle nearly as heavy as a proton.
A charged particle nearly as heavy as a proton.

why.A charged particle much lighter than a p: This confuses a proton-like mass with a different particle.
why.A neutral particle far lighter than a pr: This mistakes a nearly proton-like mass for a much smaller mass.
why.A charged particle nearly as heavy as a: This confuses the neutron’s lack of charge with having a charge.

activities.explanation: This is the neutron, which is neutral and nearly as heavy as a proton.

activities.prompt: Neutrons have nearly the mass of protons but carry no charge. Protons are positive. What happens to proton repulsion without neutrons?
options: Repulsion decreases because neutrons no longer reduce it.
Repulsion increases because neutrons no longer reduce it.
Repulsion stays same because neutrons have no charge.
Repulsion vanishes because neutrons have no charge.

why.Repulsion decreases because neutrons no: This wrongly suggests removing neutrons strengthens their reducing effect.
why.Repulsion stays same because neutrons ha: This confuses having no charge with having no effect.
why.Repulsion vanishes because neutrons have: This confuses reducing repulsion with removing it completely.

activities.explanation: Without neutrons, the reduction in proton repulsion is lost.

activities.prompt: Most atom mass comes from protons and neutrons inside the nucleus. Hydrogen has no neutron, while helium has neutrons. Which explanation fits both facts?
options: Helium gains no mass because neutrons have no charge.
Hydrogen gains extra mass because it lacks neutrons.
Helium loses mass because neutrons push protons together.
Helium gains extra mass because it contains neutrons.

why.Helium gains no mass because neutrons ha: This confuses electrical neutrality with having no mass.
why.Hydrogen gains extra mass because it lac: This reverses the role of hydrogen’s missing neutrons.
why.Helium loses mass because neutrons push: This mistakes reduced repulsion for a loss of mass.

activities.explanation: Neutrons add mass in the nucleus, helping explain helium’s greater mass.

lessons.title: Atomic Number, Shells, Valency and Isotopes

activities.prompt: What can we discover by taking a closer look inside an atom?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Atoms, Shells and Isotopes
activities.body: In a neutral atom, protons and electrons have equal numbers. The mass number is the total of protons and neutrons. Shell capacity follows 2n². The outermost shell holds up to eight electrons. Electrons fill shells from the nucleus outwards. Valency counts electrons gained, lost or shared to complete an octet. An octet has eight electrons in the outermost shell. Isotopes share an atomic number but have different mass numbers.
keyPoints: Neutral atoms have equal protons and electrons.
Valency completes an octet of eight electrons.
Isotopes have equal atomic numbers but different mass numbers.
activities.explanation: These ideas connect particles, shells, octets, valency and isotopes.

activities.title: Balanced Particles
activities.prompt: In a neutral atom, the number of protons equals the number of electrons.
activities.explanation: A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons.

activities.title: Complete the Pair
activities.prompt: A neutral atom has equal numbers of ______ and electrons.
activities.hint: Choose the other particle in this pair.
activities.explanation: Neutral atoms contain equal numbers of protons and electrons.

activities.title: What Is an Octet?
activities.prompt: Which statement describes an octet?
options: It holds eight electrons in an inner shell.
It holds eight electrons in the outermost shell.
It holds two electrons in the outermost shell.
It holds six electrons in the outermost shell.
activities.explanation: An octet means eight electrons in the outermost shell.

activities.title: Meaning of Valency
activities.prompt: What does valency count?
options: The electrons gained, lost or shared to complete an octet.
The protons gained, lost or shared to complete an octet.
The neutrons gained, lost or shared to complete an octet.
The shells gained, lost or shared to complete an octet.
activities.explanation: Valency counts electrons gained, lost or shared to complete an octet.

activities.title: Match the Ideas
activities.prompt: Match each idea with its meaning.
pairs: Eight electrons in the outermost shell
Same atomic number, different mass numbers
activities.explanation: Neutral atoms balance protons and electrons. An octet has eight outermost electrons.

activities.title: Find the Mass Number
activities.prompt: Put these steps in order to find the mass number.
activities.explanation: The mass number is found by adding the number of protons and neutrons.

activities.title: Isotopes or Isobars?
activities.prompt: Isobars have the same atomic number but different mass numbers.
activities.explanation: That describes isotopes. Isobars belong to different elements and have the same mass number.

activities.title: Calculate Average Atomic Mass
activities.prompt: Which information must you use to calculate average atomic mass?
options: The shell capacities of the isotopes.
The valencies of the isotopes.
The natural abundances of the isotopes.
The octet counts of the isotopes.
activities.explanation: Average atomic mass must use the natural abundances of the isotopes.

activities.context: During a science lesson, a learner studies Acharya Kanada’s idea that repeated division of matter would reveal its smallest particles. These could not be divided further, and Kanada called them parmanus. They were described as infinitely small and impossible to perceive through the senses. The lesson also says Leucippus and Democritus used the Greek word atomos for indivisible particles and that Dalton proposed in 1808 that all matter consists of indivisible atoms.
activities.prompt: A learner is asked to examine a parmanu with the senses. What should the learner expect?
options: It would remain beyond perception through the senses.
It would become visible after being divided more.
It would become visible after being joined into a dyad or triad.
It would become visible if a person looked very closely.

why.It would become visible after being divi: Parmanus were described as indivisible, so further division would not reveal them.
why.It would become visible after being join: A dyad or triad was a group of parmanus, not a way to make one perceptible.
why.It would become visible if a person look: Very close looking cannot overcome the stated impossibility of perceiving them.

activities.explanation: This matches the description of a parmanu as impossible to perceive through the senses.

activities.context: During a science lesson, a learner studies Acharya Kanada’s idea that repeated division of matter would reveal its smallest particles. These could not be divided further, and Kanada called them parmanus. They were described as infinitely small and impossible to perceive through the senses. The lesson also says Leucippus and Democritus used the Greek word atomos for indivisible particles and that Dalton proposed in 1808 that all matter consists of indivisible atoms.
activities.prompt: If matter is divided repeatedly according to Kanada’s idea, what should the learner expect at the final stage?
options: Particles with no further division possible.
Particles that could still be divided into smaller pieces.
Visible pieces that could be seen with the naked eye.
Particles that change whenever matter is divided.

why.Particles that could still be divided in: Repeated division was expected to end at particles that were indivisible.
why.Visible pieces that could be seen with t: The smallest particles were not visible to the naked eye.
why.Particles that change whenever matter is: Kanada’s idea was that division ends at smallest particles, not that they keep changing.

activities.explanation: Kanada’s smallest particles could not be divided further.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Acharya Kanada believed that repeated division of matter would reveal particles that could not be divided further.
Reason (R): His reasoning focused on finding the smallest particles of matter.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and finding the smallest particles explains Kanada’s belief.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Dalton’s atomic theory began with an experimental discovery of individual atoms.
Reason (R): The idea of the atom began as an imaginary idea rather than an experimental discovery.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason is true, but the assertion wrongly describes the origin as experimental.

activities.prompt: Explain how Dalton’s description of atoms compares with Acharya Kanada’s description of parmanus.
activities.answer: Dalton’s description and Kanada’s description have a central similarity: both concern indivisible particles as the basic material of matter. Dalton proposed in 1808 that all matter is made of particles called atoms, which cannot be divided. Kanada reached a similar idea by considering what would happen if matter were divided repeatedly. He called the final particles parmanus. His description also emphasized that a parmanu was infinitely small and impossible to perceive through the senses. Thus, the main differences are the names used and the extra description given for parmanus.
points: Both descriptions concern indivisible particles.
Dalton called the particles atoms.
Kanada called them parmanus.
Parmanus were described as infinitely small and imperceptible through the senses.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a class demonstration, a student studies electric current in a gas tube at low pressure. The student sees rays travel from the negative cathode toward the positive anode and identifies them as cathode rays. A teacher explains that the same kind of rays appear even if the cathode material or gas is changed. The student is then asked to connect this observation with Thomson’s atomic model.
activities.prompt: What conclusion about the structure of an atom can the student draw from the cathode-ray observation?
options: The atom contains negatively charged particles whose mass is much smaller than that of an atom.
The atom is indivisible because the rays have no mass.
The atom contains only positive charge because the particles move toward the positive anode.
The rays are positively charged particles that are heavier than atoms.

why.The atom is indivisible because the rays: This denies both their negative charge and their measurable mass.
why.The atom contains only positive charge b: Moving toward the positive anode does not mean that the particles are positive.
why.The rays are positively charged particle: This reverses both the charge and relative mass of the particles.

activities.explanation: Cathode rays were negatively charged particles with much smaller mass than atoms.

activities.context: During a class demonstration, a student studies electric current in a gas tube at low pressure. The student sees rays travel from the negative cathode toward the positive anode and identifies them as cathode rays. A teacher explains that the same kind of rays appear even if the cathode material or gas is changed. The student is then asked to connect this observation with Thomson’s atomic model.
activities.prompt: Which conclusion about electrons is best justified by the fact that changing the cathode material or gas does not change the nature of the rays?
options: Electrons occur only in the original gas tube.
Electrons are a fundamental component of every atom.
Each gas supplies a different kind of negatively charged particle.
The cathode material alone determines the particles present in the rays.

why.Electrons occur only in the original gas: The observation was not limited to electrons in one original tube.
why.Each gas supplies a different kind of ne: The particle nature remained the same even when the gas changed.
why.The cathode material alone determines th: The nature of the rays was independent of the cathode material.

activities.explanation: The unchanged rays showed that electrons occur in every atom.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Radioactivity showed that atoms are indivisible.
Reason (R): Radioactivity involves the emission of invisible energy and particles called radiation.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false because radioactivity showed that atoms are not indivisible, while the reason is true.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between radioactivity and cathode rays.
activities.answer: Radioactivity is the emission of invisible energy and particles called radiation. This is different from the cathode-ray investigation. In Thomson’s experiment, electric current was studied through a gas at low pressure, and rays moved from the negative cathode toward the positive anode. These cathode rays were streams of negatively charged particles with a much smaller mass than atoms. The particles were later called electrons. Radioactivity therefore showed that atoms contain smaller particles, while cathode rays helped reveal the electron as a fundamental component of every atom.
points: Defines radioactivity correctly
Describes the direction of cathode rays
Explains the charge and small mass of cathode-ray particles
Links both discoveries to smaller components within atoms
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student visits a school display about gold foil. A narrow beam of alpha particles is aimed at an extremely thin sheet of gold foil. Most particles cross the foil without changing direction, while some turn sharply and a few bounce back. The display explains how these observations tested Thomson’s model and led Rutherford to describe the inside of an atom.
activities.prompt: Based on the display, which conclusion best explains why some alpha particles bounced back?
options: Positive charge is spread evenly through each atom, so strong changes in direction are not expected.
A minute region in each atom holds a concentrated amount of positive charge.
Electrons form a solid centre that blocks and sends back many particles.
The alpha particles were electrically neutral, so the atoms could not affect their paths.

why.Positive charge is spread evenly through: This is the kind of distribution associated with the inadequate model; it cannot account for sharp scattering.
why.Electrons form a solid centre that block: Rutherford’s picture does not place electrons in a solid central barrier.
why.The alpha particles were electrically ne: Alpha particles are positively charged, so saying they are neutral is false.

activities.explanation: Concentrated positive charge in a tiny region accounts for sharp deflection and backward scattering.

activities.context: A student visits a school display about gold foil. A narrow beam of alpha particles is aimed at an extremely thin sheet of gold foil. Most particles cross the foil without changing direction, while some turn sharply and a few bounce back. The display explains how these observations tested Thomson’s model and led Rutherford to describe the inside of an atom.
activities.prompt: Which statement best uses both the majority of undeflected particles and the particles that changed direction sharply?
options: Most particles crossed because the atom is mainly empty space, and the exceptions show that positive charge is concentrated in a tiny region.
Most particles crossed because alpha particles have no charge, and the exceptions show that the beam was faulty.
Most particles crossed because electrons fill the atom, and the exceptions show that electrons are concentrated in the nucleus.
Most particles crossed because the atom has no empty space, and the exceptions show that positive charge is concentrated in a large region.

why.Most particles crossed because alpha par: Alpha particles are charged, and the observations were not merely a faulty beam.
why.Most particles crossed because electrons: Electrons revolve around the nucleus rather than forming it.
why.Most particles crossed because the atom: Most of an atom is empty space, and the positive charge is concentrated in a tiny nucleus.

activities.explanation: This combines empty space with a tiny region containing concentrated positive charge.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The backward-scattered alpha particles provide evidence that positive charge is concentrated in a tiny region.
Reason (R): Their strong deflection is consistent with encountering a small region containing the atom’s concentrated positive charge.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason explains how concentrated positive charge accounts for the backward scattering.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The large number of undeflected alpha particles shows that most of an atom is empty space.
Reason (R): Alpha particles are tiny, positively charged particles emitted by some radioactive elements.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but the charge of alpha particles does not explain why most of them passed through undeflected.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between Thomson’s model and Rutherford’s interpretation of the gold foil experiment.
activities.answer: Thomson’s model predicted that alpha particles would pass straight through the gold foil or bend only slightly. Rutherford’s interpretation was based on what actually happened: most particles passed through undeflected, but some were sharply deflected and a few bounced back. Since Thomson’s model could not explain these results, Rutherford concluded that positive charge is concentrated in a tiny region called the nucleus. His interpretation also stated that most of an atom is empty space and that electrons revolve around the nucleus, somewhat like planets orbiting the Sun.
points: Thomson predicted straight passage or only slight bending.
Most particles passed through undeflected, but some were sharply deflected and a few bounced back.
Thomson’s model could not explain the observations.
Rutherford identified a tiny nucleus, mostly empty space, and electrons revolving around it.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: At a school science exhibition, a student is explaining an atom using Bohr’s model. She says that electrons move in fixed circular shells around the nucleus, and that each shell has a definite energy. One electron is shown in a shell farther from the nucleus than another electron. The student also tells visitors that the atom is neutral, so its protons and electrons must be present in equal numbers. She asks visitors what happens if an electron changes shells.
activities.prompt: According to the model, what happens when an electron changes from a nearer shell to a farther shell?
options: It absorbs a fixed amount of energy.
It releases a fixed amount of energy.
It loses energy continuously until it reaches the farther shell.
It keeps the same energy because the change is between allowed shells.

Releasing energy would correspond to moving toward a lower-energy shell.
why.It loses energy continuously until it re: Energy is not lost continuously, and movement between shells involves a fixed energy amount.
why.It keeps the same energy because the cha: The energy changes by a fixed amount even when both shells are allowed.

activities.explanation: A farther shell has higher energy, so reaching it requires absorption of a fixed amount.

activities.context: At a school science exhibition, a student is explaining an atom using Bohr’s model. She says that electrons move in fixed circular shells around the nucleus, and that each shell has a definite energy. One electron is shown in a shell farther from the nucleus than another electron. The student also tells visitors that the atom is neutral, so its protons and electrons must be present in equal numbers. She asks visitors what happens if an electron changes shells.
activities.prompt: For the display to represent a neutral atom, what must be true about its protons and electrons?
options: The count of protons is the same as the count of electrons.
There are more protons than electrons.
There are more electrons than protons.
Their numbers do not affect whether the atom is neutral.

Having more protons than electrons would not meet the condition for neutrality.
Having more electrons than protons would also not meet the condition for neutrality.
why.Their numbers do not affect whether the: The two counts must match for the atom to be neutral.

activities.explanation: A neutral atom must contain equal numbers of protons and electrons.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): An electron absorbs a fixed amount of energy when it moves from a lower-energy shell to a higher-energy shell.
Reason (R): A shell farther from the nucleus has higher energy.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason shows why moving outward requires energy absorption.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): An electron can move between shells without any energy change.
Reason (R): An electron absorbs or releases a fixed amount of energy when moving between levels.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false because the reason states that a shell change involves a fixed energy amount.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Journey Inside the Atom

activities.title: The Tiny Parts of Matter
activities.prompt: What are the tiny particles that make up all matter?
options: atoms
electrons
protons
neutrons
activities.explanation: Good choice. Everything around you is made of matter, which contains tiny atoms.

activities.title: The First Atom Idea
activities.prompt: The idea of the atom began as an experimental discovery.
activities.explanation: The idea of the atom began as an imaginary idea, rather than an experimental discovery.

activities.title: Thinkers and Their Contributions
activities.prompt: Match each thinker with their contribution.
activities.explanation: Well done. These thinkers helped develop the idea of the atom.

activities.title: Mystery Rays in a Tube
activities.prompt: What did Thomson discover in the cathode rays?
options: streams of positive particles
streams of neutral particles
streams of negative particles
rays of visible light
activities.explanation: Great work. Cathode rays were streams of negatively charged particles, later called electrons.

activities.title: Journey Through Atom History
activities.prompt: Put these discoveries from earliest to latest.
items: 1897: Thomson studied electric current through gases
1911: Geiger and Marsden tested Thomson’s model
1913: Bohr proposed a new atom model
activities.explanation: Excellent ordering. Each discovery helped scientists understand the atom better.

activities.title: The Gold Foil Surprise
activities.prompt: What happened to most alpha particles in the gold foil experiment?
options: All alpha particles stopped.
Most passed through undeflected.
All particles bent equally.
None entered the foil.
activities.explanation: Correct. Most passed through undeflected, but some were sharply deflected.

activities.title: The Atom’s Tiny Centre
activities.prompt: Rutherford called the tiny region of positive charge the ______.
activities.hint: Most of an atom is empty space.
activities.explanation: Yes. The nucleus holds the atom’s positive charge in a tiny region.

activities.title: Electrons and Energy
activities.prompt: Electrons move between allowed shells without absorbing or releasing energy.
activities.explanation: An electron absorbs or releases a fixed amount of energy when moving between levels.

activities.title: Solving the Mass Puzzle
activities.prompt: Which neutral particle did Chadwick discover in 1932?
options: electron
proton
neutron
alpha particle
activities.explanation: Great choice. The neutron has nearly the mass of a proton but no electrical charge.

activities.title: Chemistry Word Challenge
activities.prompt: Match each term with its correct meaning.
pairs: Same atomic number, different mass numbers
Capital first letter, small second letter
activities.explanation: Excellent. These meanings help you compare atoms and write their symbols.

chapters.title: Atomic Foundations of Matter
chapters.summary: In this chapter: physical and chemical changes: mass is conserved; constant proportions in compounds; molecules and covalent bonds; naming compounds and ionic bonds.

lessons.title: Physical and Chemical Changes: Mass Is Conserved

activities.prompt: What might make a fizzy reaction’s measured mass look different?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Mass Is Conserved
activities.body: Physical changes can alter how a substance looks without changing its mass. Salt dissolving in water and torn paper show this. During a chemical reaction, matter is neither created nor destroyed. If gas escapes, the measured mass can fall. If the gas stays inside, the total mass before and after stays equal. This law means matter is accounted for before and after the reaction.
keyPoints: Physical changes do not change mass.
Escaped gas can change a measured mass.
Matter is neither created nor destroyed.
activities.explanation: Mass stays conserved when all matter is included.

activities.prompt: A child mixes baking soda and vinegar, then wonders why the mass reading changes. What is happening?
steps: Mixing baking soda and vinegar produces carbon dioxide during a chemical change.
Gas escaped in the first experiment, so the final reading missed some mass.
In the modified experiment, gas stayed in the balloon, so readings matched.
The Law of Conservation of Mass says matter cannot be created or destroyed.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Salt in Water
activities.prompt: What happens to mass when salt dissolves in water?
options: It stays practically the same
It becomes much smaller
It becomes much larger
It disappears completely
activities.explanation: There is practically no change in mass.

activities.title: A New Gas
activities.prompt: What do baking soda and vinegar produce during their chemical change?
options: Carbon dioxide
A white precipitate
Torn paper
Dissolved salt
activities.explanation: Carbon dioxide is produced during this chemical change.

activities.title: Experiment Results
activities.prompt: Match each experiment detail with its result.
activities.explanation: The first readings differed because gas escaped. The modified readings matched because the gas stayed inside.

activities.title: The Important Year
activities.prompt: In ______, Antoine Lavoisier proposed the Law of Conservation of Mass.
activities.hint: Enter the year given in your book.
activities.explanation: Antoine Lavoisier proposed this law in 1789.

activities.title: A White Solid
activities.prompt: What forms when sodium sulfate and barium chloride are mixed?
options: A white precipitate
A carbon dioxide cloud
A sheet of paper
Some dissolved salt
activities.explanation: The white precipitate formed is barium sulfate.

activities.title: The Law of Conservation of Mass
activities.prompt: Which statement follows from the Law of Conservation of Mass?
options: Matter cannot be created or destroyed
Mass can change in every reaction
Matter disappears during some reactions
New matter forms during every reaction
activities.explanation: The law applies to every chemical reaction. Matter is neither created nor destroyed.

activities.prompt: Baking soda and vinegar react in an open cup. What will the final mass reading show?
options: The final reading will be smaller than the first.
The final reading will be larger than the first.
The final reading will match the first reading.
The final reading will change in an unknown way.

why.The final reading will be larger than th: Gas formation is wrongly thought to add matter to the cup.
why.The final reading will match the first r: Keeping the cup open is wrongly thought to keep all gas inside.
why.The final reading will change in an unkn: Escaping gas is wrongly thought to cause an unpredictable mass change.

activities.explanation: Carbon dioxide escapes, so some matter leaves the measured cup.

activities.prompt: The same reaction is done with the gas held inside a balloon. What will the final mass reading show?
options: The final reading will be smaller than the first.
The final reading will be larger than the first.
The final reading will match the first reading.
The final reading will change by an unknown amount.

why.The final reading will be smaller than t: The gas stays inside, so total mass before and after is equal.
why.The final reading will be larger than th: The gas is wrongly thought to escape even while held inside.
why.The final reading will change by an unkn: Gas is wrongly assumed to escape without being kept inside.

activities.explanation: Produced gas is wrongly thought to create extra matter.

activities.prompt: Mixing sodium sulfate and barium chloride forms a white precipitate. What happens to total mass?
options: The total mass stays the same after mixing.
The total mass falls because a precipitate forms.
The total mass rises because a precipitate forms.
The total mass changes because the mixture turns white.

why.The total mass falls because a precipita: Forming a precipitate is wrongly thought to remove matter.
why.The total mass rises because a precipita: The white precipitate is wrongly thought to add matter.
why.The total mass changes because the mixtu: A color change is wrongly treated as creating or destroying matter.

activities.explanation: The precipitate is matter, so the total mass stays equal.

activities.prompt: A child tests whether a chemical reaction keeps total mass. Which setup is fairest?
options: Measure the reaction while the gas stays in a balloon.
Measure the reaction while the gas escapes from an open cup.
Measure only the solid before the reaction begins.
Measure only the mass after the reaction has finished.

why.Measure the reaction while the gas escap: Letting gas escape removes matter from the measured setup.
why.Measure only the solid before the reacti: Ignoring gas omits matter made during the reaction.
why.Measure only the mass after the reaction: A final reading alone cannot show the before-and-after total.

activities.explanation: Keeping the gas inside lets the measurement include all produced matter.
