lessons.title: Constant Proportions in Compounds

activities.title: Constant Proportions in Compounds
activities.body:
Elements combine in a fixed ratio by mass to form a compound.

A compound has definite proportions of its elements regardless of its source.

Water contains hydrogen and oxygen in a mass ratio of 1:8.
keyPoints: Decomposing 9 g of purified water always gives 1 g of hydrogen and 8 g of oxygen.
This rule is called the Law of Constant Proportions.
activities.explanation: Now try some questions.

activities.prompt: Why can two samples of the same compound be so similar?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.prompt: Two jugs hold purified water from different places. Will the water have the same element proportions?
steps: Purified water contains hydrogen and oxygen in a 1:8 mass ratio.
The ratio stays fixed because compounds have definite proportions.
Nine grams gives one gram hydrogen and eight grams oxygen.
Both jugs must give these same element masses.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Decomposing 9 g of purified water always gives 8 g of hydrogen.
activities.explanation: It always gives 1 g of hydrogen and 8 g of oxygen.

activities.prompt: Sodium chloride contains sodium and chlorine in a mass ratio of ______:35.5.
activities.hint: Check the sodium part of the stated ratio.
activities.explanation: Sodium chloride contains sodium and chlorine in the mass ratio 23:35.5.

activities.prompt: Match each compound with its elements.
activities.explanation: Each compound contains its listed elements in definite proportions.

activities.prompt: Which compound always contains copper, carbon and oxygen in the same proportion?
options: Water
Copper carbonate
Sodium chloride
Cinnabar
activities.explanation: Copper carbonate always contains copper, carbon and oxygen in the same proportion.

activities.prompt: A copper carbonate sample comes from another source. What stays the same?
options: The proportions of hydrogen and oxygen.
The mass ratio of sodium and chlorine.
The percentages of mercury and sulfur.
The proportions of copper, carbon and oxygen.
activities.explanation: Its element proportions stay fixed, even when the source changes.

activities.prompt: The Law of Definite Proportions is sometimes called Proust’s Law.
activities.explanation: This rule is also called the Law of Constant Proportions and Proust’s Law.

activities.prompt: Water is purified at two different places. What should happen to their element proportions?
options: The first sample will have more hydrogen because its source differs.
Both samples will keep the same hydrogen and oxygen proportions.
The second sample will have more oxygen because its source differs.
Each sample will set its own ratio during purification.

why.The first sample will have more hydrogen: This mistake lets the source change a compound's fixed proportions.
why.The second sample will have more oxygen: This mistake lets the source change a compound's fixed proportions.
why.Each sample will set its own ratio durin: This mistake treats purification as creating new element proportions.

activities.explanation: This is right because definite proportions do not change with the source.

activities.prompt: Nine grams of purified water is decomposed. How much oxygen should form?
options: About 1 gram of oxygen
About 7 grams of oxygen
About 9 grams of oxygen
About 8 grams of oxygen

why.About 1 gram of oxygen: This mistake uses the hydrogen mass for oxygen.
why.About 7 grams of oxygen: This mistake subtracts hydrogen but misses the fixed 1:8 ratio.
why.About 9 grams of oxygen: This mistake assumes all the water becomes oxygen.

activities.explanation: Nine grams always gives 1 gram hydrogen and 8 grams oxygen.

activities.prompt: Nine grams of purified water is decomposed twice. Both times, the student expects 1 gram hydrogen and 8 grams oxygen. Is this expectation correct?
options: No. Only the first heating can follow the fixed ratio.
No. Each heating may choose a different element ratio.
Yes. The ratio changes after the water is purified.
Yes. Every 9 grams always gives those same element masses.

why.No. Only the first heating can follow th: This mistake thinks a fixed rule works only once.
why.No. Each heating may choose a different: This mistake lets each experiment choose its own element ratio.
why.Yes. The ratio changes after the water i: This mistake thinks purification changes the ratio in water.

activities.explanation: This is right because every 9 grams gives the same element masses.

activities.prompt: Two sodium chloride samples come from different sources. Which test compares their element ratios fairly?
options: Measure sodium in one sample and chlorine in the other sample.
Measure both elements in each sample, then compare their mass ratios.
Compare only the sodium masses because the sources are different.
Use unequal sample masses so each element can seem equal.

why.Measure sodium in one sample and chlorin: This mistake mixes the samples, so one full ratio is never measured.
why.Compare only the sodium masses because t: This mistake leaves chlorine out of the fair comparison.
why.Use unequal sample masses so each elemen: This mistake changes sample size, so the ratios cannot be compared fairly.

activities.explanation: This is right because both samples have the same two elements.

lessons.title: Molecules and Covalent Bonds

activities.prompt: How do atoms join together to make the world around us?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Atoms Join
activities.body: One element’s atoms can form a molecule of that element. Different elements’ atoms can form a molecule of a compound. A molecule is electrically neutral, meaning it has no net charge. It contains more than one atom. A valence shell is an atom’s outer shell. Atoms may share, gain or lose electrons to become stable. A covalent bond uses a shared pair of electrons. Bonding lowers total energy and makes atoms more stable.
keyPoints: Atoms of one element can form molecules.
Atoms of different elements can form a molecule of a compound.
Shared electron pairs form covalent bonds in stable arrangements.
activities.explanation: Atoms can join through shared or transferred electrons to form stable arrangements.

activities.prompt: Why do two hydrogen atoms join by sharing electrons instead of staying apart?
steps: Hydrogen atoms have incomplete valence shells, so they can share electrons.
Two hydrogen atoms share one electron each, forming a hydrogen molecule.
This sharing lowers the atoms' total energy and makes the arrangement more stable.
The shared pair of electrons holds the atoms together in a covalent bond.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What Is a Molecule?
activities.prompt: What must a molecule contain?
options: Only one atom
More than one atom
No atoms
Only one shell
activities.explanation: A molecule contains more than one atom and has no net electric charge.

activities.title: A Hydrogen Molecule
activities.prompt: One hydrogen molecule contains ______ hydrogen atoms.
activities.hint: Think about the hydrogen example.
activities.explanation: One hydrogen molecule contains two hydrogen atoms.

activities.title: How Hydrogen Atoms Join
activities.prompt: How do two hydrogen atoms form a hydrogen molecule?
options: They share one electron each.
They transfer one electron each.
They gain electrons from other elements.
They remain as separate atoms.
activities.explanation: Two hydrogen atoms form their molecule by sharing one electron each.

activities.title: Match Each Term
activities.prompt: Match each term with its correct meaning.
pairs: An electrically neutral entity with more than one atom
A bond formed by a shared pair of electrons
An element that exists only as separate atoms
activities.explanation: Each pair connects a term with its meaning in the lesson.

activities.title: Forming a Hydrogen Molecule
activities.prompt: Put these steps in the correct order.
items: The shared pair holds both atoms together.
activities.explanation: The atoms share one electron each, and the shared pair holds them together.

activities.title: Why Bonding Helps
activities.prompt: Which explanation correctly describes a covalent bond?
options: Shared electrons hold atoms together and lower their total energy.
Shared electrons separate atoms and raise their total energy.
Transferred electrons share the outer shell between two atoms.
Transferred electrons lower energy by holding atoms apart.
activities.explanation: A covalent bond forms through shared electrons. Bonding lowers total energy and makes the arrangement more stable.

activities.prompt: Two atoms share one electron each. What kind of chemical bond forms?
options: A covalent bond forms through the shared pair.
A chemical bond forms by transferring electrons.
A covalent bond forms by moving electrons between atoms.
A chemical bond forms without any shared electrons.

why.A chemical bond forms by transferring el: Wrong: it mistakes electron sharing for electron transfer.
why.A covalent bond forms by moving electron: Wrong: it mistakes electron transfer for electron sharing.
why.A chemical bond forms without any shared: Wrong: it assumes a chemical bond needs no shared electrons.

activities.explanation: Correct: sharing a pair of electrons forms a covalent bond.

activities.prompt: A molecule has atoms from two different elements. What kind is it?
options: A compound molecule, because different elements combined.
An element molecule, because all atoms are alike.
A neutral atom, because only one atom is present.
A separate atom, because different elements cannot join.

why.An element molecule, because all atoms a: Wrong: it confuses a compound with a molecule of one element.
why.A neutral atom, because only one atom is: Wrong: it treats a many-atom molecule as one separate atom.
why.A separate atom, because different eleme: Wrong: it wrongly assumes different elements cannot combine.

activities.explanation: Correct: atoms of different elements form a compound molecule.

activities.prompt: One atom gives an electron to another. What bonding process is happening?
options: Transfer of valence electrons, making the atoms bond.
Sharing of a pair of electrons, making the atoms bond.
Sharing of all valence electrons, making the atoms bond.
No bonding, because electrons cannot move between atoms.

why.Sharing of a pair of electrons, making t: Wrong: it mistakes electron transfer for electron sharing.
why.Sharing of all valence electrons, making: Wrong: it mistakes electron transfer for sharing all valence electrons.
why.No bonding, because electrons cannot mov: Wrong: it wrongly assumes electrons cannot move between atoms.

activities.explanation: Correct: transferring one or more valence electrons is a bonding process.

activities.prompt: Two atoms have higher energy before bonding. What should happen after they bond?
options: Their total energy lowers, and their arrangement becomes more stable.
Their total energy rises, and their arrangement becomes less stable.
Their total energy stays high, and their arrangement becomes less stable.
Their total energy lowers, and their arrangement becomes less stable.

why.Their total energy rises, and their arra: Wrong: it reverses both the energy change and the stability change.
why.Their total energy stays high, and their: Wrong: it assumes bonding leaves energy high and reduces stability.
why.Their total energy lowers, and their arr: Wrong: it wrongly links lower energy with lower stability.

activities.explanation: Correct: bonding lowers total energy and makes the arrangement more stable.

activities.prompt: A student claims every molecule has one element. Why is the claim wrong?
options: Some molecules contain atoms from different elements.
Some molecules contain only one atom.
Some molecules transfer electrons between different elements.
Some molecules contain no atoms at all.

Wrong: it confuses a molecule with one atom.
why.Some molecules transfer electrons betwee: Wrong: it mistakes electron transfer for a rule about element count.
Wrong: it wrongly assumes a molecule can contain no atoms.

activities.explanation: Correct: atoms of different elements can form a compound molecule.

lessons.title: Naming Compounds and Ionic Bonds

activities.prompt: What do the names of compounds secretly tell us?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Counting Atoms and Making Ions
activities.body: Prefixes count atoms in covalent compounds. Mono- means one, di- means two, and tri- means three. The first element keeps its usual name, and mono- is usually left out. A sodium atom that loses an electron becomes a positive cation. A chlorine atom that gains one becomes a negative anion. Opposite charges form an ionic bond. Ionic compounds form repeating crystals. The cation’s name comes before the anion’s name.
keyPoints: Prefixes show how many atoms are present.
Electron changes produce charged ions.
Cation names come before anion names.
activities.explanation: These rules help you name compounds and describe ionic bonding.

activities.prompt: A model shows sodium and chlorine becoming charged. How do they attract and join?
steps: A sodium atom loses one electron, so it becomes a positively charged sodium cation.
A chlorine atom gains one electron, so it becomes a negatively charged chloride anion.
Their opposite charges attract, so an ionic bond holds the cation and anion together.
The cation is named first, so the compound name places sodium before chloride.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Choose the Counting Prefix
activities.prompt: Which prefix shows that three atoms are present?
options: mono-
di-
tri-
activities.explanation: Tri- shows that three atoms are present.

activities.prompt: The prefix mono- is normally used before the first element.
activities.explanation: Mono- is normally left out before the first element.

activities.title: Match the Science Words
activities.prompt: Match each change or pattern with its correct result.
activities.explanation: Electron changes produce ions. Opposite charges form bonds, and repeating ions form crystals.

activities.title: Name the Chlorine Ion
activities.prompt: A chlorine atom that gains an electron becomes a ______ anion.
activities.hint: This ion has a negative charge.
activities.explanation: Gaining an electron makes the chlorine atom a negatively charged chloride anion.

activities.prompt: Ionic compounds have ions arranged in a repeating pattern.
activities.explanation: Ionic compounds form three-dimensional crystals with ions in a repeating pattern.

activities.title: Choose the Correct Description
activities.prompt: Which option correctly describes an ionic compound?
options: Anion first; random ion pattern
Anion first; repeating ion pattern
Cation first; random ion pattern
Cation first; repeating ion pattern
activities.explanation: The cation’s name comes first. The ions form a repeating crystal pattern.

activities.prompt: A covalent name has no prefix before its first element. The second element has di-. How many atoms of each element are present?
options: The first element has one atom, and the second has two atoms.
The first element has two atoms, and the second has one atom.
The first element has two atoms, and the second has two atoms.
The first element has three atoms, and the second has one atom.

why.The first element has two atoms, and the: An omitted mono still means one, but di does not mean one.
The learner wrongly treats the missing prefix as di-.
why.The first element has three atoms, and t: The learner wrongly treats the missing prefix as tri-.

activities.explanation: Mono is omitted before the first element, and di means two.

activities.prompt: A learner keeps crossed valencies when a common factor can be removed. What is wrong with the formula?
options: It does not show the simplest ratio between the atoms.
It shows too few atoms of both combining elements.
It hides which valencies were crossed over.
It swaps the combining elements without changing their ratio.

why.It shows too few atoms of both combining: The learner wrongly removes the factor instead of keeping crossed valencies.
why.It hides which valencies were crossed ov: Crossed valencies are used to write the formula, not hidden from it.
why.It swaps the combining elements without: The common factor changes subscripts, not the order of elements.

activities.explanation: Removing the common factor gives the simplest ratio between the atoms.

activities.prompt: Sodium loses an electron. Chlorine gains one. How should you order this name?
options: Put sodium before chloride in the compound name.
Put chloride before sodium in the compound name.
Put sodium after chloride in the compound name.
Put only sodium in the compound name.

why.Put chloride before sodium in the compou: The learner reverses the rule and puts the anion first.
why.Put sodium after chloride in the compoun: The learner still puts the anion first by placing sodium last.
The learner wrongly leaves out the anion's name.

activities.explanation: The cation's name comes before the anion's name.

lessons.title: Properties and Masses of Compounds

activities.prompt: What makes compounds behave so differently in water?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Understanding compounds
activities.body: Ionic compounds generally dissolve in water and have high melting and boiling points. They do not conduct electricity in the solid state. In water, their free-moving ions conduct electricity. Most covalent compounds do not dissolve in water, but dissolve in kerosene and petrol. They usually have low melting and boiling points. Molecular mass sums all atom masses in a molecule. Water's molecular mass is 18 u. Formula unit mass is a formula unit's mass.
keyPoints: Ionic compounds are generally soluble in water.
Most covalent compounds dissolve in kerosene and petrol.
Molecular mass is found by adding all atom masses.
A formula unit shows the simplest whole-number ratio of ions.
activities.explanation: These properties help you compare ionic and covalent compounds.

activities.prompt: Why can an ionic compound conduct electricity in water but not as a solid?
steps: Water generally dissolves the ionic compound.
Its ions can then move freely in the water.
Moving ions let the water solution conduct electricity.
The solid does not conduct because its ions cannot move freely.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

options: It usually dissolves.
It never dissolves.
It forms separate molecules.
It conducts in the solid state.
activities.explanation: Ionic compounds are generally soluble in water, so they usually dissolve.

activities.prompt: An ionic compound conducts electricity while it is solid.
activities.explanation: Good try. Ionic compounds do not conduct electricity in the solid state.

activities.title: Matching compound properties
activities.prompt: Match each description with its stated property.
pairs: Most covalent compounds in kerosene and petrol
Generally has high melting and boiling points
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a usual solubility or melting and boiling point property.

activities.title: The molecular mass of water
activities.prompt: The molecular mass of water is ______ u.
activities.hint: Use the molecular mass given for water.
activities.explanation: Well done. The molecular mass of water is 18 u.

activities.title: Conducting electricity
activities.prompt: When do ionic compounds conduct electricity?
options: When their ions move freely in water
When their ions are fixed in a solid
When their molecules move in petrol
When their ions are joined in a solid
activities.explanation: Ionic compounds conduct electricity when their ions can move freely in water.

activities.title: Finding molecular mass
activities.prompt: Put the steps for finding molecular mass in order.
activities.explanation: Molecular mass is found by adding the masses of all atoms in a molecule.

activities.title: Meaning of a formula unit
activities.prompt: What does a formula unit represent in an ionic compound?
options: The simplest whole-number ratio of ions
The separate molecules that form it
The combined masses of all its atoms
The total number of all its ions
activities.explanation: A formula unit represents the simplest whole-number ratio of ions in an ionic compound.

activities.title: Formula unit mass
activities.prompt: The mass of a formula unit is called its molecular mass.
activities.explanation: Good try. The mass of a formula unit is called its formula unit mass.

activities.prompt: An ionic compound is dissolved in water. What is most likely?
options: The solution conducts electricity because its ions can move.
The solution fails because its ions stay still.
The solution conducts because the solid also conducts.
The solution fails because water blocks all ions.

why.The solution fails because its ions stay: It confuses solid-state behavior with water-solution behavior.
why.The solution conducts because the solid: It wrongly thinks a solid ionic compound conducts electricity.
why.The solution fails because water blocks: It wrongly thinks water prevents ions from conducting electricity.

activities.explanation: Ions move freely in water, so the solution conducts electricity.

activities.prompt: An ionic solid and a covalent solid are heated until they melt. Which result fits most samples?
options: The ionic solid needs a higher temperature to melt.
The covalent solid needs a higher temperature to melt.
Both solids need the same high melting temperature.
Both solids need the same low melting temperature.

why.The covalent solid needs a higher temper: Covalent compounds usually have low melting points.
why.Both solids need the same high melting t: It wrongly assumes both types have high melting points.
why.Both solids need the same low melting te: It wrongly assumes both types have low melting points.

activities.explanation: Ionic compounds generally have high melting points.

activities.context: During the first vinegar-and-baking-soda experiment, a student recorded the initial mass of the reaction setup and then measured the final mass after carbon dioxide formed. The final reading did not match the initial reading. In a modified experiment, the student kept the produced gas inside a balloon. This time, the final reading matched the initial reading because the gas did not escape.
activities.prompt: If the student releases the gas from the balloon before taking the final reading, what should happen?
options: The final reading would be lower because carbon dioxide would escape.
The final reading would be higher because carbon dioxide would escape.
The final reading would remain equal because matter cannot be destroyed.
The final reading would be higher because the balloon would add matter.

why.The final reading would be higher becaus: Escaping gas would reduce, not increase, the measured mass.
why.The final reading would remain equal bec: It overlooks that the escaped gas is outside the measured setup.
why.The final reading would be higher becaus: The balloon does not create extra matter.

activities.explanation: Escaping carbon dioxide leaves less matter to be measured.

activities.context: During the first vinegar-and-baking-soda experiment, a student recorded the initial mass of the reaction setup and then measured the final mass after carbon dioxide formed. The final reading did not match the initial reading. In a modified experiment, the student kept the produced gas inside a balloon. This time, the final reading matched the initial reading because the gas did not escape.
activities.prompt: What comparison of the two experiments explains why their final readings were different?
options: The readings differed because gas escaped in one setup but not in the other.
The first setup created extra matter during the reaction.
The modified setup destroyed the carbon dioxide before weighing.
The balloon changed the amount of baking soda and vinegar reacting.

why.The first setup created extra matter dur: Matter was not created during either reaction.
why.The modified setup destroyed the carbon: The carbon dioxide remained in the balloon in the modified setup.
why.The balloon changed the amount of baking: Keeping the gas did not change the quantities of the reacting substances.

activities.explanation: The escaped gas caused the first reading not to match the initial reading.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The final reading in the first vinegar-and-baking-soda experiment did not match the initial reading.
Reason (R): The carbon dioxide gas produced during the reaction escaped.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The escaped gas directly explains why the final reading was lower than the initial reading.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Matter can neither be created nor destroyed during a chemical reaction.
Reason (R): Antoine Lavoisier proposed the Law of Conservation of Mass in 1789.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but the historical proposal does not explain why matter is conserved.

activities.prompt: Explain how allowing gas to escape caused the first experiment's readings to differ and how the modified experiment demonstrated conservation of mass.
activities.answer: In the first vinegar-and-baking-soda experiment, the final reading did not match the initial reading because the carbon dioxide gas escaped from the reaction setup. Losing the gas meant that part of the matter involved in the reaction was no longer being measured, so the readings differed. In the modified experiment, the gas remained in the balloon. The total mass before and after the reaction was therefore equal, showing that matter was neither created nor destroyed during the chemical reaction.
points: Identifies the escaping carbon dioxide as the cause
Explains that the measured setup lost some matter
States that the balloon kept the gas included
Concludes that the equal readings demonstrated conservation of mass
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A school laboratory decomposes 9 g of purified water and records two portions: 1 g of hydrogen and 8 g of oxygen. A water sample from another source is checked, and copper carbonate is examined too. Later, cinnabar is heated. Students are asked why the element proportions do not change with the source or sample, and how this rule connects all these compounds.
activities.prompt: If a second 9 g sample of purified water is decomposed, what should the student expect?
options: Hydrogen: 1 g; oxygen: 8 g.
Hydrogen: 8 g; oxygen: 1 g.
Hydrogen: 1 g; oxygen: 9 g.
Hydrogen: 8 g; oxygen: 8 g.

This reverses the correct mass ratio.
This gives the whole sample to hydrogen and assigns an incorrect mass to oxygen.
This makes the two portions equal instead of following the 1:8 ratio.

activities.explanation: This matches the fixed 1:8 mass ratio in water.

activities.context: A school laboratory decomposes 9 g of purified water and records two portions: 1 g of hydrogen and 8 g of oxygen. A water sample from another source is checked, and copper carbonate is examined too. Later, cinnabar is heated. Students are asked why the element proportions do not change with the source or sample, and how this rule connects all these compounds.
activities.prompt: Based on cinnabar's 86.22% mercury and 13.78% sulfur by mass, how should a student describe its element proportions?
options: Mercury would account for the larger share of the original mass, and sulfur for the smaller share.
Sulfur would account for the larger share of the original mass, and mercury for the smaller share.
Mercury and sulfur would each account for half of the original mass.
Only sulfur would be present because mercury would be lost during heating.

why.Mercury and sulfur would each account fo: The stated percentages are not equal.
why.Only sulfur would be present because mer: Cinnabar contains both mercury and sulfur.

activities.explanation: The stated mercury percentage is greater than the sulfur percentage.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Water from different sources has hydrogen and oxygen in the same mass ratio.
Reason (R): A compound has definite proportions of its elements regardless of its source.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the second statement explains why the ratio does not change with the source.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Water contains hydrogen and oxygen in a mass ratio of 1:8 by volume.
Reason (R): Water has definite proportions of its elements regardless of its source.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false because the 1:8 ratio is given by mass, while the reason is true.

activities.prompt: Explain why decomposing 9 g of purified water always gives 1 g of hydrogen and 8 g of oxygen.
activities.answer: Water is a compound, so it contains hydrogen and oxygen in a fixed mass ratio of 1:8. Therefore, decomposing 9 g of purified water always gives 1 g of hydrogen and 8 g of oxygen. The masses add to the original 9 g, and their proportions remain fixed. Whether the water came from one source or another does not change this composition, because a compound has definite proportions of its elements regardless of its source. This fixed behaviour is called the Law of Constant Proportions, also called the Law of Definite Proportions or Proust’s Law.
points: Water contains hydrogen and oxygen in a 1:8 mass ratio.
The 9 g sample gives 1 g of hydrogen and 8 g of oxygen.
A compound keeps definite proportions regardless of source.
The rule is also called the Law of Constant Proportions, the Law of Definite Proportions, or Proust’s Law.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: At a school laboratory, a learner examines samples of hydrogen and helium. The hydrogen sample contains hydrogen molecules, while the helium sample contains only separate helium atoms. The learner is told that atoms can become more stable by sharing, gaining or losing valence electrons. In the hydrogen sample, the atoms share electrons, whereas helium remains as separate atoms. The learner wonders why hydrogen and helium form different arrangements and what force holds the atoms together.
activities.prompt: If the hydrogen atoms in the case did not share electrons, what would be true?
options: No hydrogen molecule would form.
The hydrogen sample would become a compound.
The helium atoms would begin sharing electrons.
Each hydrogen atom would become a molecule.

why.The hydrogen sample would become a compo: A compound requires atoms of different elements.
why.The helium atoms would begin sharing ele: The helium sample remains separate and does not affect hydrogen.
why.Each hydrogen atom would become a molecu: A molecule must contain more than one atom.

activities.explanation: A hydrogen molecule forms through electron sharing.

activities.context: At a school laboratory, a learner examines samples of hydrogen and helium. The hydrogen sample contains hydrogen molecules, while the helium sample contains only separate helium atoms. The learner is told that atoms can become more stable by sharing, gaining or losing valence electrons. In the hydrogen sample, the atoms share electrons, whereas helium remains as separate atoms. The learner wonders why hydrogen and helium form different arrangements and what force holds the atoms together.
activities.prompt: Why can the helium sample in the case not be described as a compound?
options: Its atoms remain unbonded rather than joining with atoms from another element.
A compound must contain atoms from only one element.
The hydrogen atoms share electrons with the helium atoms.
A molecule must contain just one atom.

why.A compound must contain atoms from only: This reverses the definition of a compound.
why.The hydrogen atoms share electrons with: The case states that helium remains as separate atoms.
This reverses the definition of a molecule.

activities.explanation: Helium exists only as separate atoms and does not combine with another element.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The hydrogen atoms in a hydrogen molecule each share one electron.
Reason (R): Sharing valence electrons can help atoms with incomplete valence shells become stable.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason explains why the hydrogen atoms share electrons and form a stable molecule.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A molecule of a compound contains atoms of different elements.
Reason (R): A molecule is an electrically neutral entity containing more than one atom.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but the definition of a molecule does not explain why a compound contains different elements.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between a molecule of an element and a molecule of a compound.
activities.answer: Both are electrically neutral entities containing more than one atom. A molecule of an element forms when atoms of that same element combine; a hydrogen molecule is an example because it contains two hydrogen atoms. A molecule of a compound forms when atoms of different elements combine. Therefore, the difference is the source of the atoms: one molecule uses atoms from the same element, while the other uses atoms from different elements. The compound molecule therefore contains different kinds of atom.
points: Defines both as neutral entities with more than one atom
Explains that an elemental molecule contains atoms of one element
Explains that a compound contains atoms of different elements
Uses hydrogen as an example
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: At school, Arjun is preparing labels for two particle models. One model shows a sodium atom that has lost an electron, while the other shows a chlorine atom that has gained one. He also writes a name for a covalent compound whose first element has one atom and whose second element has three atoms. The teacher asks him to place the two ions in a repeating three-dimensional pattern and explain his choices.
activities.prompt: How should Arjun describe the two particle models?
options: The sodium particle is the positive ion and the chlorine particle is the negative ion.
The sodium particle is the negative ion and the chlorine particle is the positive ion.
The sodium particle is the negative ion and the chlorine particle is also the negative ion.
The sodium particle is the positive ion and the chlorine particle is also the positive ion.

why.The sodium particle is the negative ion: This option reverses the charges caused by losing and gaining an electron.
Chlorine becomes negative after gaining an electron; sodium becomes positive.
why.The sodium particle is the positive ion: Chlorine does not become positive after gaining an electron.

activities.explanation: Losing an electron makes sodium positive, while gaining one makes chlorine negative.

activities.context: At school, Arjun is preparing labels for two particle models. One model shows a sodium atom that has lost an electron, while the other shows a chlorine atom that has gained one. He also writes a name for a covalent compound whose first element has one atom and whose second element has three atoms. The teacher asks him to place the two ions in a repeating three-dimensional pattern and explain his choices.
activities.prompt: Which prefixes should Arjun use for the covalent compound with one atom of its first element and three atoms of its second element?
options: Use mono- before the first element and tri- before the second.
Keep the first element unprefixed and use tri- before the second.
Use di- before the first element and mono- before the second.
Keep the first element unprefixed and use mono- before the second.

why.Use mono- before the first element and t: The prefix mono- is normally omitted before the first element.
why.Use di- before the first element and mon: One atom does not require the prefix di-.
why.Keep the first element unprefixed and us: Three atoms require tri-, not mono-.

activities.explanation: One atom in the first element needs no usual prefix, while three atoms require tri-.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The sodium model represents a cation, while the chlorine model represents an anion.
Reason (R): The sodium atom has lost an electron and the chlorine atom has gained one.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Losing an electron makes sodium a cation, while gaining an electron makes chlorine an anion.

lessons.title: How Sound Is Produced

activities.prompt: What makes a sound, and how do different objects create it?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Sound Starts with Vibration
activities.body: Sound begins with vibration, which means movement. Objects vibrate to make sound. Pulling a string can cause this. Air inside a hollow pipe can vibrate. The sound-maker is called the source. Humans and some animals use vibrating vocal cords. The tongue, lips, mouth and nasal cavity change sound into speech or music. A tuning fork is a U-shaped metal instrument with a stem. Its two sides are prongs or tines.
keyPoints: Objects vibrate to produce sound
Vocal cords help produce speech and music
Tuning fork prongs vibrate when struck
activities.explanation: Vibration is the common link between these sound-makers.

activities.prompt: A child strikes a metal object. Why is it the sound's source?
steps: The metal object is struck, so it begins to vibrate.
Vibration produces sound, so the struck object can be heard.
The metal object is the sound's source because it makes the sound.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What happens when an object vibrates?
options: It creates sound
It creates silence
It stops movement
It hides the source
activities.explanation: Vibration and sound go together.

activities.prompt: Which can be the source of a sound?
options: A metal object at rest
A string held still
A vibrating metal object
A hollow pipe with still air
activities.explanation: The source is the object that produces the sound.

activities.prompt: Humans and some animals have vocal ______ that vibrate to produce sound.
activities.hint: Join these with “vocal” to name the parts.
activities.explanation: Vocal cords vibrate to produce sound in humans and some animals.

activities.prompt: Match each object or body part with its sound action.
pairs: Vibrate when struck on a pad
Tongue, lips, mouth and nasal cavity
Convert sound into speech or music
activities.explanation: Each pair shows an object or part and its sound action.

activities.prompt: Put the steps for human sound production in order.
items: The tongue, lips, mouth and nasal cavity help convert it
The sound becomes speech or music
activities.explanation: Vibrating vocal cords start the sound. The body parts then help convert it.

activities.prompt: Which statement about a tuning fork is correct?
options: Its prongs stay still when struck.
Its prongs vibrate when struck.
Its sides are called striking pads.
Its hollow centre makes the sound.
activities.explanation: The prongs vibrate when the fork is struck on a pad. They are also called tines.

activities.prompt: A child pulls a loose string. A sound follows. What causes the sound?
options: The pulled string vibrates and produces the sound.
The still string produces the sound without any movement.
The child's fingers produce the sound while the string stays still.
The sound pulls the string and makes it move.

why.The still string produces the sound with: This mistake ignores that the string must vibrate.
why.The child's fingers produce the sound wh: This mistake ignores that pulling makes the string vibrate.
why.The sound pulls the string and makes it: This mistake reverses the order of vibration and sound.

activities.explanation: Pulling makes the string vibrate, and vibration makes sound.

activities.prompt: A singer's vocal cords vibrate. The tongue and lips move. What do they help do?
options: They help turn the sound into speech or music.
They help make the vocal cords stop vibrating.
They help make sound without needing vibration.
They help make the hollow pipe produce the sound.

why.They help make the vocal cords stop vibr: This mistake says the mouth stops the source from vibrating.
why.They help make sound without needing vib: This mistake thinks shaped sound no longer needs vibration.
why.They help make the hollow pipe produce t: This mistake mixes up a singer with a hollow pipe.

activities.explanation: These parts turn sound into speech or music, so this is right.

activities.prompt: One tuning fork is struck on a pad. Another stays still. What should the child expect?
options: The struck fork's prongs should vibrate and make sound.
Both forks' prongs should vibrate because both are metal.
The still fork's prongs should also vibrate and make sound.
Neither fork's prongs should vibrate because only pads move.

why.Both forks' prongs should vibrate becaus: This mistake assumes that being metal makes both sets vibrate.
why.The still fork's prongs should also vibr: This mistake assumes staying still also causes the prongs to vibrate.
why.Neither fork's prongs should vibrate bec: This mistake says the pad vibrates instead of the prongs.

activities.explanation: This is right because striking the pad makes the prongs vibrate.

activities.prompt: A toy object vibrates. A sound is heard. Why is the toy the sound's source?
options: It is the source because it vibrates and produces sound.
It is the source because a listener hears the sound.
It is the source because nearby air always moves.
It is the source because another object stays still.

why.It is the source because a listener hear: This mistake confuses hearing a sound with producing it.
why.It is the source because nearby air alwa: This mistake confuses the source with nearby vibrating air.
why.It is the source because another object: This mistake uses another object's stillness to explain the source.

activities.explanation: This is right because a vibrating object produces sound.

lessons.title: How Sound Travels

activities.prompt: Could you hear a bell if all the air disappeared?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Sound Needs a Medium
activities.body: Sound starts at a source and moves to a listener through a medium. A medium is the material carrying the sound. Sound can travel through solids, liquids and gases. A vacuum has no matter, so sound cannot travel through it. This is why a bell becomes fainter as air leaves its jar.
keyPoints: Sound needs a medium to travel.
Sound travels through solids, liquids and gases.
A vacuum has no matter, so sound cannot travel through it.
activities.explanation: Sound travels through matter, but not empty space.

activities.prompt: Why does a bell grow quiet as air leaves its jar?
steps: The air around the bell is a medium for sound.
As air is removed, less matter remains to carry the sound.
The listener hears a fainter bell because less sound reaches them.
A vacuum has no medium, so sound cannot travel through it.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Sound in a Bell Jar and Space
activities.body: A bell's sound becomes fainter as air is removed from its jar. When the jar contains a near vacuum, almost no sound can be heard. This vacuum bell jar experiment shows that sound needs a medium in order to travel. Outer space has a near vacuum, so sound cannot travel through it. Astronauts cannot directly hear each other during a spacewalk. They use special devices in their spacesuits to communicate.
keyPoints: A bell becomes fainter as air leaves its jar.
Almost no sound is heard in a near vacuum.
Special devices help astronauts communicate in space.
activities.explanation: These experiments and space travel show why sound needs matter.

activities.prompt: Where can sound travel?
options: Through a vacuum and liquids
Through near vacuum and gases
Through solids, liquids and gases
Through empty space and solids
activities.explanation: Sound can travel through all three materials listed.

activities.prompt: Match each item with its lesson partner.
pairs: becomes fainter as air is removed
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a key idea about how sound travels.

activities.prompt: Sound travels from its source to the listener through a ______.
activities.hint: This is the material carrying the sound.
activities.explanation: The medium carries sound from its source to the listener.

activities.prompt: Why can astronauts not directly hear each other during a spacewalk?
options: Space has a near vacuum
Spacesuits block all sound
Speech travels through light
Helmets have no air
activities.explanation: Outer space has a near vacuum, so sound cannot travel through it.

activities.prompt: Astronauts use special ______ in their spacesuits to communicate.
activities.hint: These help them communicate during a spacewalk.
activities.explanation: Special devices help astronauts communicate in their spacesuits.

activities.prompt: Put the bell jar events in order.
items: Air is removed from the jar
The jar contains a near vacuum
Almost no sound can be heard
activities.explanation: Removing air reduces the medium and makes the sound fainter.

activities.prompt: A child taps a solid wooden stick. What reaches someone holding it?
options: Sound travels through the solid stick to the listener.
No sound travels because the stick is solid.
Sound travels only through the air beside the stick.
Sound stays at the tapped end of the stick.

why.No sound travels because the stick is so: This mistake thinks solid materials block all sound.
why.Sound travels only through the air besid: This mistake thinks only gases can carry sound.
why.Sound stays at the tapped end of the sti: This mistake thinks sound cannot move through a solid.

activities.explanation: The stick is solid, and sound can travel through solids.

activities.prompt: Underwater, a diver taps a bell. What sound reaches a nearby listener?
options: Sound travels through the water to the listener.
No sound travels because water is a liquid.
Sound travels only through the air above the water.
The solid bell stops the sound before the water.

why.No sound travels because water is a liqu: This mistake thinks liquids cannot carry sound.
why.Sound travels only through the air above: This mistake thinks only gases can carry sound.
why.The solid bell stops the sound before th: This mistake thinks the solid bell blocks all sound.

activities.explanation: Water is a liquid, and sound can travel through liquids.

activities.prompt: A bell is almost silent in a near vacuum. Why?
options: The near vacuum has no matter to carry sound.
The listener stands too far away from the bell.
The solid glass of the jar stops all sound.
The remaining air pushes the sound out of the jar.

why.The listener stands too far away from th: This mistake blames distance instead of the missing medium.
why.The solid glass of the jar stops all sou: This mistake thinks solid glass blocks all sound.
why.The remaining air pushes the sound out o: This mistake thinks remaining air carries the sound away.

activities.explanation: The near vacuum lacks matter, so almost no sound can be heard.

activities.prompt: A learner tests whether sound needs matter. Which comparison is fairest?
options: Compare a bell in air with a bell in a near vacuum.
Compare two bells at different distances in the same air.
Compare a bell in air with a bell under water.
Compare a bell in air with a bell inside a solid box.

why.Compare two bells at different distances: This changes distance, not whether a medium is present.
why.Compare a bell in air with a bell under: Both air and water are media, so this does not test absence.
why.Compare a bell in air with a bell inside: Both air and a solid box provide matter for sound.

activities.explanation: The air and near vacuum change whether matter can carry sound.

lessons.title: Understanding Sound Waves

activities.prompt: How does sound travel through the air and make our ears ring?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Sound Waves Move
activities.body: Sound spreads in several directions from its source. An unrestricted medium allows sound to spread in all directions. A sound wave is a disturbance of alternating compressions and rarefactions. A compression has higher air density. A rarefaction has lower air density. The direction of propagation means the direction in which a wave travels. In a longitudinal wave, particles vibrate parallel to the wave’s direction.
keyPoints: Sound spreads in several directions.
Compressions and rarefactions alternate in a sound wave.
Particles vibrate parallel to the wave’s direction.
activities.explanation: These ideas describe how sound moves and what its wave contains.

activities.prompt: A child hears a speaker in an open space and wonders why people around it hear the sound.
steps: Sound spreads in several directions from its source, so it can reach people around the speaker.
When the medium is unrestricted, sound spreads in all directions.
The direction from the speaker toward a listener is the direction of propagation.
Therefore, people around the speaker can hear the sound.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which region has higher air density?
options: a rarefaction
a compression
a sonic boom
a wave source
activities.explanation: A compression is a region where air density is higher.

activities.prompt: A sound wave is a disturbance of alternating ______ and rarefactions.
activities.hint: This region has higher air density.
activities.explanation: Compressions and rarefactions alternate in a sound wave.

activities.prompt: Match each clue to the correct term.
activities.explanation: Higher density means compression, while lower density means rarefaction. Parallel vibration identifies a longitudinal wave.

activities.prompt: What can an aircraft travelling faster than sound produce?
options: a compression
a rarefaction
a sonic boom
a mark on a slinky
activities.explanation: The lesson says that faster-than-sound aircraft can produce a sonic boom.

activities.prompt: In a longitudinal wave, particles vibrate across the wave’s direction.
activities.explanation: Particles vibrate parallel to the wave’s direction in a longitudinal wave.

activities.prompt: Put these regions in the order they can appear in a sound wave.
activities.explanation: Compressions and rarefactions are produced one after another. A sound wave alternates between them.

activities.prompt: Which statement about sound spreading is correct?
options: Sound spreads in one direction when its medium is unrestricted.
Sound spreads in no directions when its medium is unrestricted.
Sound always spreads in one direction from its source.
Sound spreads in all directions when its medium is unrestricted.
activities.explanation: Sound spreads in all directions when its medium is unrestricted.

activities.prompt: A child speaks in a space with no barriers. People hear the voice around the child. What happens to the sound?
options: It spreads in all directions.
It spreads only forward.
It spreads only backward.
It spreads only to one side.

This is wrong because it thinks sound travels only forward.
This is wrong because it thinks sound travels only backward.
This is wrong because it thinks sound travels to only one side.

activities.explanation: This is right because unrestricted sound spreads in all directions.

activities.prompt: A sound disturbance moves through air. What pattern does the sound wave make?
options: Alternating compressions and rarefactions.
Only compressions, with no rarefactions.
Only rarefactions, with no compressions.
Random regions, with no repeated order.

This is wrong because it forgets that rarefactions also occur.
This is wrong because it forgets that compressions also occur.
This is wrong because compressions and rarefactions occur one after another.

activities.explanation: This is right because a sound wave has alternating compressions and rarefactions.

lessons.title: Energy and Graphs of Sound Waves

activities.prompt: What happens to energy when sound moves through air?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Sound Waves Carry Energy
activities.body: Sound is energy. A vibrating sound source transfers energy to the surrounding medium. The wave moves through collisions between particles. It transfers energy, but does not carry the medium’s particles along. A microphone changes sound energy into electrical energy. On a sound-wave graph, density is on the vertical axis. Density rises above average at a compression. The highest point is a crest, and the lowest point is a trough.
keyPoints: A sound wave transfers energy.
Sound energy can become electrical energy.
Graphs show density, crests and troughs.
activities.explanation: These ideas connect sound energy with the features of a sound-wave graph.

activities.prompt: A child speaks near a wall. Does the sound carry air particles to the wall, or only energy?
steps: The vibrating voice transfers energy to the nearby air.
Collisions between air particles pass that energy onward.
At the wall, the air transfers energy to it, making it vibrate.
Therefore, sound transfers energy without carrying the medium’s particles along.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: A sound wave carries the medium’s particles along with it.
activities.explanation: A sound wave transfers energy rather than carrying the medium’s particles along.

activities.prompt: What does a sound wave transfer through its medium?
options: Energy
Particles
Source
Collisions
activities.explanation: A sound wave transfers energy through the surrounding medium.

activities.prompt: Sound is a form of ______.
activities.hint: This is what a sound wave transfers.
activities.explanation: Sound is a form of energy.

activities.title: Match Sound Ideas
activities.prompt: Match each sound-related idea with its correct partner.
activities.explanation: Sound energy changes at a microphone. A graph marks density, crests and troughs.

activities.prompt: What happens to density in a compression?
options: It rises above average.
It falls below average.
It stays exactly average.
It changes randomly.
activities.explanation: The density increases above average in a compression.

activities.prompt: Put these sound-energy changes in order.
items: Collisions transfer energy through the medium.
activities.explanation: A vibrating source starts the energy transfer. The microphone converts the sound energy into electrical energy.

activities.prompt: During a compression, density is above its average value.
activities.explanation: The density increases above average in a compression.

activities.prompt: A vibrating source makes sound. Why can sound travel through the medium?
options: The wave transfers energy between particles.
The source carries particles through the medium.
The medium’s particles move to the source.
The wave carries particles far from the source.
activities.explanation: Collisions between particles transfer energy as the wave moves. The particles are not carried along.

activities.prompt: A guitar string is plucked beside a microphone. What energy change should the microphone make?
options: Sound energy becomes electrical energy.
Electrical energy becomes sound energy.
Sound energy becomes light energy.
Sound energy stays sound energy.

This reverses the stated direction of the energy conversion.
It imagines the microphone changing sound into light.
It assumes the microphone does not change the energy type.

activities.explanation: The microphone converts sound energy into electrical energy.

activities.prompt: A bell is struck and rings. What does the vibrating bell do to the surrounding air?
options: It transfers energy into the surrounding air.
It pulls air particles along with the bell.
It changes air into electrical energy.
It makes the air particles stop colliding.

why.It pulls air particles along with the be: It mistakes energy transfer for transport of particles.
It assigns the microphone’s conversion to the bell.
why.It makes the air particles stop collidin: It thinks energy transfer requires particles to stop colliding.

activities.explanation: A vibrating source transfers energy to the surrounding medium.

lessons.title: Characteristics of Sound Waves

activities.prompt: Why do sounds travel differently through solid ground, water, and air?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Sound Wave Basics
activities.body: Wavelength is the distance between neighbouring crests or troughs, measured in metres. Frequency counts density oscillations at one point per unit time. Its unit is hertz, written as Hz. Time period is the time for a complete density oscillation. A shorter period means higher frequency. Speed equals wavelength multiplied by frequency. It depends on the medium. Sound travels fastest in solids, then liquids, then gases. Warm, humid air increases its speed.
keyPoints: Wavelength is measured in metres.
Frequency is measured in hertz, written as Hz.
A shorter time period means higher frequency.
Sound speed depends on its medium.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you describe and compare sound waves.

activities.prompt: Two nearby bells make sounds in the same air. One takes less time for each complete density oscillation. Which bell has the higher frequency?
steps: The first bell changes from maximum density to minimum density and back in less time.
So more complete oscillations happen at a fixed point in each unit time.
Frequency counts these oscillations per unit time, so the first bell has higher frequency.
The second bell takes longer for each cycle, so its frequency is lower.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Measuring Wavelength
activities.prompt: What distance does wavelength measure?
options: Between neighbouring crests
Between a crest and trough
Between a wave and its start
Between a trough and the next crest
activities.explanation: A wavelength is the distance between consecutive crests or consecutive troughs.

activities.title: Match the Terms
activities.prompt: Match each sound-wave term with its correct description.
pairs: measured in hertz, written as Hz
time for one complete density oscillation
activities.explanation: Each pair connects a sound-wave term with its unit or defining relation.

activities.title: Calculating Sound Speed
activities.prompt: How is the speed of a sound wave calculated?
options: Its wavelength multiplied by its frequency
Its frequency divided by its wavelength
Its wavelength added to its frequency
Its wavelength divided by its frequency
activities.explanation: The speed equals the wavelength multiplied by the frequency.

activities.title: Period and Frequency
activities.prompt: A shorter time period corresponds to a ______ frequency.
activities.hint: Think about changes in the time for each oscillation.
activities.explanation: The lesson says that a shorter time period corresponds to a higher frequency.

activities.title: Speed Through Media
activities.prompt: Put these media in order from fastest to slowest sound travel.
activities.explanation: Sound travels fastest in solids, more slowly in liquids and slowest in gases.

activities.title: Changing Air Conditions
activities.prompt: What happens when air temperature or humidity increases?
options: The speed of sound increases.
The speed of sound decreases.
The speed of sound stays fixed.
The sound wave loses its frequency.
activities.explanation: Increasing either temperature or humidity of air increases the speed of sound.

activities.prompt: At a fixed point, Sound A completes each density cycle faster than Sound B. Which sound has the higher frequency?
options: Sound A has the higher frequency.
Sound B has the higher frequency.
Both sounds have equal frequencies.
The frequencies cannot be compared.

The mistake reverses the link between a shorter period and frequency.
The mistake ignores the different cycle times.
The mistake believes cycle times do not show frequency.

activities.explanation: Completing each cycle faster means more cycles happen per unit time.

activities.prompt: Several sounds start together at one place. Each travels an equal distance through a solid, a liquid, or a gas. Which sound arrives first?
options: The sound in the solid arrives first.
The sound in the liquid arrives first.
The sound in the gas arrives first.
All three sounds arrive at the same time.

The mistake puts liquids before solids in the speed order.
The mistake puts gases before solids in the speed order.
why.All three sounds arrive at the same time: The mistake ignores that the medium changes sound speed.

activities.explanation: Sound travels fastest in solids, so this sound arrives first.

activities.prompt: A sound wave keeps the same speed, but its wavelength becomes longer. Using speed = wavelength × frequency, what must happen to its frequency?
options: The frequency must decrease.
The frequency must increase.
The frequency must stay the same.
The frequency cannot be found from this information.

The mistake treats wavelength and frequency as both increasing together.
The mistake forgets that wavelength multiplied by frequency gives speed.
why.The frequency cannot be found from this: The mistake thinks speed does not connect wavelength and frequency.

activities.explanation: With speed unchanged, a longer wavelength needs a lower frequency.

lessons.title: Hearing, Reflection and Ultrasonic Uses

activities.prompt: How do sound waves help us explore places hidden from sight?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How We Hear Sound
activities.body: Pitch is how humans perceive frequency. Loudness is how humans perceive amplitude. Humans normally hear 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Sound bounces from surfaces. This is reflection of sound. An echo is reflected sound returning after a short time. Sounds above 20 kHz are ultrasonic waves. Echolocation uses reflected sound waves to locate objects. Sonar sends ultrasonic waves into water to study underwater objects.
keyPoints: Pitch and loudness describe human hearing.
Multiple reflections can create reverberation.
Ultrasonic waves help sonar study underwater objects.
activities.explanation: These ideas connect hearing, reflection and underwater sound.

activities.prompt: Why does a clap keep sounding in a hall with many reflecting surfaces?
steps: You clap once in a hall with many reflecting surfaces.
The sound reaches a surface and bounces back, because sound reflects.
Several reflected sounds return, so the sound continues after your clap.
This continuing sound is reverberation, because multiple reflections keep it going.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What does loudness describe?
options: Frequency
Amplitude
Pitch
activities.explanation: Loudness is how humans perceive the amplitude of a sound wave.

activities.prompt: High-pitch sounds generally have a higher frequency.
activities.explanation: High-pitch sounds generally have a higher frequency.

activities.prompt: Humans normally hear sounds from ______ Hz to 20,000 Hz.
activities.hint: This is the lower limit of normal hearing.
activities.explanation: Normal human hearing starts at 20 Hz and ends at 20,000 Hz.

activities.prompt: Match each sound term to its meaning.
pairs: Reflected sound returning after a short time
activities.explanation: Each sound feature has the matching meaning shown in the pairs.

activities.prompt: Which waves does sonar send into water?
options: Infrasonic waves
Ultrasonic waves
Multiple reflections
activities.explanation: Sonar sends ultrasonic waves into water to study underwater objects.

activities.prompt: Put these sound ranges in order from lowest to highest.
activities.explanation: The ranges run from lowest frequency to highest frequency.

activities.prompt: Two sounds reach your ears. One has a higher frequency. Which sound has the higher pitch?
options: The sound with the higher frequency.
The sound with the lower frequency.
The sound with the greater amplitude.
The sound with the smaller amplitude.

This confuses higher pitch with lower frequency.
This wrongly treats smaller amplitude as higher pitch.

activities.explanation: Pitch is how humans perceive the frequency of a sound.

activities.prompt: Two sounds have the same frequency. One wave has a greater amplitude. Which sound will be heard as louder?
options: The sound with the greater amplitude.
The sound with the smaller amplitude.
The sound with the higher frequency.
The sound with the lower frequency.

This confuses greater loudness with smaller amplitude.

activities.explanation: Loudness is how humans perceive the amplitude of a sound wave.

activities.prompt: A machine makes a sound above 20,000 Hz. A person listens normally. Will the person hear this sound directly?
options: No, because the sound is above human hearing.
No, because the sound is below 20 Hz.
Yes, because every sound can be heard.
Yes, because the sound is infrasonic.

This wrongly treats the sound as below 20 Hz.
This assumes all sounds are within the human hearing range.
This confuses ultrasonic waves with infrasonic waves.

activities.explanation: The sound is above 20,000 Hz, so it is ultrasonic.

activities.prompt: You shout at a wall and hear your words return after a short time. What caused the returning sound?
options: It bounced from the wall and returned to you.
It passed through the wall and came back.
It changed into a higher-pitched sound.
It became louder before returning to you.

why.It passed through the wall and came back: This wrongly treats the returning sound as passing through the wall.
This confuses reflection with a change in frequency.
why.It became louder before returning to you: This confuses reflection with a change in amplitude.

activities.explanation: Sound reflects from the wall and returns as an echo.

activities.prompt: A bell rings in a room with many reflecting surfaces. The bell stops, but sound continues. Why?
options: Several reflections keep the sound continuing.
One reflection makes the sound last longer.
The bell changes into a lower-pitched sound.
The sound changes into a quieter echo.

why.One reflection makes the sound last long: This misses the need for multiple reflections.
why.The bell changes into a lower-pitched so: This confuses reverberation with a change in pitch.
This confuses reverberation with an echo.

activities.explanation: Several reflections make sound continue after the source stops.
