lessons.title: Human Impact on Earth’s Processes

activities.prompt: How can our everyday choices change the health of our planet?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How People Change Earth’s Processes
activities.body: People change Earth’s processes through pollution and forest removal. Burning fossil fuels raises carbon dioxide, causing extreme weather and biodiversity loss. Extra carbon dioxide makes seawater more acidic, threatening plankton and coral reefs. Warmer seawater can absorb less carbon dioxide. Forest clearing can fill sinks and reduce photosynthesis. It can reduce rainfall, destroy habitats and reduce biodiversity. Vehicle emissions form ground-level smog with sunlight.
keyPoints: Human pollution raises atmospheric carbon dioxide.
Extra carbon dioxide acidifies seawater and threatens marine life.
Forest removal affects rainfall, habitats and biodiversity.
activities.explanation: These actions can affect air, seawater, forests and biodiversity.

activities.prompt: A town burns fuels and clears forests. What may happen nearby?
steps: Burning fossil fuels and clearing forests can fill natural carbon sinks.
More atmospheric carbon dioxide can lead to extreme weather and biodiversity loss.
Extra atmospheric carbon dioxide makes seawater more acidic.
Acidified seawater can threaten plankton, coral reefs and marine ecosystems.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Rising carbon dioxide from fossil fuels can lead to extreme weather.
activities.explanation: Rising carbon dioxide from fossil fuels can lead to extreme weather.

activities.prompt: Excess fertiliser nitrogen can enter rivers and lakes as ______.
activities.hint: Think about what fertiliser nitrogen becomes in rivers and lakes.
activities.explanation: Excess fertiliser nitrogen can enter rivers and lakes as nitrates.

activities.prompt: Match each human action with its possible result.
activities.explanation: Each pairing shows an effect described in the lesson.

activities.prompt: Extra atmospheric carbon dioxide makes seawater more acidic. What can ocean acidification threaten?
options: Coral reefs
Forest rainfall
Vehicle engines
Fertiliser nitrates
activities.explanation: Ocean acidification can threaten coral reefs. It can also threaten plankton and marine ecosystems.

activities.prompt: Put this chain of events in order.
activities.explanation: Burning fossil fuels raises atmospheric carbon dioxide. Extra carbon dioxide makes seawater more acidic, threatening coral reefs.

activities.prompt: What happens to carbon dioxide in warmer seawater?
options: It is absorbed less effectively
It is absorbed more effectively
It becomes fertiliser nitrogen
It forms ground-level smog
activities.explanation: Warmer seawater can absorb carbon dioxide less effectively.

activities.prompt: A busy street has many cars on a sunny day. What may form near the ground?
options: Ground-level smog may form soon
More oxygen may fill the air
Cleaner rain may fall nearby
Warmer seawater may appear

why.More oxygen may fill the air: This wrongly treats vehicle emissions as adding oxygen.
why.Cleaner rain may fall nearby: This wrongly assumes vehicle emissions make rain cleaner.
why.Warmer seawater may appear: This wrongly connects traffic emissions directly to seawater warmth.

activities.explanation: Vehicle emissions react with sunlight to form ground-level smog.

activities.prompt: Fertiliser nitrogen enters a lake as nitrates. What may happen before oxygen falls?
options: Algal blooms may use up oxygen
Fish may move to safer water
More carbon dioxide may be absorbed
More local rainfall may be seen

why.Fish may move to safer water: This puts a later effect before algal blooms form.
why.More carbon dioxide may be absorbed: This wrongly connects lake nitrates to carbon dioxide uptake.
why.More local rainfall may be seen: This wrongly connects lake nitrates to local rainfall.

activities.explanation: Extra fertiliser nitrogen can cause algal blooms that use up oxygen.

activities.prompt: One seawater sample is warmed while another stays cool. Which absorbs carbon dioxide better?
options: Cool seawater absorbs carbon dioxide better
Warm seawater absorbs carbon dioxide better
Both absorb carbon dioxide equally
Neither absorbs carbon dioxide at all

why.Warm seawater absorbs carbon dioxide bet: This reverses the warming effect on carbon dioxide uptake.
why.Both absorb carbon dioxide equally: This wrongly ignores the warming effect on carbon dioxide uptake.
why.Neither absorbs carbon dioxide at all: This wrongly assumes seawater cannot absorb carbon dioxide.

activities.explanation: Warmer seawater absorbs carbon dioxide less effectively than cool seawater.

activities.context: During a coastal field visit, a student observes warmer Arabian Sea water and notices that the southwest monsoon has changed. The student wonders whether Earth's spheres are separate. The Sun provides most of Earth's energy, while Earth's hot interior and chemical reactions also move energy and matter. The class considers water, air, living organisms, land and ice as connected parts of one system and asks what may link the warmer sea to the changed monsoon.
activities.prompt: Which explanation best accounts for the connection between the warmer Arabian Sea water and the changed southwest monsoon?
options: Increased evaporation from the warmer sea can contribute to the altered monsoon pattern.
The change is caused only by the Sun, because the Sun provides most of Earth's energy.
The atmosphere is separate, so the warmer sea cannot influence the monsoon.
The cryosphere is responsible because it includes solid water.

why.The change is caused only by the Sun, be: This mistakes the Sun's major energy contribution for the only mechanism.
why.The atmosphere is separate, so the warme: This wrongly treats the atmosphere as separate from other spheres.
why.The cryosphere is responsible because it: This confuses the cryosphere's solid water with the warmer sea water.

activities.explanation: Correct: increased evaporation from warmer Arabian Sea water can change the southwest monsoon.

activities.context: During a coastal field visit, a student observes warmer Arabian Sea water and notices that the southwest monsoon has changed. The student wonders whether Earth's spheres are separate. The Sun provides most of Earth's energy, while Earth's hot interior and chemical reactions also move energy and matter. The class considers water, air, living organisms, land and ice as connected parts of one system and asks what may link the warmer sea to the changed monsoon.
activities.prompt: What should the student investigate next to test whether the change affected Earth as a connected system?
options: Trace how energy and matter move among the hydrosphere, atmosphere and other spheres.
Focus only on the hydrosphere and ignore the other spheres.
Classify each sphere separately without looking for interactions.
Consider only the Sun's energy and leave Earth's interior and chemical reactions out.

why.Focus only on the hydrosphere and ignore: This ignores the principle that a disturbance in one sphere can affect others.
why.Classify each sphere separately without: This treats the spheres as independent instead of interacting.
why.Consider only the Sun's energy and leave: This overlooks energy and matter moved by Earth's hot interior and chemical reactions.

activities.explanation: Correct: tracing energy and matter reveals interactions among Earth's spheres.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A disturbance in one sphere can cause changes in other spheres.
Reason (R): Warmer Arabian Sea water can increase evaporation and change the southwest monsoon.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the change in the monsoon provides an example of the stated interaction.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The Sun is the only source of Earth's energy.
Reason (R): Earth's hot interior and chemical reactions also move energy and matter.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false because energy and matter are also moved by Earth's interior and chemical reactions.

activities.prompt: Explain how the warmer Arabian Sea water and the changed southwest monsoon illustrate Earth as one connected system.
activities.answer: Warmer Arabian Sea water can increase evaporation. That change involves the hydrosphere, because the water is moving from the sea into the air. The atmosphere is therefore involved, and a change in the southwest monsoon can follow. This is an example of a disturbance in one sphere causing changes in another. Earth is one system made of interacting spheres. Life on Earth depends on a continuous flow of energy and matter, supplied mainly by the Sun and also moved by Earth's hot interior and chemical reactions.
points: Warmer Arabian Sea water can increase evaporation.
Evaporation connects the hydrosphere and atmosphere.
A change in one sphere can cause changes in another.
Energy and matter move through Earth's interacting spheres.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A school garden’s soil receives different amounts of energy because sunlight arrives at different angles at different latitudes. The class compares two school sites. A gardener places seedlings under a transparent cover; visible light supports photosynthesis, while infrared radiation warms the soil. The class also compares the solar constant with insolation measured at the surface and learns that greenhouse gases trap some heat leaving Earth. One student wonders why the readings differ.
activities.prompt: At the site where sunlight arrives at a lower angle, what should happen to insolation and photosynthesis?
options: Less solar energy would reach the ground, so plants would receive less light energy for photosynthesis.
More solar energy would reach the ground, so plants would receive more light energy for photosynthesis.
Less solar energy would reach the ground, but plants would receive more light energy for photosynthesis.
The ground would receive the same energy, but the plants would receive more light energy for photosynthesis.

why.More solar energy would reach the ground: Wrong: a lower angle does not increase the energy reaching the surface.
why.Less solar energy would reach the ground: Wrong: reduced insolation does not increase the energy available for photosynthesis.
why.The ground would receive the same energy: Wrong: changing the sunlight angle changes the amount of energy received.

activities.explanation: Correct: a lower angle results in less insolation and less available light energy.

activities.context: A school garden’s soil receives different amounts of energy because sunlight arrives at different angles at different latitudes. The class compares two school sites. A gardener places seedlings under a transparent cover; visible light supports photosynthesis, while infrared radiation warms the soil. The class also compares the solar constant with insolation measured at the surface and learns that greenhouse gases trap some heat leaving Earth. One student wonders why the readings differ.
activities.prompt: When the class compares surface insolation with the solar constant, what result should it expect?
options: The surface value would be below the value indicated by the constant.
The surface value would be above the value indicated by the constant.
The two values would always be identical because all solar energy reaches the ground.
The values cannot be compared because changing sunlight angles also changes the constant.

why.The surface value would be above the val: Wrong: the surface receives less insolation than the constant indicates.
why.The two values would always be identical: Wrong: not all the energy represented by the constant reaches the surface.
why.The values cannot be compared because ch: Wrong: the constant still gives average solar energy received per unit time.

activities.explanation: Correct: less insolation reaches the surface than the constant suggests.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Uneven heating occurs because different latitudes receive sunlight at different angles.
Reason (R): The different angles cause the amount of solar energy received by the surface to differ.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The change in received energy directly explains why heating is uneven.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Visible light provides the energy needed for photosynthesis.
Reason (R): Infrared radiation warms Earth's surface.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but warming the surface does not explain the role of visible light in photosynthesis.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between insolation and the solar constant, and explain why their values are not the same.
activities.answer: The solar constant and insolation describe related but different quantities. The solar constant gives the average solar energy received per unit time, while insolation is the amount of solar radiation that reaches Earth's surface. Less insolation reaches the surface than the solar constant suggests, so a surface measurement is lower than the value indicated by the constant. Different latitudes also receive sunlight at different angles, so the amount reaching the surface is not the same everywhere. This uneven reception produces uneven heating.
points: Defines insolation as radiation reaching Earth's surface
Defines the solar constant as average energy received per unit time
Explains that surface insolation is lower than the constant suggests
Connects different sunlight angles with uneven heating
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: During a school activity, a student noticed that rain and wind were occurring low in the atmosphere, where almost all weather phenomena take place. In a higher layer, ozone was absorbing ultraviolet rays. The student also learned that extra carbon dioxide had strengthened the greenhouse effect, so the atmosphere was trapping more outgoing heat. The student wondered why Earth could support life and how changes in the atmosphere might affect weather and climate.
activities.prompt: If more carbon dioxide were added to the atmosphere as described in the case, what would be the most likely result?
options: More of Earth's heat would be retained, making the greenhouse effect stronger.
Less of Earth's heat would be retained, making the greenhouse effect weaker.
The ozone layer would absorb more ultraviolet rays.
Weather phenomena would stop occurring low in the atmosphere.

why.Less of Earth's heat would be retained,: This is the opposite of the stated effect of extra carbon dioxide.
why.The ozone layer would absorb more ultrav: Extra carbon dioxide strengthens heat trapping rather than increasing ozone's ultraviolet absorption.
why.Weather phenomena would stop occurring l: Extra carbon dioxide does not stop weather phenomena in the troposphere.

activities.explanation: Extra carbon dioxide strengthens the greenhouse effect, so more outgoing heat is trapped.

activities.context: During a school activity, a student noticed that rain and wind were occurring low in the atmosphere, where almost all weather phenomena take place. In a higher layer, ozone was absorbing ultraviolet rays. The student also learned that extra carbon dioxide had strengthened the greenhouse effect, so the atmosphere was trapping more outgoing heat. The student wondered why Earth could support life and how changes in the atmosphere might affect weather and climate.
activities.prompt: If the ozone layer became thinner, what change should the student expect?
options: More harmful ultraviolet radiation would reach Earth's surface.
Less heat would be trapped by the atmosphere.
More weather would occur in the stratosphere.
The atmosphere would contain less nitrogen and oxygen.

why.Less heat would be trapped by the atmosp: The ozone layer's stated role concerns ultraviolet radiation rather than heat trapping.
why.More weather would occur in the stratosp: A change in the ozone layer would not move most weather into the stratosphere.
why.The atmosphere would contain less nitrog: A change in the ozone layer would not reduce the atmosphere's mainly nitrogen and oxygen composition.

activities.explanation: The ozone layer blocks harmful ultraviolet radiation.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The ozone layer blocks harmful ultraviolet radiation.
Reason (R): Ozone in the stratosphere absorbs ultraviolet rays and heats the atmosphere.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The absorption of ultraviolet rays by ozone explains how it blocks harmful radiation.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Without the atmosphere, Earth would be too hot for life.
Reason (R): Earth's gravity holds the atmosphere in place.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Earth would be too cold rather than too hot, while the reason is true but does not support the assertion.

activities.prompt: Explain how the troposphere and stratosphere differ in their roles within the atmosphere.
activities.answer: Almost all weather phenomena occur in the troposphere, so it has an important role in weather and climate. Ozone in the stratosphere absorbs ultraviolet rays and heats the atmosphere. The ozone layer also blocks harmful ultraviolet radiation. The main difference is that the troposphere is associated mainly with weather, while the stratosphere has an important role involving ozone and ultraviolet radiation. Together, the atmospheric layers regulate energy flow, weather, climate and life.
points: Almost all weather occurs in the troposphere.
Ozone in the stratosphere absorbs ultraviolet rays.
The ozone layer blocks harmful ultraviolet radiation.
Atmospheric layers regulate energy flow, weather, climate and life.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A hiker visits a valley near the coast on a sunny day. While walking, the hiker notices air moving differently on the slopes than over nearby land, showing that uneven heating can create local winds. Later, at night, the hiker sees a large mass of seawater moving continuously. The moving water forms a circular pattern, which Earth’s rotation helps to create.
activities.prompt: During the sunny part of the visit, what should the hiker expect on the sunlit valley slope?
options: Cool valley air will rise up the slope, creating a valley breeze.
Warm valley air will rise up the slope, creating a valley breeze.
Cool air will flow down the slope, creating a mountain breeze.
Air over the slope will remain still because uneven heating has no effect.

why.Warm valley air will rise up the slope,: Cool, not warm, valley air rises during sunny conditions.
why.Cool air will flow down the slope, creat: Downslope flow at night describes a mountain breeze.
why.Air over the slope will remain still bec: Uneven heating creates pressure differences that drive winds.

activities.explanation: This correctly describes a valley breeze.

activities.context: A hiker visits a valley near the coast on a sunny day. While walking, the hiker notices air moving differently on the slopes than over nearby land, showing that uneven heating can create local winds. Later, at night, the hiker sees a large mass of seawater moving continuously. The moving water forms a circular pattern, which Earth’s rotation helps to create.
activities.prompt: Which explanation best accounts for the circular pattern in the moving seawater?
options: Earth’s rotation helps organize the continuous seawater movement into a circular pattern.
Cool air flowing down nearby slopes at night creates the seawater pattern.
Warm air rising near the equator creates the circular seawater pattern.
Daytime valley air rising up sunlit slopes creates the seawater pattern.

why.Cool air flowing down nearby slopes at n: Slope breezes are local winds, not explanations for ocean currents.
why.Warm air rising near the equator creates: Equatorial rising air relates to planetary pressure belts, not gyres.
why.Daytime valley air rising up sunlit slop: Valley breezes are local winds and do not form ocean-current patterns.

activities.explanation: Earth’s rotation helps form circular ocean-current patterns called gyres.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A valley breeze can form when cool valley air rises up sunlit slopes.
Reason (R): Uneven heating can produce local winds such as valley and mountain breezes.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

activities.prompt: Which part includes rocks, soil, landforms and Earth’s interior?

The hydrosphere
The cryosphere
The biosphere

activities.prompt: What does the solar constant give?
options: Average solar energy per unit time
Solar radiation at one point
Heat leaving Earth each day
Energy stored in seawater
activities.explanation: The solar constant gives the average solar energy received per unit time.

activities.prompt: The atmosphere contains mainly nitrogen and oxygen.
activities.explanation: Nitrogen and oxygen make up most of the atmosphere.

activities.prompt: Almost all weather occurs in the stratosphere.
activities.explanation: Almost all weather phenomena occur in the troposphere.

activities.prompt: Almost all weather phenomena occur in the ______.
activities.hint: Almost all weather phenomena occur here.
activities.explanation: The troposphere contains almost all weather phenomena.

activities.prompt: Earth’s rotation helps form circular ocean-current patterns called ______.
activities.hint: These patterns are circular.
activities.explanation: Earth’s rotation helps form circular ocean-current patterns called gyres.

activities.prompt: Match each sphere with what it includes.
pairs: Rocks, soil, landforms and Earth’s interior
Water in oceans, rivers, lakes and groundwater
Solid water such as ice, snow and glaciers
activities.explanation: Earth is one system made of interacting spheres.

activities.prompt: Match each energy feature with its role.
activities.explanation: Different forms of energy interact with Earth’s surface and atmosphere.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in the order of energy reaching and leaving Earth.
items: Some gases absorb sunlight before it reaches Earth’s surface.
Greenhouse gases absorb heat sent back into the atmosphere.
activities.explanation: Solar energy reaches Earth, and some gases absorb sunlight before the surface. Infrared warms the surface, and greenhouse gases absorb outgoing heat.

activities.prompt: How can clearing forests affect a local area?
options: Less local rainfall and fewer habitats
More local rainfall and more habitats
More photosynthesis and transpiration
Stronger ocean currents and gyres
activities.explanation: Deforestation reduces photosynthesis and transpiration. It can also reduce local rainfall and destroy habitats.
